items.title: The Working Environment Act
items.text: The Act requires systematic health and safety work (§ 3-1) and a fully sound psychosocial working environment (§ 4-3).

items.title: § 4-3 amended
items.text: The section on the psychosocial working environment is amended by Act of 16 June 2023 no. 37.

items.title: Chapter 1A in force
items.text: The regulation on the performance of work gains its own chapter on the psychosocial working environment, and § 4-3 is amended again.

blocks.text: The chapter was added to the regulation on the performance of work on 1 January 2026. It has five sections:

items.text: Work must be organised, planned and carried out so that the psychosocial working environment is fully sound. Arbeidstilsynet writes that being busy or having a demanding job is not forbidden, but the strain must not become too great – and that the assessment as a rule concerns organisation and management, not individuals.

Survey the factors, and assess the risk in the short and long term: each factor separately, how they affect each other, and together. In cooperation with employees, adapted to the business, repeated regularly and when things change, and documented.
Draw up the necessary plans and put the necessary measures in place to eliminate or reduce the risk, together with employees. Measures should as far as possible address the causes.
Employees and their representatives must get the information they need about the risk factors and the measures, and the training they need.
Employees must take part in the work, cf. Working Environment Act § 2-3. Arbeidstilsynet stresses that this does not make the individual responsible for solving the problems alone.

blocks.text: Read more about [the risk assessment](/artikler/risikovurdering-av-psykososialt-arbeidsmiljo) and about [getting from results to measures](/artikler/fra-resultater-til-tiltak).
Who must take part

center.title: The employer
center.text: Is responsible for compliance with the Act (aml § 2-1). The survey is the employer's duty.

items.title: The safety representative
items.text: Is consulted in the health and safety work and must in particular see that the psychosocial working environment is taken care of (aml § 6-2). Every business must have one; with fewer than 5 employees the parties may agree another arrangement in writing (§ 6-1).

items.title: The working environment committee
items.text: Required where at least 30 people are regularly employed, and with 10–30 when either party demands it (aml § 7-1). Among other things it deals with establishing and maintaining the health and safety work (§ 7-2).

items.title: The employees
items.text: The survey must be done in cooperation with them and their union representatives (aml § 3-1 first paragraph), and they have a duty to take part (§ 2-3 and regulation § 1A-5).

blocks.title: Whistleblowing routines belong here too
blocks.text: If the business regularly employs at least five people, it must have written routines for internal reporting, drawn up together with the employees (aml § 2 A-6). Whether people actually dare to use them is a question of the climate for speaking up. Read more about [freedom to speak up](/artikler/ytringsklima).
What the documentation should show

Arbeidstilsynet writes that the survey, the risk assessment and the results must be set down in writing in a way that makes it possible to follow the work up, and that the documentation must serve as the basis for measures. Its scope and form are adapted to the nature, size and risks of the business. At the very least it should show:

items: what was surveyed, when, and how
that employees and the safety representative took part
the risk assessment, with reasons for each factor and group
which measures were chosen, with who is responsible and by when
the follow-up: whether the measures worked

blocks.title: The survey is more than one questionnaire
blocks.text: A questionnaire for employees is one way to survey. Safety inspections, incident reports, sickness absence figures and conversations with employees can give a fuller picture of the risk. What matters is that the documentation shows what was found, how it was assessed and what was done.
What happens if the requirement is not met

Arbeidstilsynet supervises compliance with the Act. If it finds shortcomings, it can issue an order with a deadline (aml § 18-6). An order can be followed by a coercive fine until it is complied with (§ 18-7). If the Act has been breached negligently or wilfully, the business can be given an infringement fine (§ 18-10).
Arbeidstilsynet's means, from the lightest to the heaviest:

items.title: Order
items.text: In writing, with a deadline for when it must be carried out.

items.title: Coercive fine
items.text: Running for each day, week or month after the deadline – or as a one-off fine – until the order is complied with.

items.title: Stoppage
items.text: If the order is not complied with by the deadline, the business's activities can be stopped in whole or in part.

items.title: Infringement fine
items.text: For negligent or wilful breaches: up to 50 times the basic amount or four per cent of annual turnover.

blocks.text: When Arbeidstilsynet considers an infringement fine, it must among other things weigh whether the business could have prevented the breach through guidelines, training, checks or other measures. A survey that has been done, assessed and followed up – and can be shown – is therefore also the best answer to an inspection.

Read more about [the requirements for the survey](/artikler/krav-til-kartlegging-av-psykososialt-arbeidsmiljo), [what is new from 2026](/artikler/nye-regler-psykososialt-arbeidsmiljo-2026), [the risk assessment](/artikler/risikovurdering-av-psykososialt-arbeidsmiljo) and [how results become measures](/artikler/fra-resultater-til-tiltak).

faq.q: Does the mapping requirement apply to small organisations?
faq.a: Yes. Section 3-1 applies to every employer with employees. The regulation says mapping shall be adapted to the organisation's nature, activities and size – a small organisation can keep it simple, but not skip it.

faq.q: Is an employee survey enough?
faq.a: It can be an important source, but the requirement covers the whole chain: survey, risk assessment, measures and follow-up, in cooperation with employees and their representatives. Safety inspections, incident reports and conversations with employees can give a fuller picture.

faq.q: What changed on 1 January 2026?
faq.a: The regulation on the performance of work gained a new chapter 1A on the psychosocial working environment. Arbeidstilsynet writes that the provisions spell out sections 4-1 and 4-3 of the Act and the employer's duty to systematic health and safety work under section 3-1.

faq.q: How often must we map?
faq.a: The regulation says the survey must be repeated regularly and when changes may affect the risk. It sets no fixed interval. Arbeidstilsynet gives changes in organisation, staffing, tasks, management, technology, working hours or operating conditions as examples.

faq.q: Who is responsible for the survey?
faq.a: The employer. Working Environment Act § 2-1 says the employer must ensure the Act is complied with. Tasks can be shared out, but the safety representative and employees take part – carrying out the survey is not their responsibility.

faq.q: Do we need a safety representative?
faq.a: Yes, as a rule. Every business covered by the Act must elect a safety representative (§ 6-1). With fewer than 5 employees the parties may agree another arrangement in writing, including having none. Arbeidstilsynet can still decide that you must have one.

faq.q: Must we survey every factor the regulation names?
faq.a: Not necessarily. The list in § 1A-1 applies «among other things», and Arbeidstilsynet writes that it does not set a minimum. Which factors you must survey depends on the nature, activities and risks of your business. Most of the factors are still relevant to most businesses.

faq.q: What can Arbeidstilsynet do if we have not surveyed?
faq.a: Issue an order with a deadline to put it right (aml § 18-6), possibly with a coercive fine until it is done (§ 18-7). For negligent or wilful breaches, the business can be given an infringement fine (§ 18-10).

verneombud.title: The safety representative and the survey | Orgpuls
verneombud.description: The safety representative's rights and duties when the psychosocial working environment is surveyed: the law, the role at each step, and what to do.

card.title: Safety representatives
card.text: The safety representative's rights and duties when the working environment is surveyed, step by step.

verneombud.h1: The safety representative and the survey: rights, duties and how it works
verneombud.lead: The safety representative must see that the psychosocial working environment is taken care of, and must be consulted when measures are planned and carried out. When the working environment is surveyed, the safety representative is one of the representatives the employer must cooperate with – in the survey, in the risk assessment and when measures are chosen. Responsibility for getting it done lies with the employer.

blocks.text: What you are entitled to

Section 6-2 of the Working Environment Act says the safety representative shall see to it that the employees' psychosocial working environment is safeguarded. The safety representative shall also be consulted during the planning and implementation of measures that matter for the working environment. Section 1A-2 of the regulation on the performance of work also requires the mapping and risk assessment to be done together with the employees and their representatives.

center.title: The safety representative
center.text: Looks after the employees' interests in matters concerning the working environment (aml § 6-2 first paragraph).

items.title: Sees to
items.text: The employees' psychosocial working environment being taken care of (§ 6-2 second paragraph letter f).

items.title: Is consulted
items.text: When measures are planned and carried out, and in the systematic health and safety work (§ 6-2 fourth paragraph).

items.title: Alerts
items.text: The employer to conditions that may harm health – and the employer must answer (§ 6-2 third paragraph).

items.title: Takes part
items.text: When Arbeidstilsynet inspects the business (§ 6-2 seventh paragraph).

Every business must elect a safety representative. The number depends on size and the nature of the work, and with several departments or shift teams there should as a rule be one per department or shift. Who the representative is must be announced at the workplace.

The safety representative looks after employees' interests in working environment matters, must in particular see that the psychosocial working environment is taken care of, must be consulted in the health and safety work and takes part when Arbeidstilsynet inspects.

In immediate danger to life or health, the safety representative can stop the work until Arbeidstilsynet has decided. That rarely concerns the psychosocial environment, but it shows how strong the role is.
The survey and risk assessment must be done in cooperation with employees and their representatives. Arbeidstilsynet writes that this means the safety representative, where the business has one.

blocks.text: Your role at each step

items.title: Take part when the rhythm and the questions are chosen.
items.text: **Ask:** When will the survey be done, and who helps choose the questions?

items.title: Encourage colleagues to answer, and be able to explain why it is safe.
items.text: **Ask:** How is anonymity secured, and how small are the groups that are shown?

items.title: Assess the figures together with management – not get a summary afterwards.
items.text: **Ask:** Do I see the same figures as management, and am I involved when the risk is assessed?

items.title: Take part when measures are chosen, and see that they address the causes.
items.text: **Ask:** Does every measure have someone responsible and a deadline, and does it address the cause?

items.title: See that measures are done, and that someone checks whether they worked.
items.text: **Ask:** How, and when, will we see whether the measures worked?

blocks.text: Read more about [the safety representative's role in the survey](/artikler/verneombudets-rolle-i-kartleggingen) and about [the risk assessment](/artikler/risikovurdering-av-psykososialt-arbeidsmiljo).
What the safety representative should have access to

items.title: The same basis as management
items.text: To take part in the risk assessment, the safety representative needs the same results as management – not just a summary afterwards.

items.title: The measures
items.text: Which measures were chosen, who is responsible, when they are due, and how they will be followed up.

items.title: How anonymity is secured
items.text: The safety representative should be able to explain to colleagues why it is safe to answer: what is stored, and how small the groups shown can be.

items.title: The documentation
items.text: What was surveyed, how the risk was assessed and what was done. It must form part of the systematic health and safety work.

blocks.text: When you want to raise it with management

Do you know the survey should have been done, but not how to raise it? Start with questions, not demands: when was the psychosocial working environment last surveyed, what came out of it, and what happened with the findings? You can point to chapter 1A of the regulation, which since 1 January 2026 sets out the requirements more clearly. Read more about [what is new from 2026](/artikler/nye-regler-psykososialt-arbeidsmiljo-2026).

blocks.title: Advice from practice
blocks.text: Raise it as a question of rhythm, not of a tool: «When did we last map, and what happened to the findings?» The answer usually says more than any survey.
When management does not act

The law gives the safety representative a set route. If you become aware of conditions that could harm health, you must make the employer aware of them, and the employer must give you an answer. If the report has not been taken into account within a reasonable time, you must inform Arbeidstilsynet or the working environment committee (aml § 6-2 third paragraph).

items.title: Raise it
items.text: With your line manager or the managing director, preferably in writing.

items.title: Point to the figures
items.text: Which factors, which groups, and how they have developed.

items.title: Ask for an answer
items.text: And for what will be done, and when. The employer must answer.

items.title: Take it further
items.text: With no answer within a reasonable time: to the working environment committee, where there is one, or to Arbeidstilsynet.

blocks.text: Employees can also report censurable conditions through the safety representative (aml § 2 A-2). Read more about [freedom to speak up](/artikler/ytringsklima).
When a department is not shown

In an anonymous survey, results are usually not shown for groups below a certain size, often five answers. When a small department is not shown, nobody is hiding anything from you: the figure has not been calculated for anyone, precisely so that nobody can tell who answered what. The answers still count in the figures for the whole. Read more about [what anonymous means in an employee survey](/artikler/anonym-medarbeiderundersokelse).

faq.q: Must we have a safety representative?
faq.a: The main rule in section 6-1 of the Working Environment Act is yes: a safety representative shall be elected in every organisation. Only organisations with fewer than five employees may agree in writing on another arrangement.

faq.q: Can management see who answered what?
faq.a: Not in an anonymous survey. Answers should be stored without anything that could link them to the person who answered, and results for groups below a certain size should not be shown. Ask how this is handled before the survey goes out.

faq.q: What if management does not want to?
faq.a: The duty to survey, assess risk and put measures in place applies regardless, and the responsibility is the employer's (aml § 2-1). If you get no answer within a reasonable time on conditions that may harm health, you must inform Arbeidstilsynet or the working environment committee (aml § 6-2 third paragraph).

faq.q: How many safety representatives do we need?
faq.a: It depends on size, the nature of the work and the working conditions (aml § 6-1). If the business has several separate departments or works in shifts, there should as a rule be at least one per department or shift team. With more than one, there must be a chief safety representative.

faq.q: Should the safety representative take part in the risk assessment?
faq.a: Yes. Regulation § 1A-2 requires the survey and risk assessment to be done in cooperation with employees and their representatives, and Arbeidstilsynet writes that this means the safety representative where there is one. The same applies to the measures (§ 1A-3).

faq.q: What do I do if the employer does not answer?
faq.a: The employer must answer the safety representative. If the report has not been taken into account within a reasonable time, the safety representative must inform Arbeidstilsynet or the working environment committee (aml § 6-2 third paragraph).

smaaBedrifter.description: An employee survey for small businesses: what the law requires by headcount, anonymous from 5 answers, set up in under an hour. Free to start.

card.title: Small businesses
card.text: 5–25 employees and no HR department: an anonymous employee survey for NOK 265 a month.

smaaBedrifter.h1: Employee survey for small businesses – set up in under an hour
smaaBedrifter.lead: Small businesses rarely have an HR department, but they have the same legal requirements as large ones. Orgpuls is an employee survey that handles sending, reminders and documentation. You spend your time on what comes out of it.

blocks.text: What about anonymity when we are few?

It is the first question in a small organisation, and it is the right one to ask. By default, Orgpuls shows no group until at least 5 people have answered. If you are 12, you see figures for the whole organisation, but not for a department of 3.

The limit lives in the database. If you are very few, the managing director can lower it to 3 or 4 – you then see figures for smaller groups, but it also becomes easier to recognise who said what. That is why 5 is strongly recommended. A round keeps the limit it started with, and nobody can set it below 3. The answer is stored without name, e-mail address or IP address, and no column can link an answer to a person.
What the law requires – by headcount
The duty to survey the working environment applies from the first employee. Other requirements come as you grow:

items.title: Survey, assess the risk, put measures in place and follow up
items.text: Adapted to the size of the business. aml § 3-1 and chapter 1A of the regulation.

items.title: Safety representative
items.text: With fewer than 5 employees you can agree another arrangement in writing. aml § 6-1.

items.title: Written routines for internal reporting
items.text: Also with fewer when conditions call for it. aml § 2 A-6.

items.title: Working environment committee if either side asks for one

blocks.text: Read more about [what the law requires of the survey](/lovkrav).
Simpler – but not optional

The regulation says the survey and risk assessment must be adapted to the nature, activities and size of the business. Arbeidstilsynet writes that this applies to the scope, methods and content, and that the documentation can be adapted too. A small business can do it more simply than a large one. But the duty to survey, assess risk, set measures and follow up applies all the same.

blocks.title: In a small business, everything shows
blocks.text: When one person goes on sick leave or leaves, everyone notices. That is why a simple, fixed rhythm pays off more for a small business than for a large one – not less.
The time it takes

head: What
Time
rows: Signing up with the organisation number

blocks.text: When people do not sit at a PC

You send the survey by e-mail or SMS, or share it as a link or a QR code in the break room. Everyone answers on their phone, in Norwegian. You paste employees in from a spreadsheet – you do not need an HR system.
A year in a small business

items.title: Sign up
items.text: Use your organisation number, and add employees from a spreadsheet.

items.title: Send the main survey
items.text: About 4 minutes per employee, with one reminder from the system.

items.title: Go through the results
items.text: Together with employees and the safety representative. Read [how to do it](/artikler/slik-gar-dere-gjennom-resultatene-med-de-ansatte).

items.title: Choose two or three measures
items.text: Each with an owner and a deadline. Read [from results to measures](/artikler/fra-resultater-til-tiltak).

items.title: Measure again
items.text: Run a short pulse on the factors where measures are running, and the next main survey in a year.

blocks.text: What you get

items: Annual mapping of 11 factors, with short pulses in between
The findings that lift the most, turned into measures with an owner and a deadline
A report that follows section 3-1 letter c of the Working Environment Act
Access for the safety representative at no extra cost

blocks.title: Price
blocks.text: The free plan: an annual main survey with standard questions, results and measures – for as long as you like. Small: NOK 265 a month excl. VAT for up to 25 employees, with pulses, industry modules and your own questions. No set-up fee and no lock-in. Try everything free for 15 days – no card details.

faq.q: Do small businesses have to map the working environment?
faq.a: Yes. Section 3-1 of the Working Environment Act applies to every organisation with employees. The regulation says mapping shall be adapted to the organisation's size, so it can be simple – but it must be done and documented.

faq.q: What if only 4 answer?
faq.a: With the default limit of 5, a dash is shown instead of a number. The figure is not hidden from you in particular – it is not calculated for anyone. That is the price of nobody being able to recognise an answer. If the managing director lowered the limit to 3 or 4 before the round started, the figure is shown.

faq.q: Do we need an HR system?
faq.a: No. You can paste employees in from a spreadsheet or add them one at a time. An e-mail address is optional.

faq.q: Can we cancel at any time?
faq.a: Yes. The agreement is monthly, with no lock-in and no start-up fee.

faq.q: Do we need a safety representative when we are few?
faq.a: As a rule, yes (aml § 6-1). With fewer than 5 employees you may agree another arrangement in writing, including having none. The agreement lasts 2 years unless otherwise agreed, and Arbeidstilsynet can still decide you must have one.

faq.q: Do we need whistleblowing routines?
faq.a: Yes, if you regularly employ at least 5 people (aml § 2 A-6). The routines must be written, drawn up with your employees, and at least encourage reporting, describe how to report, and how reports are handled.

faq.q: Is there a free version?
faq.a: Yes. After the trial you can stay on the free plan for as long as you like: an annual main survey with standard questions, results and measures. Pulses, industry modules and your own questions need a plan.

byggOgAnlegg.h1: A work environment survey for construction – reaching people on site, rig and workshop
byggOgAnlegg.lead: In construction many employees do not sit at a PC, and the e-mail goes unread. Orgpuls sends the work environment survey by SMS, and everyone answers on their phone in about 4 minutes.

blocks.text: When the channel decides the response rate

Where people work outdoors, the channel decides much of the response rate. An SMS or a QR code in the site hut reaches people where they are. Orgpuls sends one reminder to those who have not answered – from the system, not the manager – and nobody learns who is missing.
See the difference between site and workshop
With the Usual plan you see the result per department and team, so you see where workload, time pressure and speaking up differ. By default, a department is shown once at least 5 have answered.

The example on the front page is Nordvik Anlegg AS – an imaginary company with departments on site, in the workshop and in administration. The departments with enough answers are shown there. Administration has 5 employees and 3 answers, so it only counts in the whole.
What matters most outdoors

items: **Workload and time pressure** – when progress runs the day
**Contact and communication** – when people work alone or on different rigs
**Speaking up** – whether it is safe to report mistakes before they get expensive
**Conflicting demands** – when the client, the project manager and the foreman each want something else

blocks.title: When people speak up early
blocks.text: A deviation that surfaces in week two costs less than one that surfaces at the final settlement. Speaking up is not just wellbeing – it is money.

faq.q: Does everyone need an e-mail address?
faq.a: No. The survey can be sent by SMS, or shared as a link and a QR code. An e-mail address is optional.

faq.q: How long does it take an employee?
faq.a: About 4 minutes for the main survey and under 1 minute for a pulse. Everyone can answer on a phone.

faq.q: Can we see results per project or department?
faq.a: Yes, per group as you set the groups up, on the Usual plan. By default a group is shown once at least 5 have answered; small teams can lower the limit to 3.

faq.q: What does it cost?
faq.a: Small costs NOK 265 a month for up to 25 employees, Usual NOK 565 for 26–100 employees. Prices exclude VAT, with no lock-in and Free to start.

card.title: Health and care

helseOgOmsorg.kicker: Health, care and work with people
helseOgOmsorg.h1: Work environment mapping in health and care – where the emotional demands are greatest
helseOgOmsorg.lead: In work with people, it is often something other than the workload that weighs on you. Orgpuls measures the emotional demands, whether anyone is left alone with them, and whether people have experienced violence or threats. Everyone answers anonymously on their phone, whatever their shift.

blocks.text: What the law points to in work with people

items.text: Psychosocial working environment factors include emotional demands and strain in work with people.
The employee shall, as far as possible, be protected against violence, threats and undue strain from contact with others.
The factors shall be mapped and risk-assessed one by one and together, with the employees, and repeated regularly.

blocks.text: What we ask about
Orgpuls measures 11 factors with 3 statements each. Some of them fit work with people particularly well (translated):

items: «I am rarely left alone in emotionally demanding situations»
«We talk about difficult incidents afterwards»
«I am allowed to react as a human being at work»
«I can call for help quickly if something happens while I am alone»
«I get support from my manager when the job gets demanding»

blocks.title: Violence and threats are shown only as a count
blocks.text: The question «Have you experienced violence or threats at work in the last twelve months?» is reported only as a count for the whole organisation, never per department. So nobody can work out who answered yes – not even in a small department.
When people work in shifts

You send the survey by e-mail or SMS, or share it as a link and a QR code in the staff room. It stays open for several days, so every shift has time to answer: about 4 minutes for the main survey, under 1 minute for a pulse. One reminder goes to those who have not answered – from the system, not the manager.
Small units, the same anonymity

By default no group is shown until at least 5 have answered, and the limit can never be set below 3. If a department has too few answers, they still count in the organisation's figures. If a department could be worked out from the others, Orgpuls holds back one more.

faq.q: Can we ask about violence and threats?
faq.a: Yes, and assessing that risk is a requirement under section 4-3, sixth paragraph, of the Working Environment Act. In Orgpuls the answer is reported only as a count for the whole organisation, so nobody can be identified.

faq.q: What about employees without a work e-mail?
faq.a: The survey can be sent by SMS or shared as a link and a QR code. An e-mail address is optional.

faq.q: Can we see results per department or ward?
faq.a: Yes, on the Usual plan, for departments with enough answers – at least five by default.

faq.q: What does it cost?
faq.a: Small costs NOK 265 a month for up to 25 employees, Usual NOK 565 for 26–100 employees. Prices exclude VAT, with no lock-in and Free to start.

medarbeiderundersokelse.title: Employee surveys and the working environment | Orgpuls
medarbeiderundersokelse.description: What an employee survey is, what Norwegian law requires, what it should measure, how answers stay anonymous and how findings become measures.
medarbeiderundersokelse.h1: What is an employee survey, and how should it be used?
medarbeiderundersokelse.lead: An employee survey is a questionnaire in which employees assess their own working environment, and where answers are shown only for groups in which no one can be recognised. Used well, it is part of the statutory mapping of the psychosocial working environment: it measures the factors the rules point to, the results are reviewed with employees and the safety representative, and the findings become measures that are followed up and evaluated.

blocks.text: What is an employee survey?

In an employee survey, employees respond to statements about their own working day – workload, role clarity, support from their manager and colleagues, influence over their own work and how people treat each other. Answers are combined for groups, so the organisation sees patterns rather than individuals.

The name covers a lot. Some employee surveys measure satisfaction and engagement; others measure working environment factors in a way that can be used in a risk assessment. The difference matters, because the factors are what the rules require you to map. Read more about the difference in the article on [job satisfaction surveys](/artikler/trivselsundersokelse).

The Norwegian encyclopaedia Store norske leksikon describes what such a survey can and cannot do: the results will not give a complete picture of the conditions examined, but can be a good starting point for looking further.
One source among several

The Norwegian Labour Inspection Authority (Arbeidstilsynet) writes that to get a good picture of the psychosocial working environment, an organisation should use several sources in the mapping, such as working environment surveys, safety inspections, incident reports, appraisal conversations or informal conversations.

A questionnaire is good at showing where a problem is and how large it is, and it gives everyone a voice at the same time. It is less good at explaining why. That comes out in the conversations afterwards – in the review with employees, with the safety representative and in appraisal conversations.
What does the law require?

The duty to map the working environment is not new. It is part of the provision on systematic health, environment and safety work in the Working Environment Act, and from 1 January 2026 it has been made explicit for the psychosocial working environment in a chapter of its own in the regulation on the performance of work.

items.text: map hazards and problems and on that basis assess the risk factors in the undertaking, prepare plans and implement measures to reduce the risk

items.ref: Regulation on the performance of work § 1A-2(4) (our translation)
items.text: The mapping and the risk assessment shall a. be carried out in cooperation with the employees and their representatives b. be adapted to the nature, activities and size of the undertaking c. be repeated regularly and upon changes that may affect the risk conditions in the undertaking d. be documented and form part of the undertaking's systematic health, environment and safety work.

blocks.text: The rules do not say that the mapping must be done with a questionnaire. Arbeidstilsynet writes that the scope, methods and content of the mapping and risk assessment are to be adapted to the nature, activities and size of the undertaking. An anonymous survey is a practical way to hear from everyone at once, but it should be supplemented with conversations. Read more about [the requirements for mapping](/artikler/krav-til-kartlegging-av-psykososialt-arbeidsmiljo).
What should the survey measure?
Section 1A-1 of the regulation says that psychosocial working environment factors include, among others (our translation):

items: unclear or conflicting demands and expectations in the work
emotional demands and strain in work with people
workload and time pressure that involve an imbalance between the work to be done and the time available
support and help in the work
the opportunity for contact and communication with other employees in the undertaking
harassment, including sexual harassment
violence and threats
autonomy and influence in the work

blocks.text: The list is not exhaustive. Arbeidstilsynet writes that the words «among others» mark that the provision does not give an exhaustive list of psychosocial working environment factors. Which factors you must map depends on the organisation’s nature, activities and risk profile.

Measure what protects as well. Arbeidstilsynet writes that such factors can act both as strains and as protection, and that protective factors may therefore also be relevant to include in the mapping. Support from managers and colleagues, influence over one’s own work and a sense of meaning are examples.

An established starting point is questionnaires in the QPS Nordic tradition, a Nordic questionnaire on psychological and social factors at work. The Norwegian National Institute of Occupational Health (STAMI) describes it as developed for mapping in connection with development work and measures, and for research, and intended for a survey-feedback process: the results go back to those who answered. See [which questions belong in an employee survey](/artikler/medarbeiderundersokelse-sporsmal).
Anonymity in practice

The Norwegian Data Protection Authority (Datatilsynet) writes that the purpose of a working environment survey can normally be achieved by collecting anonymous information. Not storing names is still not enough. Datatilsynet points out that combining details such as position, age and gender can quite easily identify individuals, especially in small organisations – and adds that another common problem is the use of open comment fields.

items: **Show no group with fewer than five answers.** The Norwegian central government’s employee survey (MUST), run by STAMI, uses the same threshold: units with at least five answers get a report.
**Ask for as few background details as possible.** Every extra detail splits the answers into smaller groups.
**Be careful with free text.** STAMI writes of MUST that, out of regard for privacy, employees cannot answer freely with text or comments.
**Stop anyone working it out.** If you show the figure for the whole organisation and for every group but one, the hidden group can be calculated. Then another group must be hidden too.

blocks.text: Read more about [what an anonymous employee survey means](/artikler/anonym-medarbeiderundersokelse).
Employees and the safety representative are involved from the start

Arbeidstilsynet writes that the employer cannot do this work alone, but must actively involve employees and the safety representative in the mapping, the risk assessment, and the planning and follow-up of measures. For an employee survey, this means the safety representative helps choose topics and groups, knows the timetable and takes part when the results are reviewed. Read more about [the safety representative’s role in the mapping](/artikler/verneombudets-rolle-i-kartleggingen).
From results to measures

A survey without follow-up achieves little. Arbeidstilsynet’s own survey of systematic health and safety work shows that most organisations map and assess the risks in their working environment at least once a year. Yet fewer than half do so systematically, and even fewer follow up with concrete measures based on the assessments.

Feedback appears to be an important part of the effect. In a study STAMI described in 2023, covering 30 units in seven companies, some units received feedback meetings with a presentation and interpretation of the results, and help to develop concrete measures. They had lower long-term sickness absence than units that received only the mapping and general advice. The researchers did, however, find few direct effects on the working environment factors and health complaints that were mapped.
Arbeidstilsynet describes what an action plan should contain:

An action plan should describe what the goal is, what is to be done, who is affected, who is responsible and the time frame for the measure. To find out whether the measures have the desired effect, they must be evaluated.
blocks.cite: Arbeidstilsynet, Psychosocial working environment (our translation)

blocks.text: Two more principles from Arbeidstilsynet: measures should as far as possible address the causes of the risk, for example organisational or work-related conditions; and collective measures should be considered before individual ones. See [how to review the results with employees](/artikler/slik-gar-dere-gjennom-resultatene-med-de-ansatte) and [from results to measures](/artikler/fra-resultater-til-tiltak).
Repeat, document and evaluate

Arbeidstilsynet writes that mapping and risk assessment are not to be a one-off activity. One approach is a thorough survey once a year and shorter surveys on the topics where measures are under way, a so-called [pulse survey](/artikler/pulsundersokelse). The mapping, the assessments and the measures are documented as part of the systematic health and safety work. See also [how often to measure the working environment](/artikler/hvor-ofte-bor-dere-male-arbeidsmiljoet).
Checklist

items: Agree the purpose, topics, groups and timetable with the safety representative before sending.
Measure the factors the regulation points to, and what protects.
Show no group with fewer than five answers, and keep background questions few.
Review the results with employees, and ask what lies behind the figures.
Make an action plan with goals, measures, owners and a time frame.
Evaluate the measures, and document the mapping, assessment and measures.

trivselsundersokelse.title: Job satisfaction surveys and the working environment | Orgpuls
trivselsundersokelse.description: What a job satisfaction survey measures, why satisfaction is an outcome rather than a cause, and what mapping the psychosocial working environment takes.
trivselsundersokelse.h1: What is a job satisfaction survey, and is it enough to map the working environment?
trivselsundersokelse.lead: A job satisfaction survey measures how content employees are with their jobs. On its own it is not enough to map the psychosocial working environment: satisfaction is an outcome of how the work is organised, and the rules require the organisation to map and assess the working environment factors themselves – what strains and what protects – so that measures can address the causes.

blocks.text: What is job satisfaction?

In Norwegian workplaces the everyday word is «trivsel»; research usually speaks of job satisfaction. The Norwegian encyclopaedia Store norske leksikon defines it as how content a person is with their job situation.

The encyclopaedia notes that the concept lacks a precise definition, and that the definition you choose will determine how you measure job satisfaction, for example in an employee survey. Two satisfaction surveys can therefore measure quite different things.

According to the encyclopaedia, satisfaction is shaped by three kinds of conditions: characteristics of the person, such as personality and expectations; characteristics of the job, such as workload, variety and autonomy; and characteristics of the organisation, such as leadership, culture and participation. The last two are what the employer can do something about, and they are what the rules are about.
Satisfaction is an outcome, not a cause
When Arbeidstilsynet proposed the new rules on the psychosocial working environment in 2024, it described a pattern from its inspections:

Many organisations emphasised the outcome of psychosocial and organisational working conditions, such as satisfaction or adverse health outcomes, rather than the working environment factors themselves. Many organisations described the psychosocial working environment as satisfaction at work, but reflected less on what creates satisfaction or how satisfaction is connected to the work.
blocks.cite: Arbeidstilsynet, consultation paper on the psychosocial working environment (2024, our translation)

blocks.text: The consultation paper also describes the consequence: few take good measures for the psychosocial working environment, satisfaction and welfare measures dominate, and there is no clear line back to the mapping and risk assessment.

A low satisfaction score says something is wrong, but not what. Is it the workload, unclear roles, a conflict or too little support? Without an answer, the measure easily becomes a social event while the cause remains.
Demands and resources

The job demands–resources model, developed by Bakker and Demerouti, divides the working environment into demands – such as workload, time pressure and emotional strain – and resources, such as support, influence and feedback. Arbeidstilsynet summarises the model like this in the consultation paper:

Job demands can set off a health-impairing process, while job resources can act as a buffer and limit negative health consequences. Job resources can, in addition, contribute to a motivating or health-promoting process.
blocks.cite: Arbeidstilsynet, consultation paper on the psychosocial working environment (2024, our translation)

blocks.text: A satisfaction survey captures the sum of the two processes in a single number. The same middling satisfaction can hide high demands offset by good resources, and low demands in a job with little support and influence – two situations that call for entirely different measures.

The whole picture matters. A STAMI study of 6,175 employees in 62 Norwegian organisations found that high control over one’s own work did not appear to protect against pain complaints for those who at the same time had low or middling levels of other protective factors. The researchers concluded that high job control is not enough to protect employees against the adverse effects of other working environment factors, and that the whole picture must be considered when assessing the working environment.
What do the rules require?

items.text: The work shall be organised, planned and carried out so that the psychosocial working environment factors in the undertaking are fully satisfactory with regard to the employees' health, safety and welfare.

items.ref: Regulation on the performance of work § 1A-2(1) (our translation)
items.text: The employer shall map psychosocial working environment factors that may affect the employees' health, safety or welfare. On the basis of the mapping, the employer shall assess the risk of harmful effects, in both the short and the long term. The risk assessment shall cover the individual factors separately, how they affect one another, and whether together they constitute a risk.

blocks.text: The requirement concerns the factors in the work that can affect health, safety and welfare, and how they interact – not how content employees are. The word satisfaction («trivsel») appears neither in chapter 1A of the regulation nor in Arbeidstilsynet’s comments on it. A satisfaction survey can be a useful supplement, but it does not meet the requirement on its own. Read more about [the requirements for mapping](/artikler/krav-til-kartlegging-av-psykososialt-arbeidsmiljo).
What protects belongs too

Arbeidstilsynet writes in its comments on the regulation that such factors can act both as strains and as protection, and that protective factors may therefore also be relevant to include in the mapping. Support from managers and colleagues, influence over one’s own work and a sense of meaning are resources that make demands easier to carry. Measure them, and you see both what strains and what you can build on.
One question gives one number

A satisfaction survey can be as short as a single question on how content you are, or whether you would recommend the workplace to others. Such a question can show a level and a direction over time. It cannot show the cause, and it gives no basis for assessing the risk factor by factor, as the regulation requires.
Making the survey useful

items: **Keep the satisfaction question if you like, but also measure what explains it:** workload, role clarity, support, influence, emotional demands and how people treat each other. See [which questions belong in an employee survey](/artikler/medarbeiderundersokelse-sporsmal).
**Use several sources.** Arbeidstilsynet names working environment surveys, safety inspections, incident reports, appraisal conversations and informal conversations.
**Ask employees what lies behind the figures.** See [how to review the results with employees](/artikler/slik-gar-dere-gjennom-resultatene-med-de-ansatte).
**Aim measures at the causes.** Arbeidstilsynet writes that measures should as far as possible address the causes of the risk, for example organisational or work-related conditions.
**Follow up with short surveys** on the topics where you have put measures in place. See [pulse survey](/artikler/pulsundersokelse).
**Keep answers anonymous.** See [what an anonymous employee survey means](/artikler/anonym-medarbeiderundersokelse).

blocks.title: In short
blocks.text: Satisfaction is a good signal but a poor management tool. Measure what creates it, and you will know what to do.

pulsundersokelse.title: Pulse surveys: when do short surveys make sense? | Orgpuls
pulsundersokelse.description: What a pulse survey is, what Norwegian rules say about following up the working environment, and what research says about single items and small groups.
pulsundersokelse.h1: What is a pulse survey, and when do short surveys make sense?
pulsundersokelse.lead: A pulse survey is a short survey sent more often than the annual mapping, often with only a few statements. It makes sense when it follows up specific measures or changes, with the same statements and large enough groups. It does not replace the mapping and risk assessment of the psychosocial working environment, but it can show whether the measures are being felt.

blocks.text: What is a pulse survey?

Pulse surveys are short questionnaires sent at regular intervals. A recent interview study of how organisations use them describes them as «short, frequent questionnaires» and notes «a notable lack of research examining these practices». Among the organisations in the study, the frequency varied from weekly to every three months.
That sets the pulse survey apart from the main mapping, which measures all the psychosocial factors thoroughly and is the basis for the risk assessment. The pulse is a follow-up, not a new mapping.
What do the rules say?
The Norwegian rules do not use the term pulse survey, and they do not set how often you should measure. But they set requirements that a short survey can help you meet:

items.ref: Regulation on the performance of work § 1A-2(4)(c) (our translation)
items.text: be repeated regularly and upon changes that may affect the risk conditions in the undertaking
carry out systematic monitoring and review of the systematic health, environment and safety work to ensure that it functions as intended

blocks.text: On measures, Arbeidstilsynet writes that to find out whether they have the desired effect, they must be evaluated, and that measures that do not work as planned must be adjusted, replaced or supplemented. A short survey on the topics where measures are under way is one way to evaluate. It does not give the whole answer, but it shows whether employees notice a difference.
When do short surveys make sense?

items: **After a measure.** If you measure the same statements that led to the measure, you see whether the figures move.
**Upon changes.** A reorganisation, new management or new systems can affect the risk. A short survey on the topics concerned can show whether something is happening, pending a more thorough mapping.
**To keep the work alive.** A short survey between main mappings reminds everyone that the working environment is a topic all year – provided something happens with the answers.

blocks.text: The interview study concludes that «pulse surveys should not replace annual comprehensive risk assessment surveys; rather, they should serve as a complementary tool». It also found that pulse survey processes «were generally not integrated with psychosocial risk management practices». That link is what makes the measurement useful.
What research says about measurement error
Short surveys come at a price: the fewer the statements and the fewer who answer, the less certain the figure.

items: **Single items are less reliable than scales.** A review of single-item measures in organisational research states that «multiple item measures have better psychometric properties than single-item measures», though «in some circumstances single-item measures can provide useful information». A classic study estimated the minimum reliability of a single overall job satisfaction item at between .45 and .69, where 1 is perfect.
**Small groups give unstable averages.** How reliable a group average is depends, among other things, on how many are in the group. In a small group, one answer can move the figure a lot.

**Random variation can look like change.** Regression to the mean means that a group that scored unusually low on one occasion often scores closer to the average next time – even without a measure. The effect grows with measurement error, and when only the groups that scored lowest are followed up.

blocks.text: A study of pulse surveys in one healthcare organisation found that they «provided reliable estimates of overall engagement, but scores remained stable across 8 months», with practically no differences between groups or over time despite high participation. It concluded that pulse surveys «may be adequate for estimating overall employee sentiment but not useful for detecting change over time or differences between groups».

That does not make short surveys worthless, but small shifts should not be read as change. Look for clear and lasting movements, and hold them up against what you know from conversations, safety inspections and incident reports.
Compare like with like

A pulse survey should be compared with the previous pulse survey, with the same statements and the same groups. If you change the statements, the groups or the answer scale, a change in the figures may be due to the measurement and not the working environment. The same applies when a short pulse survey is compared with the full main mapping. See [how often to measure the working environment](/artikler/hvor-ofte-bor-dere-male-arbeidsmiljoet).
Willingness to answer falls when nothing happens

Frequent surveys can wear down the willingness to answer. A study among students found that «administering multiple surveys in one academic year can significantly suppress response rates in later surveys». A workplace is not a university, but the mechanism is easy to recognise.

What seems to matter most is whether the answers are used. In the interview study, employees’ willingness to respond «was highly dependent on their perception that their responses from pulse surveys were used meaningfully», and failure to follow up could lead to disengagement, survey fatigue and erosion of trust. An older study of employee surveys found that those who did not answer more often held negative beliefs about how the organisation handles survey data – for example, that it does not act on it.

items: Say what has been done since the last survey before you send the next.
Keep the survey short, and ask only about the topics where something is happening.
Do not measure more often than you can follow up.

blocks.text: Anonymity in small surveys

Short surveys are often sent to small groups, and anonymity is then more fragile. The authors of the interview study write that calculating a group average on single items for a small number of respondents is problematic for reliability and for detecting change, and that «reporting results on small groups of as few as 3–5 people is not an acceptable practice from an ethical or a methodological point of view».

A practical starting point is to show no group with fewer than five answers, and to look at the figures for the whole organisation when groups are smaller. The Norwegian central government’s employee survey (MUST) uses the same threshold for a report, and shows the distribution across answer options only from ten answers. Read more about [what an anonymous employee survey means](/artikler/anonym-medarbeiderundersokelse).
Pulse survey and main mapping

items.title: Main mapping
items.text: All the factors, the whole organisation. The basis for the risk assessment and the action plan. Repeated regularly and upon changes.

items.title: Pulse survey
items.text: A few statements on the topics where measures are under way. Shows whether employees notice a difference. Does not replace the mapping.

blocks.text: A measure being carried out does not mean it works. A systematic review of organisational-level interventions at work found that «About half of the studies (19) reported significant effects», and that «Success rates were higher among more comprehensive interventions tackling material, organisational and work-time related conditions simultaneously». That is an argument for measuring whether measures are felt, not only whether they were carried out. See [from results to measures](/artikler/fra-resultater-til-tiltak).
Checklist

items: Tie the pulse survey to measures or changes, not just to the calendar.
Use the same statements as in the main mapping for the topics you follow up.
Keep it short: few topics, few statements.
Show no group with fewer than five answers.
Read small shifts with caution.
Say what has happened before the next survey, and involve the safety representative in the plan.

faktorYtring.title: Freedom to speak up at work: causes and measures | Orgpuls
faktorYtring.description: A low speaking-up score means people stay silent, or doubt anything happens when they speak. What the law says, what lies behind it and what helps.
faktorYtring.h1: What does a low score on freedom to speak up mean, and what can be done?
faktorYtring.lead: A low score means many people do not feel safe raising mistakes, disagreement or things that are not working – or have learnt that nothing happens when they do. Research suggests that what matters most is how the manager reacts in the moment after someone speaks up. That is also where measures should start.

blocks.text: A good climate for speaking up is not the same as agreement

Freedom to speak up is about two things: whether employees dare to raise mistakes, disagreement and what is not working, and whether anything happens when they do. A good climate does not mean everyone agrees. A workplace where nobody objects may just as easily have a weak climate as a strong one.

The term itself does not appear in the list of psychosocial factors in section 4-3 of the Working Environment Act (arbeidsmiljøloven). It is nonetheless closely tied to several rights and duties in the Act, and in practice it decides whether they are used.
The right to speak up is in the law

Chapter 2 A of the Act gives employees the right to report censurable conditions – whistleblowing – and names an unsound working environment as one example. Organisations above a certain size must have written procedures for internal reporting.

items.text: An employee has the right to report censurable conditions in the employer’s undertaking.
Undertakings that regularly employ at least five employees are obliged to have procedures for internal reporting.

The procedures shall be in writing and shall at least contain a. an encouragement to report censurable conditions b. the procedure for reporting c. the procedure for the employer’s handling of the receipt, processing and follow-up of reports.

blocks.text: The Act also prohibits retaliation against employees who report (§ 2 A-4). Under § 2 A-6, the procedures must be drawn up in cooperation with employees and their union representatives, and they must not limit the right to report.

Speaking up is nevertheless a wider idea than whistleblowing. The Act makes clear that statements about matters concerning only the employee’s own employment are, as a rule, not whistleblowing. Much of what shapes the climate – disagreement in a meeting, a suggestion for a better way of working, an objection to a deadline – falls outside chapter 2 A. It is still part of the working environment. In its commentary on section 1A-5 of the regulation on the performance of work, the Norwegian Labour Inspection Authority (Arbeidstilsynet) writes that employees must, among other things, report harassment, discrimination or other conditions that may pose a risk to health, safety and welfare in the psychosocial working environment. Such a duty only works where people feel safe using it.
How speaking up is measured in a survey
In a survey built on the QPS Nordic tradition, the factor can be measured with statements that employees agree or disagree with. Examples:

items: ‘I can report censurable conditions without fearing consequences’
‘When someone reports a problem, something is done about it’
‘Disagreement is raised openly here, not in the corridor afterwards’

blocks.text: The first statement measures safety, the second follow-through and the third the culture for open disagreement. They are three different things and should be read separately.
What the low score can tell you

head: Lowest score on
Often points to
Natural place to start
rows: Experience that speaking up has had a cost
Reports and suggestions that go unanswered
How decisions are made in meetings

blocks.text: Look also at where the score is low. A single department that stands out often says something about how objections are received there, and is frequently linked to [support from the manager](/artikler/stotte-fra-leder). If the survey has open comment fields, a strikingly low number of comments may also say something about the climate.
Why people stay silent
The climate is shaped above all by what happens just after someone has spoken up. Typical explanations for a low score are:

items: reports and suggestions that never get an answer
managers who become defensive or irritated when someone disagrees
disagreement smoothed over in the meeting and aired in the corridor afterwards
experience that whoever spoke up was seen as difficult
uncertainty about where and how to raise something

blocks.title: A common mistake
blocks.text: Meeting a low score by asking who answered what confirms exactly what employees reported. The survey was anonymous. The conversation about the result should be about situations and ways of working, not about people.
What research on psychological safety points to

Measures in this area draw on research on psychological safety, in particular the work of Edmondson. A central point is that what moves the score most is what the manager does in the moment after someone has spoken up. Three measures follow from this.

**Answer every report within five days.** Every deviation report and every suggestion gets an answer from a named person: what will happen, or why nothing will. No report is left lying. The measure targets the statement about something happening when people report, and it has a parallel in the Act. When a safety representative alerts the employer to conditions that may cause accidents or harm to health, § 6-2(3) states that the employer shall give the safety representative an answer.

**A session on what stops people speaking up.** The team writes down, anonymously, situations where they chose not to speak up. The manager listens without defending, and the meeting – about 90 minutes – ends with two concrete changes. The measure targets the fear of consequences.

**The manager asks first and speaks last.** In meetings, the manager asks for objections before decisions are made and thanks those who raise them. Disagreement is written down instead of being smoothed over. The measure targets the culture for open disagreement, and it has to be repeated in every meeting to work.
Follow-up and measuring again

The climate changes through many small experiences, not through a single decision. Ask the same statements again a couple of months after the measures are in place, and look especially at the statement each measure was aimed at. If the score has not moved, go back to the group and ask what is still holding people back. Read more about [going through the results with employees](/artikler/slik-gar-dere-gjennom-resultatene-med-de-ansatte) and [turning results into measures](/artikler/fra-resultater-til-tiltak).

faktorRolle.title: Role clarity: when expectations are unclear | Orgpuls
faktorRolle.description: A low role clarity score means many are unsure of expectations, responsibilities and what is good enough. What the rules say, likely causes and what helps.
faktorRolle.h1: What does a low role clarity score mean, and how can roles be made clearer?
faktorRolle.lead: A low score on role clarity means many employees are unsure what is expected of them, where their responsibility ends, or what counts as good enough work. Unclear demands and expectations are named as a psychosocial factor in both the Act and the regulation. The measures with research support are concrete clarifications: conversations about expectations, a review of grey zones and a training plan for new hires.

blocks.text: Three questions in one concept

Role clarity is about whether an employee knows what is expected, where their own responsibility ends and others’ begins, and what counts as good enough. If any one of the three answers is missing, a good deal of energy goes into guessing, duplicating work or waiting for decisions.

Its opposite, role ambiguity, is not the same as demanding work. An employee can be very busy and still know exactly what their job is. The problem arises when expectations are unknown, shift without explanation or have not been settled between several roles.
Unclear expectations in the Act and the regulation

Section 4-3(2) of the Working Environment Act (arbeidsmiljøloven) names unclear demands and expectations as a psychosocial factor. The same factor appears in section 1A-1 of the regulation on the performance of work, in force since 1 January 2026.

items.text: unclear or conflicting demands and expectations in the work
sufficient information and training is given so that the employee is able to carry out the work when changes occur that affect his or her working situation.

blocks.text: In its commentary on the regulation, the Norwegian Labour Inspection Authority (Arbeidstilsynet) writes that the demands and expectations may concern tasks, working methods, quality, pace, deadlines, working hours, areas of responsibility, division of roles or priorities. They may be formal or informal, and may come from managers, colleagues, partners or the employee themselves. Arbeidstilsynet links the factor to two familiar terms:
When demands and expectations are unclear or conflicting, this is often referred to as role ambiguity and role conflict respectively.
blocks.cite: Arbeidstilsynet’s commentary on the regulation on the performance of work § 1A-1 (our translation)

blocks.text: The regulation does not set a minimum list of factors every organisation must survey; that depends on the organisation’s nature, activities and risk profile. Arbeidstilsynet nonetheless writes that the listed factors will be relevant for a great many organisations.
How role clarity is typically measured
Surveys built on the QPS Nordic tradition measure role clarity with short statements about the employee’s own job. Examples of such statements:

items: ‘I know what is expected of me in my job’
‘I know where my responsibility ends and others begin’
‘I know what counts as good work here’

blocks.text: Each statement corresponds to one of the three questions above, so the factor’s overall score is rarely enough on its own.
Who scores low, and when?
The pattern in the answers often says more than the level. Three questions are worth putting to the results:

items: **Which statement is lowest?** Unclear expectations, unclear responsibility and an unclear ‘good enough’ each call for a different fix.
**New hires or everyone?** Low role clarity among newcomers points to training. Low role clarity across the board points to how the work is organised.
**Has something changed?** A reorganisation, a new manager or new tasks often cause a drop that does not correct itself.

blocks.text: The last point ties in with the requirement in section 1A-2 of the regulation that the survey and risk assessment be repeated when things change. Arbeidstilsynet mentions changes in organisation, staffing, tasks, management and technology, among others – exactly the changes that most often blur roles.
Where the ambiguity comes from
Role ambiguity rarely arises because anyone wants it. It builds up, usually gradually. Common explanations are:

items: jobs that have grown without anyone writing down what they now cover
grey zones between two roles or two departments
changes in organisation or management not followed by fresh clarification
training that stops after the first week
feedback too infrequent for people to know whether they are on target

blocks.title: Role clarity and conflicting demands
blocks.text: The Act and the regulation name unclear and conflicting demands in the same clause, and the two often occur together. An employee may know perfectly well what each expectation is, yet receive expectations from two directions that cannot be reconciled. Then the problem is role conflict, not role ambiguity. Read more about [conflicting demands](/artikler/motstridende-krav).
Three clarifications with research support

Research shows that role clarity is closely tied to job satisfaction and lower stress, and that good training at the start has a lasting effect. The measures that follow are simple in form, but someone has to take responsibility for them:

items.title: An expectations conversation with every employee
items.text: The manager and the employee write down the three most important areas of responsibility and what counts as good enough. Such a conversation takes about 30 minutes and answers the statement about what is expected directly.

items.title: A review of the grey zones
items.text: In a meeting of about 90 minutes, the team goes through the areas where it is unclear who is responsible, and assigns them. This targets the statement about where one’s own responsibility ends.

items.title: A training plan for new hires
items.text: A written plan for the first three months: what the new hire is to learn, from whom, and when they count as fully trained. The plan also makes clear what counts as good work.

blocks.text: Section 1A-4 of the regulation frames the last measure. The employer must ensure that employees receive the training, practice and instruction needed for a fully sound psychosocial working environment, and Arbeidstilsynet writes that the extent must be judged against the risk profile and the actual working conditions.
Follow up where the score was lowest

Ask the same statements again a couple of months after the measures are in place, and look especially at the group and the statement that were lowest. If the score has not moved, the ambiguity probably lay somewhere other than assumed, and it is time to go back to the group. Read more about [turning results into measures](/artikler/fra-resultater-til-tiltak).

Working Environment Act § 4-3 (Lovdata, Norwegian)

faktorMotstrid.title: Conflicting demands at work: a low score | Orgpuls
faktorMotstrid.description: A low score on conflicting demands means staff face demands that cannot all be met. What the law says, how to read the score and which measures help.
faktorMotstrid.h1: Conflicting demands: what does a low score mean, and what can the employer do?
faktorMotstrid.lead: A low score on conflicting demands means that many employees receive tasks and expectations that cannot all be met at once, with no one making clear what should give way. It is a recognised strain, and it is resolved mainly in how the work is organised: who prioritises, who has the final say, and what is dropped when something new arrives.

blocks.text: What conflicting demands are

Conflicting demands arise when two managers, two systems or two concerns ask for things that do not go together – quality and speed, for instance – and no one says which should give way. The employee is then left holding a priority call that really belongs to the organisation.
The Norwegian Labour Inspection Authority (Arbeidstilsynet) stresses that the demands do not only come from management:

The demands and expectations can be both formal and informal, and come from various quarters such as managers, colleagues, partners or the employee themselves – for example as a result of values linked to morality or profession.
blocks.cite: Arbeidstilsynet's commentary on the regulation on the performance of work § 1A-1 (our translation)

blocks.text: That last point matters. The conflict may lie between what is being asked for and what the employee considers professionally or ethically sound. Arbeidstilsynet notes that unclear and conflicting demands are often referred to as role ambiguity and role conflict respectively. This article deals with role conflict; unclear expectations are covered in the article on [role clarity](/artikler/rolleklarhet).
What the Act and the regulation say

items.text: Psychosocial working environment factors are, in addition to the matters referred to in the third to sixth paragraphs, among other things a. unclear or conflicting demands and expectations in the work

The organisation, arrangement and management of the work, working time arrangements, pay systems, including the use of performance-related pay, technology etc. shall be such that employees are not exposed to adverse physical or mental strain and such that safety considerations are safeguarded.

blocks.text: From 1 January 2026 the factor is also named in § 1A-1(2)(a) of the regulation on the performance of work. The regulation sets no limit value. Arbeidstilsynet writes that the provision «does not set prohibitions on, threshold values for, or specific requirements relating to the individual factors» (our translation). Which factors an organisation must survey depends on its nature, activities and risk profile, but the listed factors «will nonetheless be relevant to a great many organisations in different parts of working life».

In the same commentary Arbeidstilsynet lists organisational conditions that can have a major bearing on the psychosocial working environment, among them «priorities, responsibility and authority». These are the very conditions that decide whether conflicting demands get resolved or are left with the individual.
How the factor is measured

In a survey built on the QPS Nordic tradition the factor can be measured with a few statements that employees respond to, for example on a five-point scale from strongly disagree to strongly agree. Examples of statements:

head: Statement
What it captures
rows: «I rarely get tasks without knowing what should be deprioritised»
Whether new tasks come with clarity about what gives way
«The demands from different quarters hang together»
Whether requests from different managers, departments or systems pull in the same direction
«I know who decides when two things collide»
Whether there is a known line of decision when demands clash

blocks.text: The statements are worded so that agreement is the favourable answer. A low score therefore means that many disagree: they get tasks without priorities, find the demands inconsistent, or do not know who decides.
How to read a low result

Start with the statement that stands out most. The three point to different weaknesses in the organisation and call for different responses. If the third is particularly low, a line of decision is missing. If it is the first, tasks are being added without anything being removed.

Then look at which groups score lowest. A natural question is how many people commission work from the group. Employees who work for several managers or across departments may receive demands from several quarters at once. Whether that is the case in your organisation is something the figures show – not the assumption.

Finally, the factor should be read alongside the others. § 1A-2 of the regulation requires the risk assessment to cover «the individual factors separately, how they affect each other, and whether together they constitute a risk» (our translation). Arbeidstilsynet points out that the combined risk «can thus be higher than the sum of the individual factors». A low score on conflicting demands in a group that also reports a high [workload and time pressure](/artikler/arbeidsmengde-og-tidspress) should therefore be assessed as a whole.

blocks.title: A common mistake
blocks.text: Reading the result as a sign that employees are poor at prioritising. Research on role conflict points the other way: unclear priorities between several people who commission work are a strong source of stress, and the problem is solved in the organisation, not in the individual.
Where demands can collide
When the score is low, these are conditions worth examining:

items: several people commissioning work from the same staff, with no one prioritising between them
goals and targets pulling in different directions, such as quality and speed
new tasks added without anything being taken away
no clear final say when two demands collide
demands that go against professional judgement or ethics

blocks.text: The regulation requires the survey and risk assessment to be carried out in cooperation with the employees and their representatives. That is also the quickest route to an explanation: those who experience the collisions can point to where they occur.
Three measures aimed at the organisation

In its commentary on § 1A-3 of the regulation, Arbeidstilsynet writes that measures «should as far as possible be directed at the causes of the risk, for example organisational or work-related conditions» (our translation). For conflicting demands, that means measures which change how work is commissioned and prioritised.
Settle who has the final say

Decide in writing who settles the matter when demands from different quarters do not fit together, and make it known to everyone affected. It is a single decision, but it has to be honoured: when a collision occurs, the employee must know whom to turn to, and that person must actually make the call.
Draw a responsibility map

In a working session of around 90 minutes the group goes through its most important tasks and notes who commissions, who carries out and who approves each one. Where two people commission the same work, one is chosen. The map makes the collisions visible and gives a shared basis for sorting them out.
One task in, one task down

When a manager hands out a new task, they say at the same time what is to be deprioritised. The rule is ongoing and costs little, but it moves the priority call away from the employee and back to the person with the authority to make it.
How to tell whether the measures work

Each measure corresponds to one statement: the line of decision to the third, the responsibility map to the second and the prioritisation rule to the first. That makes it possible to see whether a measure hit the mark. Measure the factor again after a few months using the same statements. If the score does not move, the measure probably missed the cause, and the group should be asked again.

The measures must be planned and carried out in cooperation with the employees and their representatives, under § 1A-3 of the regulation. Arbeidstilsynet calls that cooperation «a prerequisite for the measures to be relevant, well targeted and work as intended» (our translation). Read more about getting [from results to measures](/artikler/fra-resultater-til-tiltak).
