faktorKontakt.title: Contact and communication: a low score | Orgpuls
faktorKontakt.description: A low score on contact and communication can mean isolation or that staff cannot call for help. What the law requires, how to read it and what helps.
faktorKontakt.h1: Contact and communication: what does it mean when the job allows too little contact with others?
faktorKontakt.lead: A low score means that many people have little contact with colleagues during the working day, feel isolated, or are unsure whether they can get help if something happens while they are alone. The first is about cooperation and belonging, the second about safety – and the two call for different measures.

blocks.text: Two problems under one factor

The factor covers both the social and the professional side of work. The Norwegian Labour Inspection Authority (Arbeidstilsynet) describes it as «the employee's access to social and professional interaction in everyday working life», and writes that this can be important for «information sharing, cooperation, support, belonging and the prevention of social isolation» (our translation).

For those who work alone, a further consideration comes in: the ability to get help. An employee can be on good terms with colleagues and still have no one to contact if something goes wrong on a solo shift. That is why it pays to keep the two aspects apart when reading the result.
What the law requires

items.text: The work shall be sought designed so as to allow contact and communication with other employees in the undertaking.

It shall be assessed whether there is particular risk associated with lone work in the undertaking. Measures necessary to prevent and reduce any risk in lone work shall be implemented, so that the Act's requirement for a fully satisfactory working environment is met.

blocks.text: The factor is also named in § 1A-1(2)(e) of the regulation on the performance of work, in force since 1 January 2026. § 1A-2 of the regulation requires the employer to survey psychosocial factors that may affect employees' health, safety or welfare, and to assess the risk on the basis of that survey. Where an organisation has lone work, § 4-1 of the Act also requires an assessment of whether it carries particular risk, and the implementation of the necessary measures.
Where contact is most often limited

Arbeidstilsynet itself names the forms of work concerned. Limited contact and communication «can occur in, for example, remote work, shift work, night work, lone work or work largely carried out away from the organisation's fixed workplaces» (our translation). The list is a useful starting point when results are broken down by group.
In practice it may involve:

items: solo shifts or work at sites where no one else is present
home or hybrid working without fixed meeting points
rotas that mean people are rarely at work at the same time
no fixed arrangement for raising the alarm or calling for help

blocks.text: Statements that separate isolation from safety
In a survey built on the QPS Nordic tradition the factor can be measured with statements such as these:

items: «I have the opportunity for contact with colleagues during the working day»
«I can call for help quickly if something happens while I am alone»
«I do not feel isolated in my job»

blocks.text: The first and third are about contact and belonging. The second is of a different kind: it asks about something that is either in place or not, namely a way to call for help. All three are worded so that agreement is the favourable answer, so a low score means that many disagree.

The second statement mainly concerns those who actually work alone. Answers from colleagues who never do can pull the average up and hide a problem in a smaller group. Look at this statement on its own.
Three questions to put to a low result

items.title: Which statement pulls it down?
items.text: If it is the one about calling for help, it is a safety matter that should be dealt with promptly, whatever the rest of the result shows. If it is isolation, it concerns how the work is organised over time.

items.title: Which groups score lowest?
items.text: Compare nights, weekends, home working and solo shifts with the rest. A single figure for the whole organisation can look acceptable even when one group scores low.

items.title: How is support holding up?
items.text: Contact is a precondition for getting help from others. Read the result alongside [support from colleagues](/artikler/stotte-fra-kollegaer) and support from the manager.

blocks.text: The link with support is more than practical. Research on social support at work, including the work of Johnson and Hall, shows that social support dampens the effect of high demands. In its commentary on § 1A-2 of the regulation, Arbeidstilsynet writes that «protective factors such as support and help in the work can help reduce the risk» (our translation). Where contact is lacking, that protection is weakened too.
Measures: from alarms to fixed meeting points

According to Arbeidstilsynet, what is necessary must be assessed specifically in the light of the organisation's risk profile. Three measures build on the research on social support, and one of them responds directly to the lone-work requirement in § 4-1 of the Act.
A fixed way to call for help

Everyone who works alone should know exactly how to call for help, and the arrangement must be tested regularly. It may be an alarm, a fixed phone routine or agreed check-in times. What matters is that it works when needed and that someone actually responds.
Fixed meeting points for those who work alone

A short, regular meeting – say 15 minutes a week, in person or online – where those who work alone meet colleagues and their manager. The point is regularity: the meeting should take place even in weeks when there is nothing in particular to discuss.
A fixed buddy

Whoever often works alone is paired with a regular colleague to call and talk things through with. The arrangement lowers the threshold for professional questions and gives a known person to contact when something is unclear.
Follow-up and a fresh survey

The alarm arrangement can be checked directly: does it work, does the message get through, and does everyone know how to use it? The other measures show up in the responses. Measure the same statements again after a few months, paying particular attention to the groups that scored lowest.

If the way of working changes – more home working, a new rota, new solo shifts – the survey should be repeated. § 1A-2 of the regulation requires it to be repeated «regularly and in the event of changes that may affect the risk conditions in the undertaking» (our translation). Go through the result with the groups concerned before choosing measures; see also [how to go through the results with employees](/artikler/slik-gar-dere-gjennom-resultatene-med-de-ansatte).

faktorEmosjon.title: Emotional demands: when work with people wears | Orgpuls
faktorEmosjon.description: What does a low score on emotional demands mean? The legal duties, the strain of working with people, how to read the score and research-backed measures.
faktorEmosjon.h1: Emotional demands: what a low score tells you, and how the strain can be reduced
faktorEmosjon.lead: The statements used to measure emotional demands ask about the support around the difficult part of the job. A low score therefore means that employees are left too much alone in hard encounters, that difficult incidents are not followed up, or that there is no room to react. The strain cannot be removed from work with people, but it can be shared and followed up.

blocks.text: Part of the job – but within limits

In many occupations, meeting people in difficult situations is the work itself. The Norwegian Labour Inspection Authority (Arbeidstilsynet) mentions work with patients, users, next of kin, clients, children, pupils, students and customers. No rule can remove that strain, and none tries to. The starting point is put like this:
It is not forbidden to be busy or have a demanding time at work, but the employer must ensure that the strain does not become too great.
blocks.cite: Arbeidstilsynet's commentary on the regulation on the performance of work § 1A-1 (our translation)

blocks.text: According to Arbeidstilsynet, emotional demands can involve three things:

items: having to understand or handle other people's thoughts, feelings or behaviour
having to handle or conceal one's own thoughts or feelings
having to adapt communication or behaviour when dealing with the people one works with

blocks.text: The second point is easily overlooked. The strain lies not only in what the employee encounters, but also in what they have to hold back.
The legal starting point

items.text: emotional demands and strain in work with people
Employees shall, as far as possible, be protected against violence, threats and adverse strain as a result of contact with others.

blocks.text: The factor is also named in § 1A-1(2)(b) of the regulation on the performance of work, which applies from 1 January 2026. § 1A-4(2) of the regulation further requires the employer to ensure that employees receive «the training, practice and instruction necessary for a fully satisfactory psychosocial working environment» (our translation). Arbeidstilsynet writes that training may be necessary where there is a risk of psychosocial strain, «or where prevention and handling require particular skills or knowledge». In occupations with demanding encounters with people, it is a requirement that should be assessed specifically.
The measurement looks at support, not just strain
In a survey built on the QPS Nordic tradition the factor can be measured with statements such as these:

items: «I am rarely left alone in emotionally demanding situations»
«We talk about difficult incidents afterwards»
«I am allowed to react as a human being at work»

blocks.text: Note what the statements ask. They do not ask how demanding the encounters are, but whether the employee faces them alone, whether incidents are talked about, and whether it is acceptable to be affected. These are the protective sides of the work. Arbeidstilsynet points out that psychosocial factors can «have both a straining and a protective effect», and that protective factors may also be relevant to survey.

That has a practical consequence. A workplace with very demanding client encounters may score well if the support around them is good, while a workplace with more moderate demands may score low if people are left on their own.
Three questions when the score is low

items: **Are people left alone?** The first statement says most about organisation: who is present, and how shifts and tasks are allocated.
**Are incidents followed up?** Low agreement that difficult incidents are talked about afterwards points to the routines after an incident.
**Is there room to react?** The third statement is about culture – whether being affected is seen as weakness.

blocks.text: The result should also be read together with the other factors. Arbeidstilsynet uses emotional demands as its very example of how factors affect one another:

For example, a high workload and time pressure can increase the risk associated with emotional demands and strain in work with people, while protective factors such as support and help in the work can help reduce the risk.
blocks.cite: Arbeidstilsynet's commentary on § 1A-2 of the regulation (our translation)

blocks.text: A low score here should therefore be considered alongside the results for [workload and time pressure](/artikler/arbeidsmengde-og-tidspress) and [support from colleagues](/artikler/stotte-fra-kollegaer).
Possible causes to examine

items: demanding encounters with customers or clients where the employee is alone
no fixed practice for following up after difficult incidents
a culture in which being affected is seen as weakness
too little time between heavy tasks to recover

blocks.text: What helps – and what does not
The measures build on research on emotional labour, starting from Hochschild. One finding matters particularly for how they are designed:

blocks.title: One-off debriefing is not enough
blocks.text: A single debriefing immediately after an incident has not shown an effect in systematic reviews. What works is support from colleagues and follow-up over time. Measures should therefore be built as standing arrangements, not as a reaction to individual incidents.
Nobody alone in the hardest encounters
Decide which meetings with customers or clients must always have two people present. It is a single decision, but it changes the organisation where the strain is greatest.
A short talk the same day, follow-up from the manager later

After a difficult incident, those involved have a short, voluntary talk the same day, perhaps a quarter of an hour. The manager follows up a few days later. It is the follow-up over time, not the first conversation alone, that makes the difference.
A working session on what drains people

In a working session of around 90 minutes the group shares which situations drain them most and agrees on how to help one another through them. The session may also reveal a need for training under § 1A-4 of the regulation.
Follow-up over time

Since what works is follow-up over time, the evaluation should also extend over time. Measure the same statements again after a few months, watching in particular the statement each measure was aimed at: two people present in the hardest meetings should show in the first, talks after incidents in the second and the working session in the third.

Measures must be planned and carried out in cooperation with the employees and their representatives, under § 1A-3 of the regulation. Read more about turning a survey [from results into measures](/artikler/fra-resultater-til-tiltak).

Working Environment Act § 4-3 (Lovdata, Norwegian)

faktorLeder.title: Support from managers: what a low score means | Orgpuls
faktorLeder.description: A low score on support from managers can be about availability, insight or trust. What the law says, how to read the result and which measures work.
faktorLeder.h1: Support from managers: what does a low score tell you, and what can be done?
faktorLeder.lead: A low score on support from managers means that many employees do not feel they get help from their manager when the job gets demanding, that the manager does not know the work well enough, or that it is hard to raise problems. The cause may lie as much in the manager's circumstances – number of staff, their own workload, distance from the work – as in the manager, and measures should address both.

blocks.text: Support is more than goodwill

Support from managers is about whether the manager is available when things get difficult, and whether the support is practical rather than merely well-meaning. The Norwegian Labour Inspection Authority (Arbeidstilsynet) describes several sides of support and help at work:

items.title: Emotional support
items.text: Care, understanding and recognition.

items.title: Instrumental support
items.text: Professional advice, technical assistance or feedback on the work.

items.title: Structurally anchored support
items.text: Support built into the organisation's systems, routines or clear lines of decision and responsibility.

blocks.text: The last of these matters when the result concerns managers. Support that rests only on an individual manager's personality and energy easily disappears when that manager is under pressure or leaves. Support built into regular conversations and known lines of decision holds up better.
Where managers fit in the legislation

items.text: support and help in the work

The organisation, arrangement and management of the work, working time arrangements, pay systems, including the use of performance-related pay, technology etc. shall be such that employees are not exposed to adverse physical or mental strain and such that safety considerations are safeguarded.

blocks.text: Support and help at work is also named in § 1A-1(2)(d) of the regulation on the performance of work, which applies from 1 January 2026. In its commentary Arbeidstilsynet writes that organisational conditions, including «staffing, management structure, governance» (our translation), can have a major bearing on the psychosocial working environment. That is a useful starting point: a low score is not necessarily a verdict on one person, but may reflect how management is organised.
The statements behind the score
In a survey built on the QPS Nordic tradition the factor can be measured with statements such as these:

items: «I get support from my manager when the job becomes demanding»
«My manager knows enough about what my job actually involves»
«I can raise difficult matters with my manager»

blocks.text: The three point to different things. The first is about availability when things are busy or difficult. The second is about insight: whether the manager knows the work well enough to give relevant help. The third is about trust – whether there is room to raise something uncomfortable. A low score on insight calls for a different measure from a low score on availability.
When the result concerns one manager

When results are broken down by department, the factor will often concern one particular manager. That makes it more personal than most other factors. Look at each department before drawing conclusions for the organisation as a whole; a single overall figure can hide large differences between departments.

It also means the review with employees should be planned. When the result is about the manager themselves, it may be wise for the safety representative or another manager to lead that part of the conversation, so that it can be open. Under § 6-2(2)(f) of the Working Environment Act (arbeidsmiljøloven), the safety representative shall in particular ensure «that the employees' psychosocial working environment is safeguarded» (our translation). Read more about [the safety representative's role in the survey](/artikler/verneombudets-rolle-i-kartleggingen) and [how to go through the results with employees](/artikler/slik-gar-dere-gjennom-resultatene-med-de-ansatte).
Look at the circumstances before the behaviour

Before aiming measures at how the manager behaves, it is worth looking at the manager's own working situation. A manager with a very large number of staff, a full workload of their own or a great distance from the day-to-day work cannot be available, however willing. Possible explanations to examine:

items: too many employees per manager, or managers with a full workload of their own
managers far removed from the work they manage
no regular conversations, so contact only happens when something has gone wrong
new managers without training in management

blocks.title: Remember the manager's own workload
blocks.text: § 1A-2 of the regulation requires the factors to be assessed separately and together. A manager with a high [workload and time pressure](/artikler/arbeidsmengde-og-tidspress) may be part of the reason employees experience little support. The measure must then target the manager's circumstances, not just the manager.
Measures supported by research

Studies of leadership development show an effect when the training is practical and followed up over time. Regular conversations between manager and employee are one of the simplest steps. Three measures build on this, each aimed at one of the statements.
Regular conversations every fortnight

Short, regular conversations of around 20 minutes where the employee sets the agenda. They may be moved, but are never cancelled. The arrangement provides a fixed opportunity to raise difficult matters and so answers the third statement.
A day in the ordinary work
The manager takes part in the ordinary work one day a quarter to see what the job actually involves. The measure targets insight, the second statement.
A mentor for new starters

An experienced colleague follows up new starters for their first eight weeks, so the manager is not the only person they can ask. This relieves the manager and gives new staff support when the job is demanding, which is what the first statement measures.
Has it helped?

Measure the same statements again after a few months, department by department. If the score for one statement has moved while the others stand still, the measure has hit where it was aimed. If none has moved, there is reason to go back to the group and ask what lies behind it – and to look at the manager's circumstances again.

Measures must be planned and carried out in cooperation with the employees and their representatives, under § 1A-3 of the regulation. Arbeidstilsynet writes that measures «should as far as possible be directed at the causes of the risk, for example organisational or work-related conditions» (our translation).

Working Environment Act § 4-3 (Lovdata, Norwegian)

faktorMedvirk.title: Participation and control at work | Orgpuls
faktorMedvirk.description: What does a low score on participation and control mean? The legal duty to give influence over one's work, how to read the figure, causes and measures.
faktorMedvirk.h1: A low score on participation and control: what does it mean, and what can be done?
faktorMedvirk.lead: A low score means that many employees feel they have little say over how, at what pace and in what order they do their work, or that they are not heard before changes are decided. The law requires work to leave room for self-determination and influence, and research counts control over one's own work among the best documented protective factors. The measures that work move decisions closer to the people who do the work.

blocks.text: Two sides of the same factor

Participation and control covers two things that are related but not identical. One is the room for manoeuvre in daily work: whether you can decide method, order and pace yourself. The other is influence over decisions that change the working day, such as reorganisations, new systems or new routines.

The Norwegian Labour Inspection Authority (Arbeidstilsynet) describes the factor in exactly these terms in its commentary on section 1A-1 of the regulation on the performance of work, which lists «self-determination and influence in the work» as one of the psychosocial working environment factors:

Self-determination and influence in the work concerns the extent to which employees can influence, for example, decisions of significance for their work situation, or how they carry out their tasks. This involves influence through formal participation processes, but also that the employee has real room for manoeuvre in everyday work.
blocks.cite: Arbeidstilsynet's commentary on section 1A-1 second paragraph letter h of the regulation (our translation)

blocks.text: What the Working Environment Act requires
The requirement is not new. It is set out in section 4-2 of the Working Environment Act (arbeidsmiljøloven), on arrangement, participation and development. Three paragraphs are particularly relevant:

items.ref: Section 4-2 second paragraph letter c (our translation)
items.text: In designing the individual employee's work situation, […] emphasis shall be placed on giving the employee the opportunity for self-determination, influence and professional responsibility.

During reorganisation processes that entail changes of significance for the employees' work situation, the employer shall ensure the information, participation and skills development necessary to meet the Act's requirement of a fully satisfactory working environment.

Employees and their elected representatives shall be kept continuously informed of systems used in planning and carrying out the work. They shall be given the training needed to familiarise themselves with the systems, and they shall take part in designing them.

blocks.text: The regulation also makes the survey itself a matter of participation. Under section 1A-2, the survey and risk assessment are to be carried out «in cooperation with the employees and their representatives» (our translation). An organisation that scores low on this factor should therefore look at how it follows up the result: that work, too, is to be done together with the employees.
How the factor is typically measured

In surveys built on the QPS Nordic tradition, the factor is measured with a small number of statements that employees rate on a response scale, for example from «strongly disagree» to «strongly agree». Examples of statements:

items: «I have influence over how I carry out my work»
«I am heard when something is to be changed»
«I can influence the pace of my own work»

blocks.text: The first and third statements concern room for manoeuvre in everyday work. The second concerns influence over change. The average for the factor on its own therefore tells you little.
Three questions to ask when the figure is low

items: **Is it everyday work or change?** Little influence over the working day calls for different measures from not being heard before decisions are made. Look at which statement pulls the figure down.

**Which groups are affected?** Work governed by rotas, operational systems or customers naturally leaves less room. That rarely means there is no room at all. Compare groups doing similar work before drawing conclusions.
**What does the workload look like?** Low control is more serious when demands are high at the same time. Read the figure alongside [workload and time pressure](/artikler/arbeidsmengde-og-tidspress).

blocks.text: Why control matters more when demands are high

The demand–control model developed by Karasek describes high demands combined with low control as the most straining combination. Influence over one's own work does not reduce the demands, but it makes them easier to carry. It is one of the best documented protective factors in working environment research.

The regulation rests on the same idea. The risk assessment must cover the factors individually, how they affect one another, and whether together they amount to a risk. In its commentary on section 1A-2, Arbeidstilsynet writes that «the overall risk may therefore be higher than the sum of the individual factors» (our translation). A group with low control and high time pressure should therefore come before a group where only one of the factors is weak. There is more on this in the article on [risk assessment of the psychosocial working environment](/artikler/risikovurdering-av-psykososialt-arbeidsmiljo).
Typical explanations
When employees feel they have little influence, the explanation usually lies in how the work is organised, not in the individual. These come up again and again:

items: changes are decided before the people affected have been asked
micromanagement of how tasks are to be done
systems or routines that lock order and pace
suggestions that get no answer, so people stop making them

blocks.title: A common mistake
blocks.text: Asking for input and then not responding lowers the sense of influence more than not asking at all. A reasoned no is also an answer.
Measures supported by research

Arbeidstilsynet writes that measures should, as far as possible, address the causes of the risk, such as organisational or work-related conditions. For this factor, that means moving decisions, not running motivation courses. Three measures are well suited:
Job crafting

Each employee goes through their own tasks and proposes one change in how they are done. The manager says yes, or gives reasons for a no. Such a review takes about two hours. Studies of job crafting, where employees adjust their own tasks, show measurable but moderate effects. The measure bears most directly on the statement about influence over how the work is done.
Involving those affected before the decision

Changes that affect the working day are put to the people concerned before the decision is made, not after. This is in line with section 4-2 third paragraph of the Act, and it is what employees are rating when they respond to the statement about being heard when something is to be changed.
The team plans its own week
The manager sets goals and deadlines. The team decides the order and the distribution of work. This gives control over pace without losing direction over what is to be delivered.
How to tell whether the measure worked

Measure the factor again with the same statements a couple of months after the measure is in place, in the group it was meant for. If the figure does not move, the measure probably missed the cause, and the next step is to go back to the group and ask what it would take. The approach is described in the article on [getting from results to measures](/artikler/fra-resultater-til-tiltak).

faktorIntegritet.title: Integrity and dignity at work | Orgpuls
faktorIntegritet.description: What does a low score on integrity and dignity mean? The legal protection against harassment, reading the figure in small groups, causes and measures.
faktorIntegritet.h1: Integrity and dignity: what does a low figure tell you, and how should it be followed up?
faktorIntegritet.lead: A low score means that some employees do not feel met with respect, are not allowed to use professional judgement, or do not have their boundaries respected. The Working Environment Act requires work to be arranged so that integrity and dignity are safeguarded, and that nobody is subjected to harassment. The figure is a warning that must be examined further with the employees and the safety representative – and early intervention by managers is the measure research points to.

blocks.text: A legal requirement with two sides

Section 4-3 of the Working Environment Act (arbeidsmiljøloven) contains two provisions that together make up this factor. One is a general requirement of respect in the way work is arranged. The other is a prohibition:

items.text: Work shall be arranged so that the employee's integrity and dignity are safeguarded.
Employees shall not be subjected to harassment, including sexual harassment, or other improper conduct.

blocks.text: The Act also defines what harassment is:
Harassment means acts, omissions or statements whose purpose or effect is to be offensive, frightening, hostile, degrading or humiliating.
blocks.cite: Working Environment Act section 4-3 fifth paragraph (our translation)

blocks.text: The words «purpose or effect» matter. It is not enough that the person who behaved offensively did not mean it that way. An omission – leaving someone out, for instance – can also be harassment.

Section 1A-1 of the regulation on the performance of work lists «harassment, including sexual harassment» among the psychosocial working environment factors. Integrity and dignity is not a separate item on the regulation's list, but the Norwegian Labour Inspection Authority (Arbeidstilsynet) makes clear that the list is not exhaustive: the words «among other things» show that other factors may also be relevant. The requirement in section 4-3 third paragraph of the Act applies in any case.
Respect, judgement and boundaries

In surveys built on the QPS Nordic tradition, the factor is usually measured with a small number of statements that employees rate on a response scale. The statements capture different aspects of the factor, and a low figure has to be read statement by statement:

head: Example statement
What it captures
rows: «I am met with respect regardless of who I am»
Equal treatment in how people are spoken to and treated
«I may use professional judgement when I think something should be done differently»
Whether professional and ethical judgement is taken seriously, cf. the requirement of «professional responsibility» in section 4-2 of the Act
«My boundaries for privacy are respected at work»
Personal boundaries, including in informal settings

blocks.text: A low score on the first statement points to how people treat one another. A low score on the second may rather point to management and direction. The third may concern anything from questions about private life to unwanted attention.

blocks.title: A survey is not a reporting channel
blocks.text: An anonymous survey can show that something is wrong, but not who is affected. If you learn that someone is being harassed, follow it up at once under the organisation's routine – do not wait for the next survey.
Small groups, large swings

In a small group, one or two responses can move the figure a great deal. A low result may stem from one serious situation rather than from a general culture. That is no reason to dismiss the figure, but it is a reason to interpret it with care.

Go through the figures with the safety representative before drawing conclusions. Under section 6-2 of the Act, the safety representative is to pay particular attention to whether the employees' psychosocial working environment is safeguarded, and often knows of matters that do not show up in an average. See also the article on [the safety representative's role in the survey](/artikler/verneombudets-rolle-i-kartleggingen). When the result is discussed with employees, the conversation must be set up so that nobody feels singled out.
How offensive behaviour takes hold

The bullying research group at the University of Bergen (Einarsen et al.) has shown that conflicts left unaddressed can develop into bullying, and that early intervention by managers and clear routines prevent this. Low figures on this factor may therefore have a history. Typical causes are:

items: belittling comments or exclusion that nobody steps in to stop
conflicts allowed to grow because nobody acts early
uncertainty about how to report, and what happens next
management that overrides professional judgement without explanation

blocks.text: The routines the law assumes

The employer already has duties that apply here. Under section 2 A-6 of the Act, organisations that regularly employ at least five employees must have written routines for internal whistleblowing. An unsatisfactory working environment is given in section 2 A-1 as an example of a censurable condition that may be reported.

Section 1A-4 of the regulation requires the employer to inform about measures and routines in place for the psychosocial working environment. Arbeidstilsynet gives as an example «routines for handling conflicts, harassment or violence and threats» (our translation). Employees, for their part, have a duty to take part, including by reporting harassment, under section 1A-5 of the regulation. That duty assumes people know how to report.
Three measures with research support

items: **Go through the routine for offensive behaviour in every team.** Show how to report and what happens afterwards. Make sure there is a route that bypasses the immediate manager, since the manager is not always the problem. Such a session takes about 30 minutes per team.

**Let the team agree on ground rules.** In a session of around an hour and a half, the team agrees how they speak to and about each other, and what they do when someone crosses the line. Shared rules make it easier to speak up.
**The manager steps in early.** Belittling comments and exclusion are raised at once, in a calm conversation, before they become a case. This is what the Bergen research points to.

blocks.text: If professional judgement is what scores low, it is management that has to change: who decides what, and are disagreements answered with reasons? That measure belongs with the managers, not in a team seminar.
Follow-up over time

Measure the factor again a few months after the measures are in place, looking at the same statements in the same groups. At the same time, keep an eye on whether the routine is actually being used. There is more on follow-up in the article on [getting from results to measures](/artikler/fra-resultater-til-tiltak).

faktorKollega.title: Support from colleagues: causes and measures | Orgpuls
faktorKollega.description: What does a low score on support from colleagues mean? What the law says about support and help, how to read the figure, common causes and measures.
faktorKollega.h1: When colleagues do not step up for one another: what a low score on peer support means
faktorKollega.lead: A low score on support from colleagues means that many people do not get help when they need it, that knowledge is held back, or that some do not feel part of the team. Support and help in the work is a psychosocial working environment factor under the Working Environment Act, and it protects against other strains. It is best built in the daily work, not at social events.

blocks.text: What peer support involves

Support from colleagues is both practical and personal. It may be a colleague who takes a call when you are stuck, someone who explains an operational system, or someone who asks how it went after a difficult conversation. The Norwegian Labour Inspection Authority (Arbeidstilsynet) describes its range in its commentary on section 1A-1 of the regulation on the performance of work:

Support and help may for example be emotional, such as care, understanding and recognition, or instrumental, such as professional advice, technical assistance or feedback on the work. Support and help may be structurally anchored, for example through the organisation's systems, routines or clear lines of decision-making and responsibility.
blocks.cite: Arbeidstilsynet's commentary on section 1A-1 second paragraph letter d of the regulation (our translation)

blocks.text: The last point is worth noting. Support is not only a question of how helpful individuals are. It can be built into the way work is organised.
Where the factor sits in the law

Section 4-3 second paragraph of the Working Environment Act (arbeidsmiljøloven) lists psychosocial working environment factors, and letter d is «support and help in the work». The same factor appears in section 1A-1 second paragraph letter d of the regulation. Arbeidstilsynet writes that it concerns employees «having the opportunity to get the support they need from, for example, managers and colleagues» (our translation).

The factor is closely tied to another requirement in the same section. Under section 4-3 fourth paragraph, work «shall be designed, as far as possible, to allow contact and communication with other employees in the organisation» (our translation). Without contact, there is little support.
Why support is more than job satisfaction

Research shows that support from colleagues dampens the effect of high demands. The regulation rests on the same understanding. Arbeidstilsynet writes that psychosocial factors «can be both straining and protective» (our translation), and that protective factors may also be relevant to include in the survey. Its commentary on section 1A-2 states:

For example, a high workload and time pressure may increase the risk associated with emotional demands and strains in work with people, while protective factors such as support and help in the work may help to reduce the risk.
blocks.cite: Arbeidstilsynet's commentary on section 1A-2 third paragraph of the regulation (our translation)

blocks.text: A low figure for peer support is therefore most serious in groups that also face high demands. There, the buffer that could otherwise absorb some of the strain is missing.
Help, knowledge and belonging
In surveys built on the QPS Nordic tradition, the factor is measured with a small number of statements that employees rate on a response scale. The statements cover three different aspects:

items.title: Help
items.text: «My colleagues turn up when I need help». Concerns practical help in everyday work.

items.title: Knowledge
items.text: «We share knowledge instead of holding on to it». Concerns whether experience and solutions are passed on.

items.title: Belonging
items.text: «I feel like part of the team». Concerns belonging to the group.

blocks.text: The three aspects are addressed in different ways. Where help is lacking, time and organisation are often the problem. Where knowledge is not shared, it may be about how performance is measured. Where belonging is lacking, the question is who is left outside, and why.
How to read the result

items: **Which statement pulls it down?** An average for the factor hides whether it is help, knowledge or belonging that is failing.
**New starters or long-serving staff?** Low belonging among new starters points to how they are welcomed.

**Who is at work at the same time?** People who rarely work at the same time or place naturally get less support. Read the result alongside [contact and communication](/artikler/kontakt-og-kommunikasjon).
**How high are the demands?** Low support and high strain together mean a higher overall risk. Read more about [workload and time pressure](/artikler/arbeidsmengde-og-tidspress).

blocks.text: Why support is missing
It is rarely ill will that keeps colleagues from helping one another. More often it is the conditions around the work:

items: a high pace, so nobody has time to help
competition or individual targets that make helping a loss for the helper
knowledge held by individuals
groups or cliques that keep to themselves

blocks.text: Several of these are organisational. Arbeidstilsynet writes that measures should, as far as possible, address the causes of the risk, such as organisational or work-related conditions.
Support is built in the work
Research indicates that measures which build support in daily work do better than one-off social events. Three measures are well suited.

**Regular learning meetings.** Half an hour a month in which a colleague shares something they have learnt or solved. Over time, sharing knowledge becomes a habit rather than a coincidence. The measure bears most directly on the statement about sharing knowledge.
**Make asking for help normal.** Managers ask for help themselves and give credit to those who step up for others. This signals that helping is part of the job, not an interruption to it.

**A conversation about how the team helps each other.** In about an hour, the team works out when they need each other most, and how to make it easy to get help. It gives a concrete answer to the question of belonging: who is counted on, and when?

blocks.title: The Christmas party is not the measure
blocks.text: Social events can be pleasant, but they change little about whether people get help on a busy Tuesday. If a social gathering appears in the action plan as the answer to low peer support, it should be accompanied by a measure in the work itself.
Did it improve?

Measure the factor again a couple of months after the measure is in place, with the same statements and in the same group. If the figure stands still, the measure probably did not hit the cause. The next step is then to ask the group again, as described in the article on [going through the results with employees](/artikler/slik-gar-dere-gjennom-resultatene-med-de-ansatte).

faktorMening.title: Recognition and meaning at work | Orgpuls
faktorMening.description: What does a low score on recognition and meaning mean? What the law says about coherence and development at work, reading the figure, causes, measures.
faktorMening.h1: Recognition and meaning: what does it mean when employees do not see the value of their own work?
faktorMening.lead: A low score means that many feel their work does not matter, that their effort goes unnoticed, or that they are not proud of their workplace. The Working Environment Act requires work, as far as possible, to allow employees to see the connection between individual tasks, and the Norwegian Labour Inspection Authority counts recognition as a form of support at work. The research points to two things: showing employees who their work makes a difference for, and giving specific recognition quickly.

blocks.text: Not on the regulation's list, but anchored in the Act

Section 1A-1 of the regulation on the performance of work gives eight examples of psychosocial working environment factors. Meaning and recognition are not among them as separate items. That does not make the factor irrelevant to the employer's duties. The Norwegian Labour Inspection Authority (Arbeidstilsynet) writes in its commentary on the provision:
The wording «among other things» signals that the provision does not give an exhaustive list of psychosocial working environment factors.
blocks.cite: Arbeidstilsynet's commentary on section 1A-1 second paragraph of the regulation (our translation)

blocks.text: The actual anchoring is in section 4-2 second paragraph of the Working Environment Act (arbeidsmiljøloven), which sets requirements for how each employee's work situation is designed. Two of its letters concern what gives work meaning:

items.ref: Section 4-2 second paragraph letter a (our translation)
items.text: arrangements shall be made for the employee to have opportunities for professional and personal development through their work

items.ref: Section 4-2 second paragraph letter d (our translation)
items.text: the employee shall, as far as possible, be given opportunities for variety and to see the connection between individual tasks

blocks.text: Recognition also has a place in the regulation. In the commentary on the factor «support and help in the work», Arbeidstilsynet writes that support may be emotional, «such as care, understanding and recognition» (our translation). Recognition is, in other words, part of a factor the regulation names explicitly.
A protective factor

Much of the work on the psychosocial environment is about strains: time pressure, conflicting demands, demanding service users. Arbeidstilsynet points out that the survey should also look at what protects. Its commentary on section 1A-2 says psychosocial factors «can be both straining and protective» (our translation), and that protective factors may therefore also be relevant to include in the survey.

Meaning and recognition belong here. People can carry more when the work feels meaningful and their effort is seen by someone who matters. A low score is therefore not only a question of job satisfaction; it may mean that an important counterweight to the strains is weakening.
Three statements that measure different things
In surveys built on the QPS Nordic tradition, the factor is measured with a small number of statements that employees rate on a response scale. Examples:

items: «The work I do matters»
«My effort is noticed»
«I am proud to work here»

blocks.text: The first statement concerns the value of the work, the second recognition from others, and the third the relationship to the workplace as a whole. A low average may hide that only one of them is pulling the figure down. That is the statement the measures should target.
What the figure can tell you

Start by looking at which groups stand out. Work in which people rarely see the result of what they do – in support functions far from customers and service users, for example – is a natural place to look. The question is whether employees have any chance to see the connection between their own task and the whole, as section 4-2 of the Act assumes.

Then look at how the factor relates to others. Low meaning combined with low influence may indicate that people neither see what they contribute to nor can affect it. Read more about [participation and control](/artikler/medvirkning-og-kontroll). Low recognition may also be linked to how managers give feedback, which is the subject of the article on [support from managers](/artikler/stotte-fra-leder).
When the connection is lost
The causes of a low score rarely lie in people having lost interest in their profession. More often they concern how the work is organised and how information flows:

items: feedback from customers and service users never reaches those who did the work
praise comes only at the annual appraisal, or is too general to mean anything
tasks are split up so much that the connection disappears
changes stop people doing the job the way they think it should be done

blocks.text: What the research points to

Research shows that contact with the people the work benefits raises both motivation and effort (Grant). The same research base indicates that recognition works best when it is specific and comes quickly. That gives three measures that are easy to explain but need someone to take responsibility for them.
Show who the work makes a difference for

Share feedback from customers and service users with those who actually did the job, not only with management. For employees far from the end user, this may mean telling them how their work was used further on. The measure bears on the statement that the work matters.
Specific recognition the same week
Praise what was actually done, and say why it mattered. Do not wait for the appraisal. This is what shifts the sense that effort is noticed.
A conversation about what the team is proud of

In about an hour, the team shares examples of work they are proud of and what made it possible. The conversation tells the manager what should be protected or done more of, and gives employees a shared picture of what their work is good for.

blocks.title: Rule of thumb
blocks.text: Recognition that is general or comes late has little effect. Say what the person did, why it mattered, and say it while it is still fresh.
Keep track without waiting a year

Measure the factor again a couple of months after the measures are in place, with the same statements and in the same groups. If the figure stands still, the measure probably missed the cause, and the group should be asked again. The approach is described in the article on [getting from results to measures](/artikler/fra-resultater-til-tiltak).

resultaterTilTiltak.title: From survey results to measures | Orgpuls
resultaterTilTiltak.description: After the survey, the employer must assess the risk and put measures in place with employees. How results become measures that can be followed up.
resultaterTilTiltak.h1: How do you get from work environment survey results to measures?
resultaterTilTiltak.lead: The results are used to assess risk, and where the risk calls for it, the employer must draw up plans and put measures in place – in cooperation with employees and their representatives. In practice that means reading the figures systematically, prioritising a few areas, finding the causes with the people concerned, giving each measure an owner and a deadline, and measuring again.

blocks.text: What the rules require after the survey

Since 1 January 2026 the regulation on the performance of work has had its own chapter 1A on the psychosocial working environment. It sets out a single chain: the employer must survey and assess the risk (§ 1A-2), draw up plans and implement measures (§ 1A-3), and give employees and their representatives the information they need about the risk factors and the measures (§ 1A-4).

The chain is not new. It rests on the systematic health and safety work required by section 3-1 of the Working Environment Act (arbeidsmiljøloven), which obliges the employer to identify hazards and problems, assess the risks on that basis, and draw up plans and implement measures to reduce them. What is new is that the duty now applies explicitly to the psychosocial working environment.

On the basis of the risk assessment, the employer shall draw up the necessary plans and implement the necessary measures to eliminate or reduce risk. This shall be done in cooperation with the employees and their representatives.
blocks.cite: Regulation on the performance of work § 1A-3 (our translation)

blocks.text: In its commentary, the Norwegian Labour Inspection Authority (Arbeidstilsynet) says that what counts as a ‘necessary’ measure must be judged against the organisation’s risk profile, including how serious, widespread and long-lasting the risk is. An [employee survey](/artikler/medarbeiderundersokelse) that is not followed by an assessment, and by measures where the assessment calls for them, meets only part of the duty.

items.title: Read the results in a fixed order
Find the cause with the employees
Aim the measure at the cause
Write it so it can be followed up

blocks.text: Read the results in a fixed order
It is tempting to go straight to the lowest number. A more reliable picture comes from looking at three things in turn:

items: **Level** – which factors are low for the organisation as a whole? Those are the shared challenges.
**Spread** – which departments or groups stand out? A low score in one group is often a different matter from a low score everywhere.
**Change** – what has moved since the last survey? A drop often says more than a level that has stayed put.

blocks.text: Then look at the statements behind each factor. A factor such as workload can be low because many say they lack the time to do the job well enough, or because they cannot switch off when the working day is over. Those are two different problems, and they call for different measures.
Each of the eleven factors has its own article, covering what it is about, how a low figure can be read, common causes and measures with research support:

items: [Freedom to speak up](/artikler/ytringsklima)
[Workload and time pressure](/artikler/arbeidsmengde-og-tidspress)
[Conflicting demands](/artikler/motstridende-krav)
[Contact and communication](/artikler/kontakt-og-kommunikasjon)
[Emotional demands](/artikler/emosjonelle-krav)
[Support from manager](/artikler/stotte-fra-leder)
[Participation and control](/artikler/medvirkning-og-kontroll)
[Integrity and dignity](/artikler/integritet-og-verdighet)
[Role clarity](/artikler/rolleklarhet)
[Support from colleagues](/artikler/stotte-fra-kollegaer)
[Recognition and meaning](/artikler/anerkjennelse-og-mening)

blocks.text: How do you prioritise when several scores are low?

The most common mistake is to tackle everything at once. Many measures that nobody follows up achieve less than a few that are actually carried out. Prioritise by risk, using the same considerations Arbeidstilsynet applies to necessary measures: how serious it is, how many it affects, and how long it has lasted.

The factors must also be read together. Section 1A-2 of the regulation requires the risk assessment to cover each factor on its own, how the factors affect one another, and whether together they amount to a risk. Arbeidstilsynet’s own example is that a heavy workload and time pressure can heighten the risk from emotional demands, while support and help at work can reduce it. The commentary concludes:
The overall risk may therefore be higher than the sum of the individual factors.
blocks.cite: Arbeidstilsynet’s commentary on the regulation on the performance of work § 1A-2, third paragraph (our translation)

blocks.text: A group with a low score on [workload and time pressure](/artikler/arbeidsmengde-og-tidspress) and a low score on support should therefore rank above a group with only one of the two.

blocks.title: Rule of thumb
blocks.text: Choose the area with the highest risk, and preferably one that can be acted on quickly. The first takes the working environment seriously. The second shows employees that answering made a difference.
Find the cause with the people concerned

The number shows where there is a problem, not why. The cause is best found with the employees it concerns – for example in a department meeting with the safety representative present. The regulation requires cooperation with employees and their representatives in the survey, in the risk assessment and when measures are drawn up. By representatives, Arbeidstilsynet means the safety representative where there is one, and any union representatives or other employee representatives. Questions that often open the conversation:

items: What do you think lies behind this number?
When do you notice it most – in which situations, which periods?
What would make the biggest difference, and what can we change ourselves?

blocks.text: Never ask who answered what. The survey was anonymous, and the meeting should be anonymous in practice too: talk about the work, not about individuals. Employees have a duty to take part, but Arbeidstilsynet stresses that this duty does not make the employee responsible for solving working environment problems alone. Read more about [going through the results with employees](/artikler/slik-gar-dere-gjennom-resultatene-med-de-ansatte).
Aim the measure at the cause, not the symptom

Arbeidstilsynet writes that measures should as far as possible address the causes of the risk, such as organisational or work-related conditions. A measure may reduce the extent of a risk factor or introduce something that compensates for it. A stress management course does little if the real problem is that staffing does not match the workload.
Write the measure so that it can be followed up
A measure without an owner is a wish. Word each one so that someone can later check whether it was carried out and whether it had an effect:

head: Part
Weak
Good
rows: A fixed 15-minute stand-up on Mondays and Thursdays
A higher score on the statement about where one’s own responsibility ends, at the next survey

blocks.text: Say what will happen – and what will not

Section 1A-4 of the regulation requires that employees and their representatives receive the information they need about psychosocial risk factors and about the measures and procedures in place. According to Arbeidstilsynet, this information should be given regularly and when things change, and where the organisation has a working environment committee, that committee is also a relevant forum.

Explain what you found, what you have chosen to do, and what you are leaving for now – and why. The reasons for what is not prioritised are often left out, yet without them employees cannot tell a deliberate choice from nothing happening.
Measure again, and document as you go

A new, [short survey](/artikler/pulsundersokelse) of the factors where measures are under way, a couple of months later, shows whether the figures have moved. If they have not, that is a finding in itself: the measure probably missed the cause, and it is time to go back to the group. Read more about [how often to measure the working environment](/artikler/hvor-ofte-bor-dere-male-arbeidsmiljoet).

The survey and the risk assessment must be documented and form part of the organisation’s systematic health and safety work (§ 1A-2 letter d). Arbeidstilsynet writes that the documentation must be set down in writing in a way that makes it possible to follow up the work on the psychosocial working environment, and that its scope and form should suit the organisation’s nature, size and risk profile. Paper, a spreadsheet or a digital tool will all do. What matters is being able to show what you found, how you assessed it, which measures you chose and what happened next. Read more about [the risk assessment](/artikler/risikovurdering-av-psykososialt-arbeidsmiljo).

gjennomgang.title: Going through survey results with employees | Orgpuls
gjennomgang.description: The meeting after the employee survey: what the rules require, when to hold it, a one-hour agenda, questions that open the conversation and four pitfalls.
gjennomgang.h1: How do you go through the results with your employees?
gjennomgang.lead: Go through the results with the group they concern within a couple of weeks, together with the safety representative. Show the figures as they are, spend most of the time finding causes and measures together, and write down what you agree. The meeting is where the cooperation the regulation requires actually happens – and it decides whether people answer next time.

blocks.text: What do the rules require?

Chapter 1A of the regulation on the performance of work, in force since 1 January 2026, requires the mapping, the risk assessment and the measures to be carried out in cooperation with employees and their representatives, and requires them to be informed about the risk factors and the measures. It does not say the results must be reviewed in a meeting, but a meeting is the most direct way to meet both requirements.

items.ref: Regulation on the performance of work § 1A-3 (our translation)
items.text: On the basis of the risk assessment, the employer shall draw up the necessary plans and implement the necessary measures to eliminate or reduce risk. This shall be done in cooperation with the employees and their representatives.

The employer shall ensure that employees and their representatives receive the necessary information about risk factors in the psychosocial working environment and about measures and routines that have been implemented.

blocks.text: According to the Norwegian Labour Inspection Authority (Arbeidstilsynet), the information must be sufficient and relevant, so that employees and their representatives understand what the psychosocial risks in the organisation are and how they are being handled. Representatives means the safety representative where there is one, and any union representatives. Where the organisation has a working environment committee, Arbeidstilsynet notes that it too is a relevant body for information and dialogue.

Employees, for their part, have a duty to participate under section 1A-5 of the regulation and section 2-3 of the Working Environment Act (arbeidsmiljøloven), including in mappings, risk assessments and measures. Arbeidstilsynet stresses that this duty does not make the employee responsible for solving working environment problems alone. The responsibility lies with the employer. It is worth saying so plainly in the meeting.
Why the meeting matters more than the report

A report tells you what people answered. The meeting is where they see whether anyone listened. The figures show where things fall short, but rarely why. The people doing the work know, and the meeting is where that knowledge comes out.
When should the meeting be held?

Within a couple of weeks of the survey closing. The longer you wait, the less people connect the figures with what they answered. Book the time before the survey goes out, so it does not get pushed back.

Go through the figures with the safety representative and any union representatives first, so they know them before the rest of the group. Read more about [the safety representative's role in the mapping](/artikler/verneombudets-rolle-i-kartleggingen).
Who should take part?

Go through the results with the group they concern – the whole company in a small business, otherwise department by department. The manager leads the meeting, and the safety representative takes part. If the result is about the manager, for instance a low score on support from the manager, it can be wise for the safety representative or another manager to lead that part.
A one-hour agenda

items.title: Why we ran the survey, and how many answered
What is going well – with figures
What is weakest – with figures, without explaining it away
Groups of three or four: what lies behind it, and what would help?
Choose two or three things to act on, and agree when you will follow up

blocks.text: Start with what is going well. Not to soften the blow, but because those are findings too. Arbeidstilsynet points out that psychosocial factors can be protective as well as straining. What works tells you what you must take care to keep.
Questions that open the conversation

items: Do you recognise yourselves in this figure?
What do you think lies behind it?
When do you notice this most in your working day?
What would make the biggest difference – and what can we do ourselves?
What should we stop doing?

blocks.text: Small groups get more people talking than a round in plenary. Ask the groups to write their answers down, so nobody has to stand behind a view alone.
Look for causes in the work, not in people

In its commentary on section 1A-3, Arbeidstilsynet writes that measures should, as far as possible, target the causes of the risk, such as organisational or work-related conditions. A low score on workload is rarely about people working badly; it is about staffing, priorities or tasks that have grown.

Look, too, at how the findings fit together. Arbeidstilsynet's example is that high workload and time pressure can amplify the risk from emotional demands, while support and help can reduce it. Two middling figures may therefore together be a more serious finding than one low one. See [risk assessment of the psychosocial working environment](/artikler/risikovurdering-av-psykososialt-arbeidsmiljo).
Four things to avoid

items.title: Do not look for who
items.text: «Who is it that thinks this?» breaks anonymity in practice, even though the survey was anonymous. Talk about the work, not about people.

items.title: Do not explain it away
items.text: «It was a busy period» may be true, but it is not the manager's call. Let the group say whether they recognise it.

items.title: Do not promise everything
items.text: It is better to say no to something and explain why than to promise ten things and do two.

items.title: Do not show groups that are too small
items.text: If only three in a group answered, it is easy to guess who thought what. Show the figures for a larger unit instead. See [what anonymity requires](/artikler/anonym-medarbeiderundersokelse).

blocks.text: After the meeting

Write down what you agreed, with owners and deadlines, and send it to everyone – including those who were not there. Say what you have chosen not to do, and why. This is documentation too: Arbeidstilsynet writes that the mapping, the risk assessment and their results must be set down in writing in a way that makes it possible to follow up the work on the psychosocial working environment.

When the next survey comes round – a new mapping or a short [pulse survey](/artikler/pulsundersokelse) – start by telling people what happened after the last one. People answer when they see it makes a difference. Read more about [getting from results to measures](/artikler/fra-resultater-til-tiltak).

risikovurdering.title: Risk assessment of the psychosocial environment | Orgpuls
risikovurdering.description: How to assess psychosocial risk under § 1A-2 of the Norwegian regulation: what must be assessed, a four-step approach and what has to be documented.
risikovurdering.h1: How do you carry out a risk assessment of the psychosocial working environment?
risikovurdering.lead: A risk assessment interprets what the mapping has found: which psychosocial conditions may harm employees' health, safety or welfare, how serious that is, and what must be done first. Section 1A-2 of the regulation on the performance of work requires the factors to be assessed separately, in combination and as a whole, in the short and the long term. The assessment must be made together with employees and their representatives, and documented.

blocks.text: What does the regulation require?

On the basis of the mapping, the employer shall assess the risk of harmful effects, both in the short and the long term. The risk assessment shall cover the individual factors separately, how they affect one another, and whether together they amount to a risk.
blocks.cite: Regulation on the performance of work § 1A-2, second and third paragraphs (our translation)

blocks.text: The mapping and risk assessment must also be carried out together with employees and their representatives, adapted to the organisation's nature, activities and size, repeated regularly and when things change, and documented as part of systematic health, safety and environment work (§ 1A-2, fourth paragraph).

The duty is not new. Under section 3-1(2)(c) of the Working Environment Act (arbeidsmiljøloven), the employer must «map hazards and problems and on this basis assess the risk factors in the undertaking» (our translation). The regulation makes clear that this also applies to the psychosocial working environment, and how the assessment is to be made.
How does mapping differ from risk assessment?

Mapping gathers information: how do employees experience their workload, role clarity, support and the other factors? Risk assessment interprets it: which of these conditions could harm health, safety or welfare, how likely is that, and how serious could it be? A [questionnaire](/artikler/medarbeiderundersokelse) on its own is therefore not a risk assessment. The risk assessment is what the organisation does with the findings afterwards.
What does «fully satisfactory» mean in the assessment?

The yardstick is that the psychosocial working environment must be fully satisfactory. The Norwegian Labour Inspection Authority (Arbeidstilsynet) describes this as a legal standard to be judged concretely, taking into account among other things the organisation's nature, activities and risk profile. As a rule, the assessment concerns the working environment as a whole and the organisation's systems, structure and governance – not individuals. Individual experiences and strain can still be important indicators of conditions in organisation, management or governance.

The regulation sets no prohibitions, thresholds or specific requirements for the individual factors. Some factors, such as emotional demands and time pressure, can be a natural part of the work. The question is not whether the strain exists, but whether it becomes too great.
Which three things must be assessed?

items.title: Each factor on its own
items.text: How weak is the factor, how many people does it affect, and how long has it lasted?

items.title: How the factors affect each other
items.text: Arbeidstilsynet notes that a high workload and time pressure can heighten the risk from emotional demands, while support and help at work can help reduce it.

items.title: The overall risk
items.text: Several moderately weak factors in the same group can together amount to a higher risk than a single weak factor.

blocks.text: The overall risk may therefore be greater than the sum of the individual factors.
blocks.cite: Arbeidstilsynet's commentary on § 1A-2, third paragraph (our translation)

blocks.text: Arbeidstilsynet also points out that factors can act as both strains and protections. A good climate for speaking up and good support are not merely the absence of risk, but conditions that keep risk down. They therefore belong in the assessment. A single satisfaction score does not separate what strains from what protects; see [why a job satisfaction survey is not enough](/artikler/trivselsundersokelse).
Why both the short and the long term?

According to Arbeidstilsynet, the risk assessment must cover both acute strain and strain that can build up over time, such as prolonged stress. Some things are acute: violence and threats, harassment, a conflict that has become entrenched. Others work slowly: a workload that never eases, roles that are never clarified. The latter are easier to overlook, because no single incident brings them to light.
A four-step approach
The regulation does not prescribe a particular method. A simple four-step sequence might look like this:

items.title: Flag
items.text: the factors and groups that score weakly, or that have fallen since the previous mapping.

items.title: Assess
items.text: each of them: how serious could it become, how many does it affect, and how long has it lasted? Use both the statements behind the figures and what employees say.

items.title: Look for connections
items.text: do some factors reinforce each other in the same group? Is anything protective?

items.title: Conclude
items.text: with a risk level and a brief justification, and let the conclusion determine which measures come first.

blocks.title: A risk level is an aid, not a legal requirement
blocks.text: The regulation sets no thresholds. If an organisation uses levels such as low, medium and high, they are a way of setting priorities. The reasoning – why something is judged high or low risk – matters more than the label.

The assessment must be made together with employees and their representatives. The safety representative sees everyday work from a different angle than management, and under section 6-2 of the Act must be consulted on measures. Read more about [the safety representative's role in mapping](/artikler/verneombudets-rolle-i-kartleggingen).
When must the risk assessment be repeated?

Regularly, and whenever changes may affect the risk. Arbeidstilsynet mentions changes in organisation, staffing, tasks, management, technology, working hours or operating conditions. Section 3-1(2)(d) of the Act also requires the employer, when planning and carrying out changes, to assess whether the working environment will meet the Act's requirements. A reorganisation is therefore a reason to look at the psychosocial working environment before it takes effect, not only afterwards. Read more about [how often the working environment should be measured](/artikler/hvor-ofte-bor-dere-male-arbeidsmiljoet).
What must be documented?

The documentation must make it possible to follow up the work and serve as the basis for measures. Its scope and form may be adapted to the organisation's nature, size and risk profile. As a minimum it should record:

items: what was mapped, when, and who took part
which factors and groups were assessed, and the conclusion for each
the reasoning – why something was judged high or low risk
which measures the assessment led to, with a person responsible and a deadline

blocks.text: From assessment to measures

Under § 1A-3 of the regulation, the employer must, on the basis of the risk assessment, draw up the necessary plans and implement the necessary measures to remove or reduce risk. What counts as «necessary» must, according to Arbeidstilsynet, be judged concretely from the severity, extent and duration of the risk. Measures may reduce the extent of a risk factor or compensate for it, and should as far as possible target the causes. Read more about [moving from results to measures](/artikler/fra-resultater-til-tiltak).
