arbeidsmengde.title: Workload and time pressure: causes and measures | Orgpuls
arbeidsmengde.description: A low workload score means work and time no longer match over time. What the rules require, how to read the score and which measures tend to work.
arbeidsmengde.h1: What does a low score on workload and time pressure mean – and what can the employer do?
arbeidsmengde.lead: A low score means many people feel the work they are expected to do does not match the time and resources they have, or that they cannot recover after the working day. Being busy is not unlawful, but a lasting imbalance is a risk the employer must assess and act on – preferably by changing how the work is organised.

blocks.text: Busy is allowed – too much strain is not

Workload and time pressure is one of the psychosocial factors named in section 4-3(2) of the Working Environment Act (arbeidsmiljøloven). Since 2026 it has also appeared in section 1A-1 of the regulation on the performance of work. The wording is precise: the factor is not the amount of work as such, but the imbalance between the work and the time.

items.text: workload and time pressure that involve an imbalance between the work to be done and the time available

The organisation, arrangement and management of the work, working hours arrangements, pay systems, including the use of performance-related pay, technology etc. shall be such that employees are not exposed to adverse physical or mental strain and so that safety considerations are attended to.

blocks.text: In its commentary on the regulation, the Norwegian Labour Inspection Authority (Arbeidstilsynet) explains that the factor can mean having to work a great deal, for long hours or at high speed, without enough breaks or recovery. At the same time it stresses that busy periods are not in themselves the problem:
It is not forbidden to be busy or to have a demanding job, but the employer must ensure that the strain does not become too great.
blocks.cite: Arbeidstilsynet’s commentary on the regulation on the performance of work § 1A-1 (our translation)

blocks.text: The regulation sets no threshold. What is too much has to be judged in each organisation – which is exactly why a survey is needed.
Three questions that pick up the imbalance
Surveys built on the QPS Nordic tradition usually measure the factor with a few statements that employees respond to. Examples of such statements:

items: ‘My workload is manageable over time’
‘I have enough time to do the job well enough’
‘I can switch off from work when the working day is over’

blocks.text: The statements capture three sides of the same relationship. The first asks whether the load is sustainable over time, not just in a busy week. The second is about quality: whether there is time to do the work well enough. The third concerns recovery – what Arbeidstilsynet refers to as sufficient breaks or recovery.
How to interpret a low score
An overall score for the factor says there is a problem but little about which one. Before choosing measures, put four questions to the results:

items: **Which statement pulls it down?** A low score on having time to do the job well points to tasks and staffing. A low score on switching off points to working hours, availability and expectations outside the working day.
**Who does it affect?** A department that stands out often has a local cause – an unfilled post, a new task, a seasonal peak.
**Has it changed?** A drop since the last survey means something has happened, and that is often easier to trace than the cause of a low level that has persisted for a long time.
**What surrounds it?** Low support from the manager or unclear roles in the same group make the load harder to carry.

blocks.text: The last point is grounded in the regulation. Under section 1A-2 the risk assessment must cover each factor on its own, how the factors affect one another, and whether together they amount to a risk. Arbeidstilsynet itself uses workload as the example: a heavy workload and time pressure can heighten the risk from [emotional demands](/artikler/emosjonelle-krav), while support and help at work can reduce it.
Where the strain usually comes from

According to Arbeidstilsynet, the imbalance can arise when an employee has many, large or demanding tasks and at the same time too little time, or otherwise insufficient resources, to carry them out. It also points out that organisational matters such as staffing, priorities and the organisation of working hours can have a major effect on the psychosocial working environment. In practice, the same causes recur:

items: staffing that does not fit the tasks, or absence that is not covered
unclear priorities, so that everything is equally urgent
interruptions and tasks arriving from many directions at once
deadlines set without asking the people who will do the work
new tasks added without anything being taken away
unspoken expectations of being available after hours

blocks.text: Measures with research support

Arbeidstilsynet writes that measures should as far as possible address the causes, such as organisational or work-related conditions. For workload, that means measures aimed at the individual, such as courses in stress or time management, are rarely enough on their own. Research points the same way: measures in this area draw on the demand–control–support model (Karasek) and the job demands–resources model (Bakker and Demerouti), which view strain in the light of the resources and support employees have. Measures work best when the employees themselves help find the solutions.
A regular meeting on what has to give

The manager and the team go through everything on the table and agree on what must wait or be dropped. The result is a single written, ranked list. Such a meeting takes about 20 minutes a week and makes the question ‘what do we stop doing?’ as ordinary as ‘what do we do?’.
Tracking down the time thieves

The team logs its work for a week and then spends a couple of hours finding tasks that can be removed, simplified or moved. The session should end in concrete decisions – at least three changes – before people leave, or it becomes an exercise without consequences.
Clear limits on availability

The organisation agrees when it is acceptable to send and answer messages outside working hours. It is a single decision, but it only works if the manager keeps to it as well. The measure speaks directly to the statement about switching off after work.

blocks.title: When it is urgent
blocks.text: If someone is at risk of becoming ill from the strain, do not wait for the next survey. Raise it with the person concerned and with the safety representative, and act straight away.
Did it work?

Measures on workload tend to show quickly – or not at all. Ask the same statements again a couple of months after the measure is in place, in the group concerned. If the score has not moved, the measure probably missed the cause, and it is time to go back to the group and ask again.

Remember too that the regulation requires a new survey and risk assessment when changes occur that may affect the risks. Arbeidstilsynet mentions, among other things, changes in staffing, tasks and working hours – exactly the things that most often shift the workload. Read more about [turning results into measures](/artikler/fra-resultater-til-tiltak).

nyeRegler2026.title: New psychosocial work environment rules, 2026 | Orgpuls
nyeRegler2026.description: Since 1 January 2026 Norwegian regulations have a chapter on the psychosocial working environment. What is new, and what it requires of employers.
nyeRegler2026.h1: What is new in the rules on the psychosocial working environment from 2026?
nyeRegler2026.lead: Since 1 January 2026 the regulation on the performance of work has had its own chapter 1A on the psychosocial working environment. The chapter spells out duties that already followed from the Working Environment Act: the employer must map psychosocial factors, assess the risk, put measures in place and inform employees – together with them and their representatives. What is new is mainly that the regulation says more clearly how.

blocks.text: What changed on 1 January 2026?

Chapter 1A was added to the regulation on the performance of work by a regulation of 16 December 2025 (no. 2615) and came into force on 1 January 2026. On the same day an amendment to section 4-3 of the Working Environment Act (arbeidsmiljøloven), passed by an act of 20 June 2025 (no. 37), also came into force. Section 4-3 is the Act's core provision on the psychosocial working environment.

In its commentary, the Norwegian Labour Inspection Authority (Arbeidstilsynet) describes the chapter as giving concrete form to sections 4-1 and 4-3 of the Act, and to the employer's duty under section 3-1 to carry out systematic health, safety and environment work. The duty to map and assess risks in the working environment existed before, among other places in section 7-1 of the regulation on organisation, management and employee participation. The new chapter makes clear that the duty also covers the psychosocial working environment, and describes how the work is to be done.

items.title: The Working Environment Act
items.text: The Act requires systematic health and safety work (§ 3-1) and a fully sound psychosocial working environment (§ 4-3).

items.title: § 4-3 amended
items.text: The section on the psychosocial working environment is amended by Act of 16 June 2023 no. 37.

items.title: Chapter 1A in force
items.text: The regulation on the performance of work gains its own chapter on the psychosocial working environment, and § 4-3 is amended again.

blocks.text: Psychosocial working environment conditions shall form an integrated part of the organisation's ongoing risk management.
blocks.cite: Arbeidstilsynet's commentary on § 1A-2 of the regulation on the performance of work (our translation)

blocks.text: What do the five sections say?

head: Section
Subject
Core of the requirement
rows: A fully satisfactory psychosocial working environment
Work is to be organised, planned and carried out so that the psychosocial working environment is fully satisfactory.
The employer must map the factors and assess the risk of harmful effects in the short and long term.
The necessary plans and measures to remove or reduce risk, together with employees.
Employees and their representatives must receive the necessary information and training.
The employee's duty to take part
Employees must take part in the work, cf. section 2-3 of the Act.

blocks.text: Which factors does the regulation name?
The second paragraph of § 1A-1 lists psychosocial working environment factors. According to Arbeidstilsynet, the examples are taken from sections 4-3 and 4-2(2)(c) of the Act:

items: unclear or conflicting demands and expectations at work
emotional demands and strain in work with people
workload and time pressure that create an imbalance between the work to be done and the time available
support and help at work
the opportunity for contact and communication with other employees in the organisation
harassment, including sexual harassment
violence and threats
autonomy and influence at work

blocks.text: The words «among other things» mean that the list is not exhaustive. Arbeidstilsynet also points out that the provision does not set a minimum of factors every organisation must map. That depends on the nature, activities and risk profile of the organisation, although the factors will be relevant to a great many workplaces.

blocks.title: Being busy is not unlawful
blocks.text: The regulation sets no thresholds for the individual factors. Arbeidstilsynet writes: «It is not forbidden to be busy or to have a demanding job, but the employer must make sure that the strain does not become too great» (our translation).
What does the regulation require of the mapping?
The employer shall map psychosocial working environment factors that may affect the employees' health, safety or welfare.
blocks.cite: Regulation on the performance of work § 1A-2, first paragraph (our translation)

blocks.text: On the basis of the mapping, the employer must assess the risk of harmful effects «both in the short and the long term». The risk assessment must cover each factor separately, how the factors affect one another, and whether together they amount to a risk. Arbeidstilsynet notes that factors can act as both strains and protections, and that protective factors may also be worth including. The requirement concerns the factors in the work, not how content employees are – read more about [job satisfaction surveys](/artikler/trivselsundersokelse).
The fourth paragraph sets four requirements for how the work is done. The mapping and risk assessment shall be

items.text: carried out in cooperation with the employees and their representatives (our translation)
adapted to the nature, activities and size of the organisation
repeated regularly and whenever changes occur that may affect the risk situation in the organisation
documented and made part of the organisation's systematic health, safety and environment work

blocks.text: The regulation sets no fixed interval. According to Arbeidstilsynet, the organisation's risk profile, structure and ways of working determine how and how often the work is done. As examples of changes that call for a new round, it lists changes in organisation, staffing, tasks, management, technology, working hours or operating conditions. Read more in [How often should you measure the working environment?](/artikler/hvor-ofte-bor-dere-male-arbeidsmiljoet)
What has to happen after the mapping?

Section 1A-3 ties the mapping to action: «On the basis of the risk assessment, the employer shall draw up the necessary plans and implement the necessary measures to remove or reduce risk» (our translation). This, too, must be done together with the employees and their representatives. Arbeidstilsynet writes that measures should as far as possible target the causes of the risk, such as organisational or work-related conditions.

Under § 1A-4, employees and their representatives must receive the necessary information about the risk factors and about the measures and routines put in place, along with any training required. The results of a mapping cannot simply stay with management. Section 1A-5 works the other way: employees have a duty to take part, for instance in mapping, risk assessments and measures. Arbeidstilsynet stresses that this does not make any individual responsible for solving working environment problems alone.
Who has to be involved?

By employees' representatives, Arbeidstilsynet means the safety representative (verneombud), where the organisation has one, and any union or other employee representatives. Under section 6-2 of the Act, the safety representative must ensure that the psychosocial working environment is taken care of, and must be consulted when measures are planned and carried out. Cooperation therefore means more than presenting the results afterwards. Read more about [the safety representative's role in mapping](/artikler/verneombudets-rolle-i-kartleggingen).
What should an organisation do now?

An organisation that already maps its psychosocial working environment seldom needs to start again. A sensible first step is to hold current practice up against the four requirements in the fourth paragraph of § 1A-2. Three questions reveal most gaps:

items: When was the psychosocial working environment last mapped and risk-assessed, and has that been done since later changes in organisation or staffing?
Were the safety representative and union representatives involved in the planning, and not only in the presentation of the results?
Can the organisation show in writing what was found, how the risk was assessed and which measures followed?

blocks.text: According to Arbeidstilsynet, the documentation requirement means that the mapping, the risk assessment and their results must be set down in writing in a way that allows the work to be followed up. Scope and form may be adapted to the organisation's nature, size and risk profile. It is often easiest to write things down as you go: what was mapped, what was assessed, which measures were chosen and who is responsible for them.
Do the rules apply to small organisations?

Yes. The duty applies to every employer, but the mapping and risk assessment must be adapted to the organisation's nature, activities and size. An organisation with ten employees can therefore keep it simpler than one with 200, but it cannot skip it.
Is an annual employee survey enough?

A survey can be a central part of the mapping, but it does not meet the requirements on its own. Without a risk assessment, measures, information to employees and documentation, several of the steps the regulation describes are missing. Safety inspections and one-to-one appraisal conversations can provide knowledge that a questionnaire does not capture.

kravKartlegging.title: Requirements for mapping the work environment | Orgpuls
kravKartlegging.description: Employers must map the psychosocial working environment, assess risk and act. Where the duty is found, who takes part and what must be documented.
kravKartlegging.h1: What are the requirements for mapping the psychosocial working environment?
kravKartlegging.lead: Every employer must map the psychosocial factors that may affect employees' health, safety or welfare, assess the risk and put the necessary measures in place. The duty follows from section 3-1 of the Working Environment Act (arbeidsmiljøloven) and is set out in more detail in chapter 1A of the regulation on the performance of work. The work must be done together with employees and their representatives, repeated regularly and documented.

blocks.text: Where is the requirement found?

items.text: To ensure that the employee's health, environment and safety are safeguarded, the employer shall ensure that systematic health, environment and safety work is carried out at all levels of the undertaking. This shall be done in cooperation with the employees and their union representatives. (our translation)
map hazards and problems and on this basis assess the risk factors in the undertaking, prepare plans and implement measures to reduce the risk (our translation)

Work shall be organised, planned and carried out so that the psychosocial working environment factors in the undertaking are fully satisfactory with regard to the employees' health, safety and welfare. (our translation)

items.ref: Regulation on the performance of work § 1A-2(1)
items.text: The employer shall map psychosocial working environment factors that may affect the employees' health, safety or welfare. (our translation)
The safety representative shall in particular ensure … that the employees' psychosocial working environment is taken care of. (our translation)

blocks.text: The Norwegian Labour Inspection Authority (Arbeidstilsynet) describes § 1A-2 of the regulation as giving concrete form to section 3-1 of the Act and to section 5 of the internal control regulation. Section 7-1 of the regulation on organisation, management and employee participation already required mapping and risk assessment of the working environment in general; chapter 1A makes clear that this also covers the psychosocial side. Read more about [the changes that came into force in 2026](/artikler/nye-regler-psykososialt-arbeidsmiljo-2026).
What has to be mapped?

Section 1A-1 of the regulation names, among other things, unclear or conflicting demands and expectations, emotional demands and strain in work with people, workload and time pressure, support and help at work, the opportunity for contact and communication with others, harassment, violence and threats, and autonomy and influence. In addition, section 4-3(3) of the Act requires work to be arranged so that the employee's integrity and dignity are safeguarded.

The list is not exhaustive, nor is it a minimum everyone must cover. According to Arbeidstilsynet, which factors an organisation must map depends on «the nature, activities and risk profile of the organisation» (our translation), though the factors named will be relevant to a great many. The mapping should also bring out what protects: Arbeidstilsynet points out that factors can act as both strains and protections. It is the factors that are to be mapped, not satisfaction; see [what a job satisfaction survey measures](/artikler/trivselsundersokelse).
How must the mapping be done?
The fourth paragraph of § 1A-2 sets four requirements that apply to both the mapping and the risk assessment. Arbeidstilsynet's commentary explains what each of them involves.

head: Requirement in the regulation
What it involves
rows: In cooperation with employees and their representatives
The representatives are the safety representative, where there is one, and any union or other employee representatives.
Adapted to the organisation's nature, activities and size
Scope, methods and content are adapted. Risk profile, structure and ways of working determine how and how often.
Repeated regularly and when things change
Not a one-off exercise. Changes in organisation, staffing, tasks, management, technology, working hours or operating conditions may call for a new round.
Documented and part of HSE work
Set down in writing so that the work can be followed up, and the basis for measures under § 1A-3.

blocks.text: The regulation does not prescribe a method. An anonymous [questionnaire](/artikler/medarbeiderundersokelse) is the most common, and it can be run on paper, in a spreadsheet or with a digital tool. Safety inspections and appraisal conversations can provide knowledge a questionnaire does not capture. Arbeidstilsynet notes that individual employees' experiences and strain may be relevant as indicators of conditions in organisation, management or governance.
What happens after the mapping?

blocks.center: In cooperation with employees and their representatives

items.title: Map
items.text: Gather knowledge about the factors relevant to the organisation, together with the safety representative and union representatives.

items.title: Assess the risk
items.text: Assess the factors one by one, how they affect each other, and whether together they amount to a risk – in the short and the long term. Read more about [risk assessment of the psychosocial working environment](/artikler/risikovurdering-av-psykososialt-arbeidsmiljo).

items.title: Put measures in place
items.text: Section 1A-3 requires the necessary plans and measures to remove or reduce risk. According to Arbeidstilsynet, measures should as far as possible target the causes, such as organisational or work-related conditions.

items.title: Inform and follow up
items.text: Employees and their representatives must receive the necessary information about the risk factors and the measures (§ 1A-4). Whether a measure worked only becomes clear when the organisation maps again.

blocks.title: Few measures, carried through
blocks.text: A mapping that ends with ten measures often ends with none. Two or three prioritised measures, each with a named person responsible and a deadline, are easier to carry out and to follow up.
Who has to be involved?

Mapping is the employer's responsibility, but it must be done together with employees and their representatives. In practice the safety representative and union representatives help plan the mapping, see the results and take part when measures are chosen.

Organisations that regularly employ at least 30 people must have a working environment committee. In organisations with between 10 and 30 employees, one must be set up if either party demands it (section 7-1). Among other things, the committee deals with establishing and maintaining systematic HSE work, so the mapping naturally belongs on its agenda.

Employees, for their part, have a duty to take part under § 1A-5 of the regulation, including in mapping exercises. It is good practice to explain in advance what the mapping will be used for, how anonymity is protected and when the results will be available.
What should the documentation contain?
The regulation says the mapping and risk assessment must be documented, but not in what form. Good documentation answers the questions an inspector or a new safety representative would ask:

items: when the mapping was done, and who helped plan it
how it was done: method, who was asked, and the response rate
what came out, factor by factor
how the risk was assessed, and what was prioritised
which measures were chosen, with a person responsible and a deadline
what the follow-up showed – whether the measures worked
minutes of the discussion with the safety and union representatives, and how employees were told about the results

blocks.text: Common mistakes

items: **Mapping without follow-up.** The findings are presented and nothing happens. The regulation requires mapping to lead to a risk assessment and the necessary measures.
**Measures without an owner.** «We will get better at communicating» is an intention. «The department head introduces a weekly stand-up meeting from 1 March» is a measure.
**No new measurement.** A measure is not finished until the organisation has seen whether it worked.
**Small, identifiable groups.** Figures for a department of three are not anonymous. Set a minimum group size for reporting, and keep to it.
**No documentation.** If the organisation cannot show what it did, the work is hard to follow up.

blocks.text: What can happen if the requirement is not met?

Arbeidstilsynet can issue orders to enforce the provisions in and under chapters 3 to 11 of the Act, which include sections 3-1 and 4-3 (section 18-6). An order may carry a running coercive fine until it is complied with (section 18-7). The authority can also impose an administrative fine if someone acting on behalf of the organisation has breached such provisions negligently or wilfully. The fine can be up to 50 times the National Insurance basic amount or four per cent of annual turnover, whichever is higher (section 18-10).

items.title: Order
items.text: In writing, with a deadline for when it must be carried out.

items.title: Coercive fine
items.text: Running or as a one-off fine, until the order is complied with.

items.title: Infringement fine
items.text: For negligent or wilful breaches: up to 50 times the basic amount or four per cent of annual turnover.

sporsmal.title: Employee survey: which questions to ask | Orgpuls
sporsmal.description: Which questions belong in an employee survey? The factors Norwegian rules point to, example statements, the scale and why fewer questions are better.
sporsmal.h1: Which questions belong in an employee survey?
sporsmal.lead: An employee survey used to map the psychosocial working environment should cover the factors the Working Environment Act and its regulation point to: demands and expectations, workload, emotional strain, support, influence, contact, respect, harassment and violence. The questions work best as short statements about one's own working day, answered on a five-point scale – and there should be no more of them than the organisation is willing to follow up.

blocks.text: What do the rules say about content?

Neither the Working Environment Act (arbeidsmiljøloven) nor the regulation provides a ready-made list of questions for an [employee survey](/artikler/medarbeiderundersokelse). But section 1A-1 of the regulation on the performance of work, in force since 1 January 2026, gives examples of the psychosocial factors involved. The examples are taken from sections 4-3 and 4-2(2)(c) of the Act.

items.ref: Regulation on the performance of work § 1A-1(2) (our translation)
items.text: Psychosocial working environment factors include, among others, a. unclear or conflicting demands and expectations in the work b. emotional demands and strain in work with people c. workload and time pressure that entail an imbalance between the work to be done and the time available d. support and help in the work e. the opportunity for contact and communication with other employees in the undertaking f. harassment, including sexual harassment g. violence and threats h. self-determination and influence in the work.
The work shall be arranged so that the employee's integrity and dignity are safeguarded.

blocks.text: The list is not a minimum. In its commentary on the regulation, the Norwegian Labour Inspection Authority (Arbeidstilsynet) writes that the provision does not set a minimum for which factors every organisation must map and assess, and that this depends on the nature, activities and risk profile of the organisation. At the same time, Arbeidstilsynet stresses that the factors will be relevant to a great many organisations.

Nor does the survey need to ask only about what causes strain. The commentary on section 1A-2 notes that factors can be both straining and protective, and that protective factors may therefore also be relevant to include in the mapping. Support, influence and recognition belong here.
The topics, with example statements

The table shows how the factors can be covered in eleven topics, with one example statement for each. The statements come from a survey built in the QPS Nordic tradition, where each topic is measured by several statements.

head: Topic
Basis
Example statement
rows: «I know what is expected of me in my job»
«The demands from different quarters hang together»
«I am rarely left alone in emotionally demanding situations»
«I get support from my manager when the job becomes demanding»
«My colleagues turn up when I need help»
«I have influence over how I carry out my work»
«I have the opportunity for contact with colleagues during the working day»
«I am met with respect regardless of who I am»
Not on the list; cf. the right to blow the whistle, the Act § 2 A-1
«I can report censurable conditions without fearing consequences»

blocks.text: With several statements per topic, the result depends less on how people read a single sentence. Support from the manager can also be measured with «My manager knows enough about what my job actually involves» and «I can raise difficult matters with my manager».

blocks.title: Write statements, not questions
blocks.text: «I know what is expected of me in my job» is easier to answer honestly than «Is your role clear?». The statement is concrete, is about one's own experience and has no right answer.
Harassment, violence and threats

The regulation names harassment, including sexual harassment, and violence and threats. These fit poorly as statements in an overall index, because what matters is whether something has happened. An example of a separate question: «Have you experienced or witnessed offensive behaviour, harassment or bullying at work in the last twelve months?»

The answers should only be shown as a count for the whole organisation, never per department. Where the work involves contact with patients, clients or customers, there is also reason to ask about violence and threats, since section 4-3(6) of the Act requires employees to be protected against them as far as possible.

A survey does not replace whistleblowing routines. Under section 2 A-6 of the Act, organisations that regularly employ at least five people must have written routines for internal whistleblowing, and respondents should be told where to report a concern.
Questions outside the topics

items: **Recommendation:** «How likely is it that you would recommend us as a workplace to someone you know?» Reported as a figure of its own, not as part of an index.
**Open comment:** A free-text field can catch what the statements miss. But free text can reveal who wrote it, even when no name is stored. Comments deserve the same care as figures for small groups.

blocks.text: Why a five-point scale?

The statements are usually answered on a five-step scale: **strongly disagree, somewhat disagree, neither, somewhat agree, strongly agree**. The midpoint lets people say «neither» when that is what they mean. Without it they have to take a side, which adds noise. More steps do not necessarily give more precise answers: the difference between 6 and 7 on a ten-point scale can mean different things to different people.
Why fewer questions give better answers

Every question costs time, and fatigue produces worse answers towards the end. More importantly, every question quietly promises that someone will act on the answer. Only ask what you are prepared to follow up.

The regulation also requires the mapping to fit the organisation. According to Arbeidstilsynet, the scope, methods and content of the mapping and risk assessment must be adapted to the nature, activities and size of the organisation. A small firm with no public-facing work does not need the same questions as a care home.
Anonymity decides whether the answers are honest

People answer honestly when they know the answer cannot be traced back. That takes more than not storing names: a department of three is recognisable regardless. No group should therefore be shown until a minimum number have answered. Five is a common threshold. Read more in [Anonymous employee survey: what does anonymous mean?](/artikler/anonym-medarbeiderundersokelse)
How the answers should be read

The level of a topic says less than its movement over time. A topic that has fallen a few points since the last survey while the rest stand still is a clearer signal than the figure on its own. Look at the topics before the total: the total can stand still while two topics move in opposite directions.

The topics must also be read together. Section 1A-2 of the regulation requires the risk assessment to cover the factors individually, how they affect one another, and whether together they amount to a risk. High workload combined with emotional demands is a different finding from either on its own. See [risk assessment of the psychosocial working environment](/artikler/risikovurdering-av-psykososialt-arbeidsmiljo).

The result is the start of a conversation, not the answer. Share it with employees within a couple of weeks, pick the two or three findings that matter most, and turn them into measures with an owner and a deadline. Then measure again on the topics where measures are running. Read more about [going through the results with employees](/artikler/slik-gar-dere-gjennom-resultatene-med-de-ansatte).

hvorOfte.title: How often should the work environment be mapped? | Orgpuls
hvorOfte.description: How often must the psychosocial working environment be mapped? What the regulation requires, which changes trigger a new mapping, and an annual cycle.
hvorOfte.h1: How often should the working environment be measured?
hvorOfte.lead: The rules set no fixed interval, but they require the mapping to be repeated regularly and whenever changes may affect the risk. A practical rhythm is one full mapping a year, short follow-up surveys on the topics where measures are in place, and a new mapping whenever the organisation changes.

blocks.text: What do the rules require?

On 1 January 2026 the regulation on the performance of work gained a chapter of its own on the psychosocial working environment. Section 1A-2 states that the employer shall map psychosocial working environment factors and assess the risk, and sets four requirements for how this is done.

items.ref: Regulation on the performance of work § 1A-2(4) (our translation)
items.text: The mapping and the risk assessment shall a. be carried out in cooperation with the employees and their representatives b. be adapted to the nature, activities and size of the undertaking c. be repeated regularly and upon changes that may affect the risk conditions in the undertaking d. be documented and form part of the undertaking's systematic health, environment and safety work.

blocks.text: Neither the regulation nor the Working Environment Act (arbeidsmiljøloven) says how many months may pass between rounds. In its commentary, the Norwegian Labour Inspection Authority (Arbeidstilsynet) writes that mapping and risk assessment are not to be a one-off activity, but must be carried out regularly and upon changes that may affect the psychosocial working environment.

How often is therefore a matter of judgement, adapted to the organisation. According to Arbeidstilsynet, the organisation's risk profile, structure and ways of working will affect how and how often the mapping and risk assessment are carried out. An organisation whose staff face demanding encounters with clients, or are exposed to violence and threats, may have reason to keep a closer watch than a small office.

The rhythm should also be agreed in cooperation with employees and their representatives, as letter (a) presupposes. Representatives means the safety representative where there is one, and any union representatives. Read more about [the safety representative's role in the mapping](/artikler/verneombudets-rolle-i-kartleggingen).
When does a change trigger a new mapping?

The duty to map upon changes applies whenever the last mapping took place. Arbeidstilsynet gives as examples changes in organisation, staffing, tasks, management, technology, working hours or general conditions. Section 3-1(2)(d) of the Act also requires the employer to assess, while planning changes, whether the working environment will meet the requirements of the Act.
Typical situations that call for a mapping outside the regular rhythm:

items: reorganisation, a merger or downsizing
new management, or new managers across much of the organisation
a move, new premises or a shift to working from home
new systems or ways of working that change the day for many
a demanding event or period – an accident, a conflict, a large project

blocks.text: It is then better to map the affected topics now than to wait for the next annual round. If the change mainly concerns workload and the division of responsibility, a short survey of just workload and role clarity may be enough.
Why one survey a year is not enough on its own

An annual [employee survey](/artikler/medarbeiderundersokelse) gives a snapshot. It shows where the organisation stands, but not whether last year's measures worked, because a great deal else happens between two surveys. Twelve months is also a long time to wait to learn whether something helped.

When a year passes between rounds, the survey easily becomes a project that is planned, presented and forgotten. That sits poorly with section 3-1(2)(h) of the Act, which requires the employer to monitor and review the systematic health, environment and safety work so that it functions as intended.
Main mapping and follow-up survey
One approach is to distinguish between two kinds of survey with different purposes:

items.title: Main mapping – once a year
items.text: The full question set. Sets the starting point and documents the mapping. Hold it in the same month every year, so the figures can be compared.

items.title: Follow-up survey – between main mappings
items.text: A few statements, only on the topics where measures have been put in place. It is not a new mapping, but a check on whether the measure works.

blocks.text: A follow-up survey should be short. If it takes more than a couple of minutes, it starts to feel like a new survey, and fewer people answer. Keep it to the topics where a measure is running – often two or three topics with three statements each. Such short checks are often called a [pulse survey](/artikler/pulsundersokelse).
An example annual cycle

items.title: Main mapping: the full question set
Review with employees, risk assessment and measures with an owner and a deadline
Follow-up survey on the topics with open measures
Follow-up survey and planning for next year

blocks.text: July is holiday season, and December is busy for many. Keep the surveys out of both. The March review is where findings become measures; see [from results to measures](/artikler/fra-resultater-til-tiltak).

blocks.title: Rule of thumb
blocks.text: Measure as often as you can follow up. A survey nobody has time to act on is worse than none.
How to keep people willing to answer

If people are to answer again and again, they need to see that the last round led to something. This ties in with the duty to inform in section 1A-4 of the regulation. Arbeidstilsynet writes that information is to be given regularly and upon changes that may affect the risk profile, organisation, tasks or measures in place.

items: Send at the same time every round, for example the first Tuesday of the month at nine.
Send one reminder, not three – and have it go out centrally, not from the line manager. Then no manager needs to know who has not answered.
Use text messages or a QR code where people do not sit at a computer.
Tell people what happened after the last round before you send the next.

blocks.text: Compare like with like

A main mapping should be compared with the previous main mapping, ideally taken in the same month. A follow-up survey is compared with the one before it. Mix the two and you are comparing different question sets – and a change may then be due to the questions, not the working environment.
Small organisations

The requirement to adapt the mapping to the nature, activities and size of the organisation also covers the documentation. Arbeidstilsynet writes that the scope and form of the documentation must be adapted to the organisation's nature, size and risk profile. A small business does not need an elaborate apparatus, but it must be able to show what has been mapped, assessed and followed up.

Follow-up surveys are useful in small organisations too, but keep anonymity in mind: no group should be shown with fewer than five answers. If you are few, look at the figures for the whole organisation, not per department. See [which questions belong in the survey](/artikler/medarbeiderundersokelse-sporsmal).

anonym.title: What does an anonymous employee survey mean? | Orgpuls
anonym.description: When is an employee survey truly anonymous? Why removing names is not enough, why small groups must be hidden, and which questions to ask about the setup.
anonym.h1: Anonymous employee survey: what does anonymous mean?
anonym.lead: Not storing names is not enough. A survey is only anonymous when nobody can work out who answered what – not from the data, not from small groups, not by calculating a hidden group, and not from what is written in a comment. That takes a lower limit on how small a group may be shown, and answers that are never stored with anything that could identify the respondent.

blocks.text: Why anonymity decides the quality

People answer honestly when they are confident the answer cannot be traced back. If in doubt, they answer politely – or not at all. An [employee survey](/artikler/medarbeiderundersokelse) with doubtful anonymity produces figures that look good but are not true. The mapping of the psychosocial working environment that employers must carry out under section 1A-2 of the regulation on the performance of work then rests on weak ground.
The mapping is about the working environment, not individuals

Anonymity does not get in the way of what the mapping is for. In its commentary on section 1A-1, the Norwegian Labour Inspection Authority (Arbeidstilsynet) writes that the assessment of what is fully satisfactory should, as a rule, relate to the psychosocial working environment as a whole and to the organisation's systems, structure and management. Individual experiences still matter, but as signals about the organisation:

The individual employee's experiences and strains may nevertheless be relevant as indicators of conditions in organisation, management or governance that matter for the working environment in the undertaking.
blocks.cite: Arbeidstilsynet's commentary on the regulation on the performance of work § 1A-1 (our translation)

blocks.text: What the employer needs to know, then, is how the work is experienced in a department or team – not who thinks what. Individual cases, such as a specific harassment complaint, belong in the whistleblowing routines, not in a survey.
Three ways anonymity breaks
1. The answer can be linked to the person

Many surveys go out with a personal link, and who has answered is recorded so that reminders can be sent. If that link sits alongside the answers, anonymity is a promise, not a property. What matters is whether the answer is stored with anything that could identify the respondent: name, e-mail, IP address or an exact time. A time rounded to the hour says far less than one accurate to the second.
2. The group is too small

A department of three is recognisable even if no name appears anywhere. The remedy is a lower limit: no group is shown until a minimum number have answered. Five is a common threshold. A small team may have reason to go down to three, but the fewer the answers, the easier it is to recognise who said what.

The limit must apply to everyone, administrators and senior management included. Nor should it be possible to lower it afterwards to «see the figure anyway»: a survey should keep the limit that applied when it went out. The same goes for combinations of background data. Department, age and length of service may each give large groups, yet together produce a group of one.
3. The hidden group can be calculated

This is the one most often overlooked. If you can see the figure for the whole organisation and for every department but one, you can work out the last. It then does not help that the small department is hidden. Where the sum would otherwise add up, one more group must be held back.

blocks.title: Why is there a dash?
blocks.text: A dash instead of a number means the group had too few answers. The figure is not hidden from anyone in particular – it is not calculated for anyone. The answers still count in the figures for the whole.
Reminders without knowing who is missing

Reminders raise the response rate, but they are also where anonymity easily leaks. If the manager chases people personally, the manager must know who has not answered – and therefore who has. The safest arrangement is a single reminder sent centrally, with nobody in the organisation able to read the list of who is missing.
Comments are the hardest to keep anonymous

Free text can reveal its author even when no name is stored. «As the only woman in the workshop …» needs no signature. Comments should therefore only be shown when the group has enough answers, and should not be passed on to more people than need them to follow up.

Anonymity need not mean one-way communication. It is possible to let management reply to a comment without learning who wrote it, for example by giving the writer a private link where the reply can be read. The condition is that the link between comment and person is not available to the organisation.
Questions to ask before the survey goes out

Whether the survey is run on paper, in a spreadsheet or with a digital tool, the employer and the safety representative should be able to answer these questions. If you use an external supplier, these are the questions to put to them.

items: Is the answer stored with a name, e-mail, IP address or exact time?
What is the smallest group that is shown – and can anyone lower the limit, including afterwards?
Is it prevented that someone calculates a hidden group, or narrows background data down to a few people?
Who can see the list of who has answered, and who sends the reminders?
How are comments from small groups handled, and who can read them?
Where is the data stored, who has access, and is it shared with anyone?

blocks.text: Under section 1A-2 of the regulation, the mapping must be done in cooperation with employees and their representatives. It is natural for the safety representative to help settle these questions before the survey goes out.
How to explain anonymity to employees
People believe in anonymity when it is explained concretely, not when they are handed a promise. If the survey is set up as described above, a short text before it goes out might read:

blocks.title: Example text – adapt it to how the survey is actually set up
blocks.text: «Your answers are stored without name, e-mail or IP address. No group is shown until at least five have answered – not even to management. There is no list of who answered what, and nobody can make one. We get the figures, not you.»
The text must match reality. If anyone in the organisation can see who has answered, do not say that it is impossible.

Also say what will happen with the result, and when. Anonymity makes people safe enough to answer. Seeing something happen afterwards makes them bother. Read about [going through the results with employees](/artikler/slik-gar-dere-gjennom-resultatene-med-de-ansatte) without exposing anyone, and about [which questions belong in the survey](/artikler/medarbeiderundersokelse-sporsmal).

verneombud.title: The safety representative's role in mapping | Orgpuls
verneombud.description: The safety representative must ensure the psychosocial working environment is looked after and be consulted on measures. What it means in a mapping.
verneombud.h1: What role does the safety representative play when the working environment is mapped?
verneombud.lead: The safety representative (verneombud) looks after employees' interests in working environment matters, must ensure that the psychosocial working environment is taken care of, and must be consulted when measures are planned and carried out. When the psychosocial working environment is mapped and risk-assessed, the safety representative is one of the representatives the employer must work with. Responsibility for making sure the mapping happens, however, lies with the employer.

blocks.text: What does the law say about the safety representative?
The safety representative shall safeguard the employees' interests in matters relating to the working environment.
blocks.cite: Working Environment Act (arbeidsmiljøloven) § 6-2, first paragraph (our translation)

blocks.text: Section 6-2 of the Act lists what the safety representative must particularly ensure. One item concerns the psychosocial working environment directly, and the fourth paragraph ties the safety representative to systematic HSE work, where mapping belongs.

items.text: that the employees' psychosocial working environment is taken care of. (our translation)

The safety representative shall be consulted during the planning and implementation of measures of significance for the working environment within the representative's area, including the establishment, performance and maintenance of the undertaking's systematic health, environment and safety work, cf. section 3-1. (our translation)

items.ref: Regulation on the performance of work § 1A-2(4)(a)
items.text: The mapping and risk assessment shall … be carried out in cooperation with the employees and their representatives (our translation)

blocks.text: In its commentary, the Norwegian Labour Inspection Authority (Arbeidstilsynet) states that employees' representatives means the safety representative, where the organisation has one, and any union or other employee representatives. Under § 1A-4 of the regulation, the same representatives must receive the necessary information about psychosocial risk factors and about the measures put in place.
Must every organisation have a safety representative?

The main rule in section 6-1 of the Act is yes: a safety representative must be elected in every undertaking covered by the Act. Organisations with fewer than five employees may agree in writing on a different arrangement, including having no safety representative. Unless otherwise agreed, such an arrangement lasts two years. Arbeidstilsynet may, after a specific assessment, decide that the organisation must have one after all.

Organisations with more than 10 employees may elect several safety representatives. Where an organisation has several separate departments, or work is done in shifts, at least one should normally be elected for each department or shift team. Organisations with more than one safety representative must have a senior safety representative to coordinate the work, and the names of the safety representatives must be posted at the workplace.
What does the safety representative do at each stage of the mapping?

items.title: Planning
items.text: Is consulted on how the mapping is done, what it covers and how anonymity is protected.

items.title: Carrying it out
items.text: Can help make sure employees know why they are being surveyed, and that it is safe to answer.

items.title: Results and risk assessment
items.text: Should see the same material as management, not a summary afterwards, and take part in assessing the risk.

items.title: Measures
items.text: Is consulted when measures are chosen and planned.

items.title: Follow-up
items.text: Ensures that measures are carried out and that the psychosocial working environment is taken care of.

blocks.text: What access should the safety representative have?

The Act uses the words «consulted» and «ensure». It is hard to give good advice about something you have only seen a summary of. The safety representative should therefore have access to the same [employee survey](/artikler/medarbeiderundersokelse) results as management – for the whole organisation and for the groups large enough to be shown. Under section 6-2(5), the safety representative must also be informed of, among other things, occupational diseases, accidents at work and identified faults and deficiencies in their area.

Access to the results does not mean access to individual answers. Anonymity applies to the safety representative as much as to management: no one should be able to see who answered what, and figures for groups so small that individuals can be recognised should not be shown to anyone.

blocks.title: The responsibility lies with the employer
blocks.text: The safety representative takes part and keeps watch, but is not responsible for the mapping being done. That responsibility lies with the employer under section 3-1 of the Act. A safety representative who organises a survey because management will not is taking on a task the law assigns to the employer.
How can the safety representative raise it with management?
Many safety representatives know a mapping should have been done, but not how to raise it. Some advice:

items: **Start with questions, not demands.** «When did we last map the psychosocial working environment, and what happened to the findings?»

**Point to the rules.** Since 1 January 2026 the regulation has stated expressly that mapping must be repeated regularly and documented. See [the new rules from 2026](/artikler/nye-regler-psykososialt-arbeidsmiljo-2026).
**Propose a fixed rhythm.** A mapping planned for a set time is easier to get done than a project with no date.
**Offer to help.** A safety representative who helps explain the survey gives employees a reason to trust it.

blocks.text: What if problems are not followed up?

If the safety representative becomes aware of conditions that may cause a risk of accident or ill health, they must alert the employees on the spot at once, and draw the employer's attention to it if they cannot avert the danger themselves. The employer must respond. If the report is not acted on within a reasonable time, the safety representative must notify Arbeidstilsynet or the working environment committee (section 6-2(3)).

The safety representative must also take part when Arbeidstilsynet inspects the organisation. Employees, for their part, can always report censurable conditions internally through the safety representative, and an unsatisfactory working environment is named as an example of such conditions (sections 2 A-1 and 2 A-2).
The working environment committee and union representatives

Organisations that regularly employ at least 30 people must have a working environment committee. In organisations with between 10 and 30 employees, one must be set up if either party demands it (section 7-1). Among other things, the committee deals with establishing and maintaining systematic HSE work, and Arbeidstilsynet names it as a relevant forum for information and dialogue about psychosocial risk.

Section 3-1(1) of the Act says systematic HSE work must be carried out in cooperation with employees and their union representatives. Where the safety representative has a particular responsibility for the working environment, union representatives represent employees more broadly. The mapping works best when both are involved from the start.
Situations the safety representative may face
The results are weak for one department

Raise it as a finding, not a verdict. Ask what lies behind the figure, and let the department help choose the measures. The regulation requires measures to be drawn up together with employees, and Arbeidstilsynet describes cooperation as a precondition for measures being relevant and well targeted. Read more about [risk assessment of the psychosocial working environment](/artikler/risikovurdering-av-psykososialt-arbeidsmiljo).
Someone wants to see the figures for a small group

Hold firm. A minimum group size for reporting exists to protect employees, and it is a precondition for people daring to answer honestly. A group too small to be shown still counts towards the figures for the whole.
Nothing happens after the mapping

Ask about the measures: who is responsible, and when will they be done? Without an owner and a deadline, measures become intentions. The next mapping is the best basis for that conversation, because it shows whether anything has changed.

plattform.title: The platform: mapping, measures and follow-up | Orgpuls
plattform.description: Anonymous work environment survey with results by factor and department, measures with owner and deadline, a pulse that shows what worked, and a report.
plattform.h1: One platform for the whole round: map, understand, act and see that it worked
plattform.lead: Orgpuls brings what the Working Environment Act requires of mapping into one steady rhythm. Each part can be used on its own, but the value is in how they connect: the survey becomes measures, and the next survey shows whether they worked.

blocks.text: Mapping

items.title: Baseline
items.text: Eleven psychosocial factors with three statements each, answered on a five-point scale. The wording builds on QPS Nordic and covers the factors named in section 4-3 of the Act and in the regulation. About four minutes per employee.

items.title: Pulse
items.text: Short surveys between baselines, only on the factors where a measure is running. The pulse is not a new mapping but a measurement of whether the measure works. Under a minute.

items.title: Your own questions
items.text: Up to five of your own questions per survey, for what is particular to you. They are reported separately and never enter the index.

items.title: Outside the index
items.text: A recommendation question, screening for offensive behaviour and for violence and threats – only as a count for the whole organisation – and an open field.

blocks.text: The survey is sent by e-mail or SMS, or shared as a link and a QR code. One reminder goes to those who have not answered, from the system and not the manager.
Results
The answers become an index from 0 to 100 per factor, with a risk band: 65 or above is low risk, 50–64 medium and below 50 high. The result can be read in several ways:

items: **Heatmap** – the factors against the departments, with the statements behind each figure
**Priority** – which factors matter most for whether people would recommend the workplace
**Segment profile, Compare and Development** – one department, two surveys, or the development over time

blocks.text: By default a department is shown once at least five have answered; small teams can choose 3. When a department could be worked out from the others, one more is held back. Read more about [anonymity and security](/sikkerhet).
Comments and conversations

Employees can write a comment on a statement. Management can reply without knowing who wrote it, and the writer can read the reply and answer back through a private link. If a manager wants to talk directly, they can ask – and the employee alone decides whether to make themselves known, by writing from their own e-mail.
Measures

The findings become measures on a board, from finding to effect. Each measure has an owner, a deadline and the factor it is meant to move, and ready suggestions are there to start from. **A measure cannot be closed before its effect is measured** – the next pulse must show whether the figure has moved.
Annual wheel and report

items.title: The annual wheel
items.text: You choose the rhythm once – from one baseline a year to a pulse every month – and the wheel plans the rounds itself. The safety representative and the union representatives are notified first, before the employees.

items.title: Report for inspection
items.text: The report follows the four steps of section 3-1 letter c of the Act: mapping, risk assessment, measures and follow-up. The figures are frozen when the round closes, and the report can be printed or saved as PDF.

blocks.text: Roles and access

head: Role
Sees
rows: The whole organisation, every factor and the anonymous conversations
Their own department once the threshold is met, and the conversations from it
The same figures and the same risk assessment as management, at no extra cost

blocks.text: No role sees who answered what. That link does not exist.
Getting started

Sign up with the organisation number and we fetch the name and address from the Brønnøysund registers. Add employees from a spreadsheet or one at a time, and follow the setup wizard. See [pricing](/priser), or the [use cases](/bruksomrader) for how other organisations use Orgpuls.

sikkerhet.title: Security, privacy and anonymity | Orgpuls
sikkerhet.description: How Orgpuls keeps answers anonymous: no link to a person, at least 5 answers per group by default, data in the EU. What we store, and what we do not.
sikkerhet.h1: Anonymity that does not depend on anyone keeping a promise
sikkerhet.lead: Nobody can see who answered what – not even you. It is built into how the answers are stored, not into a routine someone has to follow. That is why employees can answer honestly.

blocks.text: What we store, and what we do not

The register holds each employee’s name, e-mail and group, and a mobile number if you use SMS. If you bring in employees from Microsoft Entra ID, the person’s object ID in the directory is stored too. The answer itself goes into a table that **has no column that could hold a link to a person**. The row shows the round, the group and the hour the answer came in – not the minute.

Orgpuls recognises the invitation link by a cryptographic checksum. The invitation records that it has been used, so you get no reminder – but never the answer. No screen, export or query shows what a named person answered, not even to administrators: the information does not exist.

items.title: Recognised by a checksum
items.text: The link is looked up by a cryptographic checksum. The invitation only records that it has been used, so you get no reminder.

items.title: Stored with no link to you
items.text: The row shows the round, the group and the hour the answer came in. No column can hold a link to a person.

items.title: Shown only when enough have answered
items.text: Figures are shown per group, and only when the group has at least as many answers as the limit.

blocks.text: Fewer than 5 answers show a dash – by default

By default no group is shown until at least 5 have answered, and 5 is strongly recommended. The database enforces the limit: you can raise it up to 10, and a small team can lower it to 3 – never further. The fewer the answers, the easier it is to recognise who said what, so the managing director gets a warning before the limit is lowered. A round keeps the limit it started with, so a lower limit never opens earlier rounds. If the figures for the other groups would reveal a hidden group, Orgpuls hides one more, so nobody can work their way back to it.

items.title: At least 3 answers
items.text: A small team can lower the limit to here, after a warning to the managing director. It cannot go lower.

items.title: At least 5 answers
items.text: Strongly recommended. A round keeps the limit it started with.

items.title: Up to 10 answers
items.text: You can raise the limit. The more answers per group, the harder it is to recognise who said what.

blocks.text: Comments and conversations stay anonymous

A comment is shown only when the group it comes from has enough answers, and the group never travels with the comment. The writer gets a private key to the conversation; the database stores only a checksum of it. If a manager wants to talk directly, the manager can ask – but only the employee can make themselves known, by writing from their own e-mail.
The basis is a legal duty, not consent

The processing rests on legal obligation: GDPR Article 6(1)(c), with sections 3-1 and 4-3 of the Working Environment Act. An employee cannot consent freely to their employer, so consent is not used. The questions avoid health information, which an employer shall not ask for, and answers about violence, threats and offensive behaviour are shown only as counts.
Stored in the EU, not passed on

items: We store the data on servers in the EU (Frankfurt), under the GDPR
We do not share answers with third parties, and use no answers to train AI models
A single answer cannot be retrieved or deleted on its own, because it cannot be linked to a person (GDPR article 11)

blocks.text: The data processing agreement is ready in Orgpuls

You are the controller and Orgpuls the processor, under GDPR Article 28. The managing director reads and signs the agreement under Settings, and can print it or save it as PDF. We use three sub-processors: Supabase (database and sign-in, Frankfurt), Vercel (hosting, Frankfurt) and Brevo (e-mail and SMS), and a fourth for organisations that send the survey in Teams: Microsoft (Azure Bot Service, EU).
Questions to ask any supplier
Anonymity is easy to promise and hard to prove. Ask these questions – of us and of others:

items: Is there any column or log that could link an answer to a person – including for administrators?
How large must a group be before it is shown, and who can lower the threshold?
Can a hidden group be calculated from the total and the other groups?
Does the group come with a comment when it is shown?
Where is the data stored, and which sub-processors are used?
Are the answers used for anything else, such as training AI models?

blocks.text: Read more about [what anonymous must mean in an employee survey](/artikler/anonym-medarbeiderundersokelse).

blocks.title: Questions about privacy?
blocks.text: Write to [hjelp@orgpuls.no](mailto:hjelp@orgpuls.no). Read also [what anonymous has to mean in an employee survey](/artikler/anonym-medarbeiderundersokelse).

faq.q: Can the employer see who answered what?
faq.a: No. The answer is stored in a table with no column that could link it to a person. No screen, export or query shows what a named person answered, not even for administrators.

faq.q: What happens when a group is too small?
faq.a: By default no group is shown before at least 5 have answered; a dash is shown instead. The threshold can be raised to 10, and small teams can lower it to 3 – never lower. If a hidden group could be calculated from the others, one more group is hidden.

faq.q: Where is the data stored?
faq.a: On servers in the EU (Frankfurt), under the GDPR. The sub-processors are Supabase, Vercel and Brevo, and Microsoft for organisations that send the survey in Teams.

faq.q: Why is consent not used?
faq.a: Because an employee cannot freely consent towards their employer. Processing rests on legal obligation, GDPR Article 6(1)(c), cf. Working Environment Act §§ 3-1 and 4-3.

faq.q: Are the answers used to train AI?
faq.a: No. We do not share answers with third parties and use no answers to train AI models.

blocks.text: Who is responsible

Pundit Invest AS, org. no. 922 698 422, Øvre Prinsdals vei 36L, 1266 Oslo, which provides Orgpuls, is the controller for the data described here: visits to the website, organisation signups, the newsletter, marketing and customer support. Send questions about privacy to [hjelp@orgpuls.no](mailto:hjelp@orgpuls.no).

blocks.title: Answers to employee surveys
blocks.text: When an organisation uses Orgpuls to survey its work environment, the organisation is the controller and Orgpuls the processor under a data processing agreement. Answers are stored with no link to the person who gave them. If the organisation brings in its employees from Microsoft Entra ID, we do so on its behalf and only for the groups it chooses: name, e-mail address, language, group membership and object ID in the directory, and a mobile number only if the organisation turns it on. If your employer uses Slack to send you the link, Orgpuls finds you in the workspace by your work e-mail and stores your member ID there, on your employer’s behalf. The message is a short text and the personal link, with no read receipt and no record of clicks. Slack is your employer’s own tool: the Slack admin there can read the messages, as an e-mail admin can read e-mail, and a reminder shows that you had not answered when it was sent. Your answer is stored with no connection to the message. How that is built is described under [Security and privacy](/sikkerhet). Questions about a survey you take part in go to your employer.
When you visit the website

We keep our own statistics on the use of orgpuls.com, without cookies and without storing anything on your device. For each page view your browser sends which page it is, the site you came from (the domain only) and any campaign tags in the address (utm) to our own platform. If you press a button that leads to signing up, or start or complete a signup, that is sent too, with nothing of what you typed. The IP address and the browser's identification are not stored. They are used only to make a visit code with a key that changes every day, so we can count visits within a day without being able to follow you from one day to the next. In addition, Vercel, which hosts the website, measures page views and load times without cookies.

If your browser asks not to be tracked (Global Privacy Control or Do Not Track), nothing is sent to our platform. The statistics are deleted after 13 months. The legal basis is our legitimate interest in understanding how the website is used, GDPR Article 6(1)(f).
When you register an organisation

We store your name, e-mail address, password (only as a cryptographic hash), the organisation's name, organisation number and number of employees, and information we fetch from the Brønnøysund Register Centre. We also store your answer if you tell us how you heard of us. The legal basis is the agreement with the organisation, Article 6(1)(b), and our legitimate interest in knowing which channels work, point (f).
If you sign in with Google, we receive your name and e-mail address from Google. We never receive your password there.

If you sign in with Microsoft, we receive your name and e-mail address from Microsoft, and we store two technical identifiers for the account: the ID of the Microsoft 365 organisation it belongs to (tenant ID), and the account’s object ID there. We use them only to make sure it is the same Microsoft account, from the organisation your organisation may have connected, that signs in again. We never receive your password there. The identifiers are deleted with the account. The basis is the agreement with the organisation, Article 6(1)(b), and our legitimate interest in securing the sign-in, point (f).
When you try the demo

If you ask for a demo, we store your name, the email address, the organisation and the role you give, whether you ticked the box for email from us, and a visitor code for the network you came from, made from the IP address with a key that changes every day. The IP address itself is not stored. The request is deleted after 30 days. We use it to send the sign-in link and to prevent misuse, such as many links to the same address. The basis is that you asked for the demo, Article 6(1)(b), and our legitimate interest in stopping misuse, point (f).

The demo is a copy of a fictional organisation that only you can access. It and your sign-in are deleted after 14 days without a sign-in, or as soon as you choose to create your own account. Once you have opened the link, we store your address, name, organisation and role as a contact marked «demo», so that we know who has tried Orgpuls. If you were already a contact, we keep what we had and only fill in what was missing. The basis is our legitimate interest in knowing who tries the product, point (f). We keep the contact until you ask us to delete it or object. We email you about Orgpuls only if you ticked the box, Article 6(1)(a), and you can unsubscribe in every email.
Newsletter and e-mail about Orgpuls

If you subscribe to the newsletter, we store your e-mail address, your name and organisation if given, the lists you chose and when you confirmed. The legal basis is your consent, Article 6(1)(a). We record whether a mailing was delivered, opened or clicked, to learn what is useful. You can unsubscribe with the link at the bottom of every e-mail, or choose your lists again. After you unsubscribe we keep only a cryptographic hash of the address, so that we do not send to it again.

We may send e-mail about Orgpuls to organisations' role addresses (such as post@), on the basis of legitimate interest. Personal addresses receive e-mail from us only with consent, or when you are already a customer and have not opted out. Every e-mail has an unsubscribe link. When we write to an organisation, we take its name, organisation number, industry and address from the Central Coordinating Register for Legal Entities (Enhetsregisteret), and the general manager’s name from its public role information. We use the name only to address the organisation, at its own address. The basis is legitimate interest, Article 6(1)(f), and the information comes from a public source (Article 14). You can object at any time, see below.
When you contact us

If you write to us, through the form or by e-mail, we store your name, e-mail address and what you write, to answer and follow up. The legal basis is our legitimate interest in answering enquiries, or the agreement if you are a customer.
When you download a free template

If you download one of the free templates, we store your name, your e-mail address, which template you downloaded, your organisation and role if you give them, and whether you ticked the box for e-mail from us. The legal basis is our legitimate interest in knowing who uses the templates, Article 6(1)(f). You receive e-mail about new templates and articles only if you ticked the box; the basis is then your consent, Article 6(1)(a), and you can withdraw it with the link in every e-mail. Your browser gets a cookie that remembers which templates you have downloaded, for one year.
Cookies

We use only the cookies the service needs to work: signing in, your language choice, display choices in the app, and a short-lived cookie that remembers the organisation while you sign up with Google. In the demo, the browser remembers which places in the demo guide you have visited; this is stored on your device only. If you download a free template, a cookie remembers which templates, for one year, so you need not fill in the form again. None is used for statistics or advertising.
Who helps us

items: Supabase Inc. (USA): database, sign-in, background jobs and our own visit statistics. Data is stored and processed in Frankfurt, Germany.
Vercel Inc. (USA): hosting of the website and the application, and the cookieless measurement of page views. Server functions run in Frankfurt.
Brevo SAS (France): sending e-mail and SMS, and recording delivery, opens and clicks on e-mail.
Google (Ireland): sign-in with Google, only if you choose it.
Microsoft (Ireland): sign-in with Microsoft, only if you choose it.

Microsoft Ireland Operations Ltd (Ireland): Azure Bot Service relays the Teams message with the survey link, for organisations that have switched Teams on. The service is set up in the EU (West Europe).

blocks.text: Suppliers outside the EEA are bound by the European Commission's standard contractual clauses for transfers. We do not sell personal data or share it with others for their marketing.
How long we keep data

items: Visit statistics: 13 months. The visit code changes every day.
The account and the organisation's data: for as long as the customer relationship lasts, and then as long as the Accounting Act requires for what is part of the accounts.
Demo: the request 30 days. The demo and its sign-in 14 days without a sign-in. The contact until you ask us to delete it.
Newsletter: until you unsubscribe. After that, only the hash that prevents new mailings.
Support enquiries: as long as needed to follow up the case and the customer relationship.
Free template downloads: until you ask us to delete the data. Consent to e-mail: until you withdraw it.

blocks.text: Your rights

You can ask for access to, correction and erasure of data about you, ask us to restrict processing, object to processing based on legitimate interest, and receive data you have given us in a machine-readable format. Write to [hjelp@orgpuls.no](mailto:hjelp@orgpuls.no); we answer within 30 days. If you believe we process data in breach of the rules, you can complain to the Norwegian Data Protection Authority, [Datatilsynet](https://www.datatilsynet.no).
