after that you move to the free plan: you can send the standard main survey, read the results and work on measures for as long as you like, but pulses, follow-up surveys, industry modules, your own questions, comparisons with earlier rounds and the report require a plan;
a survey that is already open finishes as planned.

blocks.text: We may change what the free plan includes. A change is announced by e-mail to the managing director and in Orgpuls at least 60 days before it applies, and it does not apply to a survey that is already open. What you have measured and recorded before the change, you can still read and download.
4. Prices and payment
The prices are on the pricing page and are stated excluding VAT. There is no setup fee.

items: **Invoicing.** The managing director chooses a plan and gives the invoice address under Settings › Payment. Invoices are sent by e-mail or as EHF. The first invoice runs from the day the trial period ends, or from the day the plan is confirmed if that is later.

**Invoicing interval.** The managing director chooses a monthly or a yearly agreement. A monthly agreement is invoiced monthly in advance. A yearly agreement is invoiced a year in advance, at ten months' price.
**Payment terms.** 14 days from the invoice date. Late payment is subject to the Norwegian Late Payment Interest Act (forsinkelsesrenteloven).

**Non-payment.** If an invoice has not been paid 30 days after its due date, and after at least one written reminder, we may restrict the service to what the free plan in section 3 includes until the invoice is paid.
**Price changes** are notified at least 60 days before they apply. You may cancel before the change takes effect.

**Changing package.** If the number of employees passes the package's limit (for example from 25 to 26 employees), the managing director chooses the larger package under Settings › Payment. The new package's price applies from the next invoicing period.

blocks.text: 5. Your responsibilities
You are the employer and the controller, and Orgpuls is the tool. This means you are responsible for:

items: entering correct information about the employees, and keeping it up to date;
informing the employees about the survey and what it is used for;
involving the safety representative and employee representatives as the Working Environment Act requires;
giving access only to people who should have it (managing director, department managers, safety representative), and keeping sign-in details to yourselves;
not trying to find out who answered what. This includes combining Orgpuls' results with other information to single out individuals, or pressuring anyone to identify themselves;
not using the service in breach of the law, or in a way that harms the service or other customers.

blocks.text: Orgpuls provides a basis for systematic health, safety and environment work, but does not fulfil the duty for you. It is you who assess risk, decide on measures and follow them up. The report is an aid, not legal advice.
6. Anonymity and privacy

Answers are stored with no link to the person who gave them. Results are not shown for a group with fewer answers than the threshold. The threshold is five answers by default and can be raised to ten. The managing director can lower it to three or four, but never below three, and a round keeps the threshold that applied when it was opened. How this is built is described under [Security and privacy](/sikkerhet).
Orgpuls processes personal data about the employees as your processor, under the data processing agreement.
For data about the users of the account (name, e-mail, sign-in) and about the organisation as a customer, Orgpuls is the controller, as described in the [privacy statement](/personvernerklaering).
7. Availability and support
We work to keep the service available around the clock. Planned maintenance that will be noticeable is announced in advance.
Support is given at [hjelp@orgpuls.no](mailto:hjelp@orgpuls.no) and through the form in Orgpuls, on working days.
8. Rights
The information you enter, and the results of the surveys, belong to you. Reports can be downloaded as PDF at any time.

Pundit Invest AS owns the software, the design and the texts in the service, including suggested measures. You receive a non-exclusive right to use the service for your own organisation during the agreement period.
The question set is based on QPS Nordic.
9. Liability
Orgpuls is not liable for indirect loss, such as lost profit, loss of data resulting from the customer's own actions, or claims from third parties.
Orgpuls' total liability under the agreement is limited to what the customer has paid in the 12 months before the damage. These limitations do not apply in the case of intent or gross negligence.
Orgpuls is not responsible for the customer complying with the Working Environment Act or the inspection authority's requirements. See section 5.
10. Cancellation and deletion
A monthly agreement has no binding period. A yearly agreement runs one year at a time.

**Moving to the free plan.** The managing director may instead move to the free plan under Settings › Payment. The subscription runs to the end of the paid period, and nothing is deleted. If nothing has been invoiced yet, the free plan begins when the trial ends.

**Deletion.** When the agreement has ended, Orgpuls deletes the organisation's data within 30 days, unless the law requires it to be kept. Reports you have downloaded are yours to keep. Download them before the agreement ends.
11. Changes to the terms
We may change the terms. Material changes are notified by e-mail to the managing director and in Orgpuls at least 30 days before they apply. You may cancel before the change takes effect.
The current version and its date are always shown on this page.
12. Force majeure

Neither party is liable for circumstances beyond its control that prevent performance, such as extensive power cuts, cyber attacks on subcontractors, strikes or orders from the authorities, for as long as the circumstance lasts.

The agreement is governed by Norwegian law. The parties shall first try to resolve disagreements through negotiation. The legal venue is Oslo District Court (Oslo tingrett), where Pundit Invest AS has its registered business office.

risikovurdering.lead: An Excel template for the risk assessment chapter 1A of the regulation on the performance of work requires: one row per factor the law names, with the legal basis, likelihood and consequence, risk level, reasoning and measures. In Norwegian.

blocks.text: What the template contains

items: **How to use it:** what the regulation requires, the three things to assess, and a way of working in four steps
**Risk assessment:** the eleven factors from the Act and the regulation, with their legal basis, ready set up. Risk and level are calculated
**Risk matrix:** likelihood × consequence, with suggested scales you can adapt
**Action plan:** measure, owner, deadline, status and how you will see whether it worked

blocks.text: What the regulation requires

On the basis of the mapping, the employer shall assess the risk of harmful effects, both in the short and the long term. The risk assessment shall cover the individual factors separately, how they affect one another, and whether together they amount to a risk.
blocks.cite: Regulation on the performance of work § 1A-2, second and third paragraphs (our translation)

blocks.text: The assessment is done in cooperation with employees and their representatives, repeated regularly and when things change, and documented. The template is made to show exactly that.
How to use it

items.title: Flag
items.text: the factors and groups that score weakly, or that have fallen since the previous mapping.

items.title: Assess
items.text: each of them: how serious could it become, how many does it affect, and how long has it lasted? Use both the statements behind the figures and what employees say.

items.title: Look for connections
items.text: do some factors reinforce each other in the same group? Is anything protective?

items.title: Conclude
items.text: with a risk level and a brief justification, and let the conclusion determine which measures come first.

blocks.title: The scales are a suggestion
blocks.text: The regulation sets no thresholds or fixed scales. Adapt the scales in the template to your business, and use the same ones every time so you can compare.
Read more about [how to assess the risk in the psychosocial work environment](/artikler/risikovurdering-av-psykososialt-arbeidsmiljo).

qps.h1: QPSNordic 34+: the Nordic questionnaire on psychological and social factors at work
qps.lead: The short version of QPSNordic, verbatim as the National Institute of Occupational Health published it, set up for printing. With a spreadsheet where you register the answers and get the count, mean and distribution per question. In Norwegian.

blocks.text: What is QPSNordic?

QPSNordic is a questionnaire for surveying psychological, social and organisational factors at work. It was developed by researchers from Norway, Sweden, Denmark and Finland in a project the Nordic Council of Ministers started in 1994, and tested in all four countries. The National Institute of Occupational Health (STAMI) published the user manual in 2001.

The manual says the questionnaire may be copied, and that you may build your own systems for registering, analysing and reporting. The short version, QPSNordic 34+, has 37 questions and seven background questions.
What you get

items: **The questionnaire** in Word, with the manual’s own introduction, the background questions and all 37 questions with their answer scales
**The answer register** in Excel: one row per form, and a summary with the count, mean, median and distribution per question

blocks.text: Before you use it

items: The short version has no scales, and the manual says the validity and reliability testing done for QPSNordic does not apply to it. Look at the questions one by one.
The manual advises against statistical analysis for groups of fewer than 10 people. The answer register therefore shows nothing until at least 10 have answered.
Employees must be told beforehand what the survey is for and how anonymity is kept. Taking part must be voluntary, and no results about individuals may be presented.

blocks.text: Spørreskjemaet kan kopieres fra Vedlegg 1 i denne brukerveiledningen. Man kan utvikle et PC-basert system for dataregistrering, statistiske analyser og rapportering. (The questionnaire may be copied from Appendix 1 of this user manual. You may develop a PC-based system for data registration, statistical analysis and reporting.)
blocks.cite: Brukerveiledning QPSNordic, p. 5

blocks.text: Source: Skogstad, A., Knardahl, S., Lindström, K., Elo, A.-L., Dallner, M., Gamberale, F., Hottinen, V. and Ørhede, E. (2001). Brukerveiledning QPSNordic (user manual). STAMI report vol. 2, no. 1. National Institute of Occupational Health in Norway.

dpa.title: Data processing agreement
dpa.lead: This agreement governs how Orgpuls processes personal data on behalf of the organisation, under the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) Article 28. It follows the requirements the Norwegian Data Protection Authority (Datatilsynet) sets out for data processing agreements, and the structure of the European Commission's standard contractual clauses between controllers and processors (Implementing Decision (EU) 2021/915). This is a translation; the Norwegian version governs.

p: The organisation using Orgpuls is the controller. Orgpuls is the processor.
The organisation decides the purpose of the processing and which data is entered. Orgpuls processes the data only to provide the service.

Orgpuls processes personal data only to carry out the mapping of the psychosocial working environment under the Working Environment Act sections 3-1 and 4-3, as the organisation sets it up in the service: sending invitations and reminders, collecting anonymous answers, and showing results, measures and the report.

This agreement and the organisation's settings in Orgpuls are the documented instructions. Orgpuls shall inform the organisation at once if, in Orgpuls' view, an instruction infringes data protection law.
The data is not used for any other purpose, is not sold and is not shared with anyone other than the sub-processors in Annex 3.

Orgpuls is built to process as little personal data as possible. About employees, only name, e-mail address and, if the organisation enters them, mobile number and preferred language are stored, together with their department. If the organisation connects Orgpuls to Microsoft Entra ID, the same data is read from there, together with the person's object ID in the directory. Answers are stored without any link to the person who gave them. Annex 1 describes the processing in full.
Everyone at Orgpuls with access to the personal data is bound by confidentiality. Access is given only to those who need it to operate and troubleshoot the service.
Orgpuls implements technical and organisational measures that ensure a level of security appropriate to the risk, under GDPR Article 32. The measures are set out in Annex 2.

The organisation authorises the sub-processors in Annex 3. Orgpuls shall notify the organisation by e-mail at least 30 days before a sub-processor is added or replaced, and the organisation may object. If the parties cannot agree, the organisation may terminate the agreement before the change takes effect.

The duty to notify does not apply to a sub-processor that is used only when the organisation itself switches on an integration, such as Microsoft for Teams. It is listed in Annex 3 before the integration can be switched on, and the organisation authorises it by switching the integration on. When the integration is switched off, it is no longer used for the organisation.
Orgpuls shall impose the same obligations on sub-processors as follow from this agreement, and is liable to the organisation for their performance.

The personal data is stored in the EEA, in Frankfurt, Germany. Some sub-processors are headquartered in the USA (Annex 3). Any transfer outside the EEA, including access from such countries, takes place only in accordance with GDPR Chapter V, for example on the basis of the European Commission's standard contractual clauses in the sub-processor's agreement.

Orgpuls assists the organisation, as far as possible, in meeting the data subjects' rights, such as access, rectification and erasure, and with the obligations in GDPR Articles 32 to 36: security, breach notification, data protection impact assessment and prior consultation.

The organisation can correct and delete employee data in Orgpuls itself. Anonymous answers cannot be linked to a person, and therefore cannot be retrieved or deleted for one particular person, under GDPR Article 11.

Orgpuls shall notify the organisation without undue delay, and no later than 36 hours after becoming aware of a personal data breach. The notice shall describe what happened, which data and approximately how many data subjects are affected, the likely consequences and the measures taken, so that the organisation can notify Datatilsynet within 72 hours under GDPR Article 33.

Orgpuls makes available the information the organisation needs to demonstrate compliance with GDPR Article 28, and allows for audits, including inspections, by the organisation or an auditor it has mandated. Audits are announced at least 30 days in advance. The organisation bears the cost, unless the audit reveals material breaches of the agreement.

The agreement applies for as long as the organisation uses Orgpuls. When it ends, Orgpuls deletes the organisation's personal data within 30 days, unless the law requires it to be kept. Before then, the organisation can print or save its reports as PDF. Backups are deleted in the sub-processor's regular cycle.
Orgpuls may present a new version of the agreement in Orgpuls. The organisation is notified, and the new version applies once it is signed. Until then, the version last signed applies.
The agreement is governed by Norwegian law. In case of conflict, this agreement takes precedence over other agreements between the parties as regards the processing of personal data.

Purpose: mapping and follow-up of the psychosocial working environment under the Working Environment Act sections 3-1 and 4-3 and chapter 1A of the Regulations concerning the performance of work. The organisation's legal basis is legal obligation, GDPR Article 6(1)(c).
The data subjects are the employees the organisation invites to the mapping, and the organisation's users of Orgpuls: the managing director, department managers and safety representatives.
About employees, the following is stored:
ul: name and e-mail address
mobile number, only if the organisation enters it or chooses to read it from Microsoft Entra ID, for sending by SMS
preferred language, if the organisation enters it or it is read from Microsoft Entra ID, so that the survey can be offered in that language
for organisations that send the survey in Teams: which conversation the Orgpuls app has with the employee in Teams, and whether Teams has turned away a message to the employee

for organisations that send the survey in Slack: the employee's member ID in the organisation's Slack workspace, found from the work e-mail address, and the Slack access the Orgpuls app was given when the organisation connected – only to send the link as a direct message
which department the employee belongs to, and any role as safety representative, union representative or manager

if the organisation brings in its employees from Microsoft Entra ID: the person's object ID in the directory, which of the chosen groups the person is in, and whether the account is active – only to keep the register up to date. Nothing is written back to the directory
for each survey: whether an invitation and a reminder were sent and whether the employee has answered, so that reminders go only to those who have not – never what the employee answered
the name of the person responsible for a measure, if the organisation chooses an employee as responsible

sections.h: Annex 1 – Answers, users and technical data
p: Answers are stored without name, e-mail address, invitation or any other link to the person who gave them: only which department the answer concerns and the hour it arrived. Results for a department are not shown until at least five have answered, or fewer — never under three — where the organisation has chosen a lower limit for small teams. Comments and replies in anonymous conversations are stored the same way. They may contain personal data if the writer includes it, and are never shown with a name. The exception is an employee who asks to be told when management answers a comment they wrote: then who wrote it is stored, encrypted and only to send the notice. The link covers the whole response. It is never visible to the organisation, Orgpuls does not hand it over to the organisation, and it is deleted when the conversation is closed, when the employee turns the notice off, and after a year at the latest.
About users, name, e-mail address, role and department are stored. Passwords are stored only as a cryptographic hash.

The questions are designed not to collect health data or other special categories of personal data, under GDPR Article 9 and the Working Environment Act section 9-3. The questions on offensive behaviour and violence are reported only as counts for the whole organisation.
The sub-processors record IP address and time in operational logs, used for operation and security. The statistics on use of the website use no cookies and do not identify visitors.
Retention: for as long as the agreement applies, unless the organisation deletes the data earlier or asks Orgpuls to do so.

ul: The data is stored in a database in Frankfurt, Germany, and is encrypted in transit and at rest.
Access control on every database table: a user sees only their own organisation, and only what their role allows.

The tables holding answers are closed to all users. Results are read only through functions that withhold departments with fewer answers than the organisation’s limit: five by default, never under three.
The link an employee answers with is stored only as a SHA-256 hash. The time of an answer is stored rounded to the hour.
Sign-in with e-mail address and password. Passwords are stored as hashes.
Free text from employees is not written to logs or analytics tools.
Orgpuls' personnel access production data only when operation or troubleshooting requires it.
The database is changed only through versioned migration scripts, and the security rules are tested automatically on every change.

faq.t: What people ask before they start
faq.d: Can't find the answer? Write to us using the <link>contact form</link>. We reply personally, in Norwegian.

items.q: Can the manager see who answered what?
items.a: No. Orgpuls never links a response to a name, email or IP. Nobody sees a group until the threshold is reached — 5 responses by default, never below 3 — and that applies to administrators too.

items.q: Why not just one survey a year?
items.a: One survey shows how things stood at one point in time. It doesn't tell you whether the measures worked. The pulse measures only the factors you are working on, so you see the trend without asking about everything every time.

items.q: Won't people get tired of answering?
items.a: The pulse asks only about the factors you have open measures on, and a factor drops out once its measures are closed. What wears people out is answering without seeing anything happen — which is why everyone gets to see the measures.

items.q: Do we need an HR system?
items.a: No. You can paste employees in, upload them as a CSV or add them by hand.

items.q: Can we change the questions?
items.a: You can switch off a factor, but not change the wording. That is what makes the figures comparable over time.

items.q: Does this cover all the requirements of the Working Environment Act?
items.a: Orgpuls covers the survey duty in § 3-1 c and the requirements for the psychosocial working environment in § 4-3, with documentation. Other HSE duties, such as incident reporting systems and sickness absence follow-up, are outside its scope.

Violence and threats lead to more sick leave and make it harder to keep and recruit people, the Labour Inspection Authority writes.
Many young people take a shop job alongside school or studies, and most do not stay in the industry over time.

challenges.title: Eight known risks in shops – and what the rules say
challenges.lead: The challenges come from Norwegian research and inspections. Under each one is what the Act and the regulation require of the employer.

items.t: Violence and threats in shops – theft and robbery
items.looks: A customer is stopped with goods in their jacket and turns threatening. The employee has seconds to decide: step in, call for help or let it go.
items.fig: 12 % had faced threats so serious they were frightened in the past year. In retail, most reports of violence and threats to the Labour Inspection Authority come from grocery shops and petrol stations.
items.solve: The retail module asks whether the routines are known, whether help comes quickly and whether people are followed up afterwards. A separate yes/no question counts incidents that were never reported. The main survey counts how many have experienced violence or threats.
items.vl: faced threats so serious they were frightened in the past year
items.law: Employees must as far as possible be protected from violence and threats (WEA § 4-3, sixth paragraph). Chapter 3A of the regulation requires the risk to be surveyed and assessed, measures to be put in place, employees to be trained, and anyone affected to be followed up (§§ 3A-2, 3A-3, 3A-5 and 3A-6).

items.t: Alone on shift at opening, closing and in the evening
items.looks: The last person walks through the shop, cashes up and locks. If something happens, there is nobody to call out to.
items.fig: 32 % work alone sometimes or more often. In chain shops with lone work, 1 in 3 had not made a separate risk assessment of it.
items.solve: The factor Alone on shift measures whether it feels safe, whether there are breaks and whether a manager is easy to reach. A yes/no question counts how many have felt unsafe alone – never per shop or shift. The answers are the basis for the risk assessment the law requires.
items.vl: work alone sometimes or more often
items.law: The employer must assess whether lone work carries a particular risk, and put the necessary measures in place (WEA § 4-1, third paragraph). When violence and threats are surveyed, lone work must be part of the assessment (regulation § 3A-2).

items.t: Difficult customers and feelings kept inside
items.looks: The complaint in the checkout queue is met with a smile, and the anger about prices is taken without answering back – shift after shift.
items.fig: 27 % have conflicts with customers, and 33 % have to hide negative feelings. Across all employed, the figures are 16 and 17 %.
items.solve: The main survey measures emotional demands with three statements. The retail module adds Boundaries with customers: whether it is fine to end a conversation that crosses the line, and whether the manager backs you up.
items.vl: have conflicts with customers, against 16 % of all employed
items.ref: WEA § 4-3 second paragraph b and third paragraph
items.law: The Act names emotional demands and strain in work with people as a psychosocial factor (WEA § 4-3, second paragraph, letter b). Work must also be arranged so that employees’ integrity and dignity are safeguarded (third paragraph).

items.t: Too few at work when it is busy
items.looks: Friday afternoon: a long queue, shelves to fill, and one person who also has to answer the phone.
items.fig: Low staffing makes violence and threats harder to prevent and handle, the Labour Inspection Authority writes. The regulation names staffing among the things the risk assessment must look at.
items.solve: The factor Staffing and pace shows whether staffing follows the busy hours, and whether it is clear what can wait. Together with Workload and time pressure you see which shops are stretched too far.
items.vl: Low staffing makes it harder to prevent and handle violence and threats, the Labour Inspection Authority writes.
items.law: Workload and time pressure is one of the factors the Act names (WEA § 4-3, second paragraph, letter c). Staffing is among what the risk assessment of violence and threats must look at (regulation § 3A-2).

items.t: Evenings, Saturdays and rotas at short notice
items.looks: The rota arrives late, and a free shift pops up on the phone the same morning.
items.fig: 85 % work Saturdays, and 60 % have early evening shifts on weekdays. Working beyond agreed hours is most common in retail and in health and care.
items.solve: The factor Shift schedule and predictability measures whether the shift schedule comes in good time, and whether employees can influence their shifts. Participation and control in the main survey shows whether they have a say.
items.vl: work Saturdays
items.law: If employees work at different times of day, there must be a work schedule showing which weeks, days and hours each person works. It is drawn up with the employee representatives and, as a rule, discussed no later than two weeks before it takes effect (WEA § 10-3).

items.t: Part-time, young and new staff who are soon on their own
items.looks: A student takes Saturday shifts, works a few hours a week and rarely meets the others.
items.fig: 37 % in retail work part-time, and 1 in 4 under 20 hours a week. 28 % of those who work alone have had no training in what to do if something happens.
items.solve: The survey goes out by text message or QR poster, so the Saturday helper answers as easily as the shop manager. It stays open for 14 days, so every shift has time to answer. Training and new staff and Position and belonging show whether new people are welcomed.
items.vl: of those who work alone have had no training in what to do if something happens
items.law: The employer must make sure employees know the hazards of the work and get the training, practice and instruction they need (WEA § 3-2, first paragraph, letter a). The regulation also requires training in preventing and handling violence and threats (§ 3A-5).

items.t: Heavy lifting and long hours on your feet
items.looks: Deliveries with heavy boxes, restocking on your knees and a whole shift standing at the till.
items.fig: 73 % work standing, against 35 % of all employed. 22 % do awkward lifts, against 14 %.
items.solve: The factor Physical work and equipment shows whether lifting aids exist, whether there is time to use them, and whether employees can vary their working position – per shop and warehouse.
items.vl: work standing, against 35 % of all employed
items.law: The workplace must be designed so that employees avoid undue physical strain. Necessary aids must be provided, and work must be arranged for variety and to avoid heavy lifting (WEA § 4-4, second paragraph).

items.looks: Comments across the counter, or a customer who comes back again and again. Many say nothing.
items.fig: 16 % had experienced unwanted sexual attention in the past year. Only 1 in 3 of them told their employer.
items.solve: The main survey asks anonymously about offensive behaviour and measures integrity and dignity. Boundaries with customers asks whether sexual comments and touching are taken seriously. The law says you must prevent harassment, including from customers.
items.vl: had faced unwanted sexual attention in the past year
items.law: Nobody may be subjected to harassment, including sexual harassment (WEA § 4-3, fifth paragraph). The Act counts any form of unwanted sexual attention whose purpose or effect is offensive, frightening, hostile, degrading, humiliating or troublesome as sexual harassment.

items.q: How long does it take employees?

items.q: What does it cost?
items.a: Small costs NOK 265 a month for up to 25 employees, and Usual NOK 565 for 26–100 employees. The retail module is included in both. Prices exclude VAT, there is no lock-in, and the first 15 days are free.

items.q: Is it anonymous when the shop has only 6 employees?
items.a: Yes. By default no group is shown until at least 5 have answered, and a shop with fewer answers only counts in the figures for the whole business. Small teams can lower the limit to 3, but the fewer the answers, the easier it is to recognise who said what.

items.q: Many employees have no work e-mail or PC. Does it work?
items.a: Yes. Send the link by text message, or put up the QR poster in the break room. The employee scans the code, enters a mobile number or e-mail address and gets their own link. Everything works on a phone.

items.q: Can employees answer in languages other than Norwegian?
items.a: Yes. The questionnaire is available in Norwegian, English, Polish and Lithuanian. When an employee's language is registered, the invitation and the questionnaire come in that language, and anyone can switch language in the questionnaire. The Polish and Lithuanian texts are machine-translated, and a language is offered only when every question in the survey has an approved translation. Ukrainian, Swedish and Danish are not ready yet.

items.q: We are a chain with many shops. Does it fit?
items.a: Yes. Make one group per shop, and you see the results for each shop with enough answers, and the shop manager can see their own. If the shops are separate companies, or you have more than 100 employees, you get a separate offer on the Several companies plan.

items.q: Is the retail module fully tested?
items.a: It is built on Norwegian research and inspections, but it is not validated yet. That is why its risk thresholds are marked provisional in the results. The main survey is built on QPS Nordic.

items.q: Will this hold up if the Labour Inspection Authority visits?
items.a: Orgpuls covers the survey and risk assessment of the psychosocial work environment. The report brings together survey, risk assessment, measures and follow-up, with dates. Incident handling, safety inspections and employment contracts live elsewhere, and the Labour Inspection Authority expects the survey to draw on several sources – a questionnaire is one of them.

seo.title: The work environment in construction: risks, figures and the law | Orgpuls
seo.description: Time pressure, many firms on one site, language and near misses in construction: figures from the Labour Inspection Authority, STAMI and Fafo.

hero.h1: The work environment in construction: risks, figures and the law
hero.lead: Time pressure, many firms on the same site, language and long days shape the working day for many in construction. This is what the Labour Inspection Authority, STAMI and Fafo have found about the work environment in the industry, and what the Working Environment Act and the regulations require of the employer.

stats.title: The work environment in construction: what the figures show
stats.lead: Around 240,000 residents of Norway work in construction, and about 21,000 more are here on short stays. The figures come from Norwegian research and official statistics.

why.title: What the law requires of employers in construction
why.lead: The Working Environment Act applies to every employer with employees, including the trade business with five in the team. On a building site there are requirements of its own on top: coordination when several companies work in one place, and a language everyone in the work team understands.

law.title: What the law asks of a construction company

rows.t: Identify hazards and problems, assess the risk, make plans and put measures in place.

The psychosocial factors of the work environment must be fully satisfactory – including workload and time pressure, and support and help at work. Nobody may be subjected to harassment or other improper conduct.
When several businesses work at the same workplace, the principal enterprise is responsible for coordinating their health and safety work.
At least one person in every work team must be able to understand and make themselves understood in a language the others in the team understand, where safety requires it.
The survey must be done together with the employees, repeated regularly and documented.

tilsyn.t: The Labour Inspection Authority prioritises building firms
tilsyn.p: In 2025 building firms were among the industries the Labour Inspection Authority prioritised in inspections of mental and musculoskeletal strain. In nearly two in three of those inspections the survey was inadequate, and action plans, named owners and deadlines for measures often fell short. More than half of all infringement fines went to the construction industry.
tilsyn.d: In Orgpuls every measure gets an owner and a deadline, and the safety representative sees the same figures as management.

gap.t: Many small firms have not done it
gap.p: Among private businesses with fewer than 20 employees, 28 % run an employee survey, and 23 % carry out none of the surveys Fafo asked about. Fafo still finds major health and safety challenges in many of the smallest construction firms.

items: 1 in 2 on sick leave in building work say the absence is related to their job. Such absence can often be prevented at the workplace.

An analysis the Labour Inspection Authority refers to found a strong link between actions that triggered accidents and uncertain management of risk. That may point to psychosocial measures also needing high priority in construction.
1 in 5 of those who worked in construction in 2015 worked in another industry in 2022. Younger people are over-represented among those who move.

challenges.title: Eight known risks on the building site – and what the rules say
challenges.lead: The challenges come from the Labour Inspection Authority, STAMI and Fafo. Under each one is what the Act and the regulations require of the employer.

items.t: Time pressure that comes before safety
items.looks: The concrete truck is booked, the scaffolding is not finished, and the client is waiting. That is when the shortcuts get taken.
items.fig: Fafo’s informants describe ever greater time pressure in projects, making it more tempting to take shortcuts. The accidents the Labour Inspection Authority has analysed typically happened in work that departed from the original plan.
items.vl: The accidents the Labour Inspection Authority has analysed typically happened in work that departed from the original plan.
items.ref: WEA § 4-1 second paragraph · § 4-3 second paragraph c
items.law: The organisation, arrangement and management of work must be such that employees are not exposed to undue strain, and so that safety is ensured (WEA § 4-1, second paragraph). Workload and time pressure is one of the psychosocial factors the Act names (§ 4-3, second paragraph, letter c).
items.solve: The factor Safety before progress asks whether safety holds when time is short, and whether people can stop an unsafe job without getting into trouble. Planning and progress shows whether the schedule is realistic. A yes/no question counts how many have been asked to do a job they thought was unsafe.

items.looks: A main contractor, three subcontractors and an electrician who arrived today. Who tells whom when the crane lifts over the roof?
items.fig: Lack of planning and communication between businesses has been a cause in many of the accidents the Labour Inspection Authority has analysed. Construction firms in the Oslo region have met the ban on hiring from staffing agencies with, among other things, more subcontractors and more overtime.
items.vl: Lack of planning and communication between businesses has been a cause in many of the accidents the Labour Inspection Authority has analysed.
items.law: When several businesses work at the same workplace, the principal enterprise is responsible for coordinating their health, environment and safety work (WEA § 2-2, second paragraph).
items.solve: The factor Coordination on site asks whether it is clear who is in charge when several companies work together, and whether you are told about the risk in the work others are doing around you. The suggested measures are concrete, such as a joint morning meeting for every company on site.

items.looks: The foreman gives instructions in Norwegian, one person in the team translates, and the rest nod. Nobody asks again.
items.fig: In a 2017 survey Fafo refers to, 29 % of employers had seen language problems lead to an accident or near miss. Among Polish and Lithuanian labour migrants living in Norway, 8 % said they did not speak Norwegian, and 30 % that they spoke quite little.
items.vl: of employers in a 2017 survey had seen language problems lead to an accident or near miss
items.law: The employer must in particular make sure that, where safety requires it, at least one person in every team can understand and make themselves understood in a language the others in the team understand (Construction Client Regulations § 19a, second paragraph).
items.solve: The factor Language and instructions asks whether safety information is given in a language each person understands well, whether there is always someone in the team who can pass messages between languages, and whether it is fine to ask again. The crew can answer in Polish and Lithuanian as well as Norwegian and English; the Polish and Lithuanian texts are machine-translated.

items.t: New, young and hired-in workers in the team
items.looks: An apprentice on their first project, two hired-in workers who arrived on Monday and a summer temp. All get tasks before they know the site.
items.fig: Young people under 25, people new in the job and hired-in workers are among the groups the Labour Inspection Authority names as most exposed to accidents. The injury rate is considerably higher in the youngest age groups.
items.vl: The injury rate is considerably higher in the youngest age groups.
items.ref: WEA § 3-2 first paragraph a and b
items.law: The employer must make sure employees know the accident and health hazards of the work and get the training, practice and instruction they need (WEA § 3-2, first paragraph, letter a). Anyone who leads or supervises others must have the competence to see that the work is done safely (letter b).
items.solve: The factor New and young people in the team asks whether new people are trained before they get risky tasks, whether they have a fixed person to ask, and whether they get time to learn. Hired-in workers who are part of the team can be added to your employee list, and then they answer like everyone else.

items.looks: A panel slips from the crane and lands where someone stood ten minutes earlier. No deviation report is written.
items.fig: Fafo describes how reporting unwanted incidents can be seen as snitching, and that many with a loose tie to the employer do not report. Fear of reprisals applies particularly to foreign workers.
items.vl: Reporting unwanted incidents can be seen as snitching, and fear of reprisals applies particularly to foreign workers, Fafo describes.
items.law: Employees must immediately tell the employer and the safety representative when they become aware of faults or defects that may endanger life or health (WEA § 2-3, second paragraph, letter b). The employer must make sure every injury at work is registered (§ 5-1).
items.solve: A yes/no question counts near misses that were not reported – only as a count for the whole business, never per project. Safety in the team asks whether you speak up to each other and learn from incidents, and Freedom to speak up in the main survey shows whether people dare to say something.

items.t: Teams that do not talk to each other
items.looks: Each team eats on its own in the site hut. When something goes wrong, it is easier to blame the others than to speak up.
items.fig: An informant in Fafo’s report describes how the divides carry into the break rooms and can cause conflict and a lack of trust between people from different countries. The Labour Inspection Authority names a good climate for speaking up between workers and managers as important for safety.
items.vl: Divides between people from different countries can carry into the break rooms and cause conflict and a lack of trust, an informant tells Fafo.
items.ref: WEA § 4-3 second paragraph d and fourth paragraph
items.law: Support and help at work is one of the psychosocial factors the Act names (WEA § 4-3, second paragraph, letter d). Work must as far as possible be designed to allow contact and communication with other employees (fourth paragraph).
items.solve: The main survey measures Support from colleagues and Integrity and dignity, and asks anonymously about offensive behaviour. That question is shown only as a count for the whole business.

items.t: Long days and a long way home
items.looks: Long days to earn the time off, and then the flight or the drive home. On Sunday evening the trip back begins.
items.fig: 12 % in civil engineering work more than 48 hours a week, against 8.2 % of all employed. Fafo’s informants name working hours as a known risk, particularly for those who commute between their home country and Norway and work long days to earn time off.
items.vl: in civil engineering work more than 48 hours a week, against 8.2 % of all employed
items.law: Normal working hours must not exceed nine hours in 24 hours and 40 hours in seven days (WEA § 10-4). Employees must have at least 11 consecutive hours off work in every 24 hours and 35 hours in every seven days (WEA § 10-8). Exceptions require a written agreement with the employee representatives in a business bound by a collective agreement, and compensating rest.
items.solve: The factor Working hours and recovery asks whether working hours give enough rest, whether travel time and commuting are manageable over time, and whether overtime is the exception rather than the rule.

items.looks: After a fall from the scaffolding, work is under way again the next morning. Nobody asks those who stood next to it how they are doing.
items.fig: 3,902 occupational injuries were registered in construction in 2024. 43 % in building work do heavy physical work, against 21 % of all employed.
items.vl: in building work do heavy physical work, against 21 % of all employed
items.law: The workplace must be designed so that employees avoid undue physical strain, and necessary aids must be provided (WEA § 4-4, second paragraph). Every injury at work must be registered (§ 5-1).
items.solve: The factor Saying you're not doing well asks whether there is a talk with those who were there after an accident or near miss, and whether people know where to get help. One of the suggestions is to gather those who were there the same week, with a manager or the occupational health service.

items.a: Job safety analyses, safety rounds and the deviation system deal with the hazards in the work. Orgpuls surveys the psychosocial work environment – time pressure, coordination, language, support and the climate for speaking up – which the law requires in § 4-3 and chapter 1A of the regulation. It does not replace physical measures: the Labour Inspection Authority and STAMI write that psychosocial measures can reinforce other measures, but have little effect on their own.

items.q: Will this hold up if the Labour Inspection Authority visits?
items.a: Orgpuls covers the survey and risk assessment of the psychosocial work environment. The report brings together survey, risk assessment, measures and follow-up, with dates. Incident handling, safety rounds, the health and safety plan for the site and HMS cards live elsewhere, and the Labour Inspection Authority expects the survey to draw on several sources – a questionnaire is one of them.

hero.k: Knowledge and office work · consultancy, IT, finance, media and real estate
hero.h1: The work environment in knowledge and office work: risks, figures and the law
hero.lead: Interruptions, expectations of being available, working from home and constant change shape the working day for many in knowledge and office work. This is what STAMI, Fafo and Statistics Norway have found about the work environment, and what the Working Environment Act and the home office regulation require of the employer.

stats.title: The office work environment: what the figures show
stats.lead: Around 400,000 people work in information and communication, finance and insurance, and technical services and real estate, and about 800,000 sit in an office almost all their working time. The figures come from Norwegian research and official statistics.

items.l: of people in office workplaces work from home or on the move outside normal hours every week, against 17% of all employed

of employees work from home several days a week since the pandemic, against 4.2% in 2019
of doctor-certified sick-leave days in the second quarter of 2026 were due to mental disorders – across all of working life

stats.h3: High satisfaction, but not everything shows
stats.note: 86% of people in office workplaces are satisfied with their job, against 83% of all employed, and sick leave is below average. Even so, 1 in 5 report mental health complaints wholly or partly caused by their job.
stats.text: An anonymous questionnaire shows what is not said at the all-hands. Among other things, the office module asks whether employees have been contacted in their free time with an answer expected. The answer is shown only as a count for the whole business.

Have been through a reorganisation

why.title: What the law requires of employers in knowledge and office work
why.lead: The Working Environment Act applies to every employer with employees – including the consultancy with six consultants. For knowledge work, the law points among other things to workload and time pressure, unclear expectations and support at work, and the home office is part of the work environment.

law.title: What the law requires in knowledge and office work

rows.t: Identify hazards and problems, assess the risk, make plans and put measures in place.
The psychosocial factors must be fully satisfactory – among them unclear or conflicting demands and expectations, workload and time pressure, and support and help at work.
Employees shall have at least 11 consecutive hours off work in every 24 hours.

Regular work from home requires a written agreement, covering among other things working hours and when the employee is to be available. The psychosocial work environment at home must also be taken care of (§§ 2 and 3).
The survey must be done together with the employees, repeated regularly and documented.

law.link: Read more about the legal requirement

tilsyn.t: The Labour Inspection Authority: risk is more about how work is organised
tilsyn.p: “More and more people in Norway work in occupations where the risk is less about machinery and physical hazards and more about how work is organised, time pressure and emotional strain,” the Authority writes in its 2025 annual report. The requirements were clarified from 1 January 2026, and the Authority is giving guidance first. In its 2025 inspections – in other industries – the survey was inadequate in nearly two out of three, and measures often lacked a person responsible and a deadline.
tilsyn.d: In Orgpuls every measure gets an owner and a deadline, and the safety representative sees the same figures as management.

gap.p: Among private businesses with fewer than 20 employees, 28% run an employee survey, and 23% do none of the surveys Fafo asked about. Among businesses with fewer than 20 employees, 19% have guidelines on the right to disconnect.

items: 1 in 3 people on sick leave in office workplaces say their absence is related to their job. Absence like that can often be prevented at the workplace.

Employees in open-plan offices with fixed desks were more likely to take both self-certified and doctor-certified sick leave than those in single or small shared offices, a STAMI doctoral thesis shows. The differences are small, but they apply to many people.
Sick leave due to mental disorders often lasts a long time, which increases the chance of dropping out of working life altogether, says NAV's director Hege Nilssen.

challenges.title: Eight known risks in knowledge and office work – and what the rules say
challenges.lead: The challenges come from STAMI, Fafo, Statistics Norway and Abelia. Under each one is what the Act and the regulations require of the employer.

items.looks: A quick question at your desk, notifications in three channels, four meetings before lunch. The work that needs concentration gets done after everyone else has gone home.
items.fig: 58% of people who work in an office sit in a shared office or open plan all or part of the time. In Fafo's evaluation of an activity-based office in the ministries, work that needs concentration was experienced as harder in the open plan.
items.vl: sit in a shared office or open plan all or part of the time
items.law: The work environment must be fully satisfactory based on an individual and overall assessment of the factors that may affect employees’ health and welfare (WEA § 4-1, first paragraph). Physical conditions such as indoor climate, light and noise must also be fully satisfactory (§ 4-4, first paragraph).
items.solve: Focus and interruptions asks whether people get uninterrupted time for work that needs concentration, and whether they are disturbed when they need quiet. Meeting culture asks whether meetings are useful. In the simplified set they come together as Concentration and workflow, with suggestions such as fixed focus blocks and a meeting review.

items.looks: The client e-mails on Sunday evening, and the manager answers in the chat at eleven at night. Nobody has said you must reply – but everyone does.
items.fig: 22% of people in office workplaces feel they are expected to be available in their free time, against 19% of all employed. Expectations are often informal and unspoken, Fafo writes.
items.vl: feel expected to be available in their free time, against 19 % of all employed
items.law: Employees must have at least 11 consecutive hours off work in every 24 hours and 35 hours in every seven days (WEA § 10-8). Exceptions require a written agreement with the employee representatives in a business bound by a collective agreement, and compensating rest.
items.solve: Availability asks whether it is accepted not to answer outside working hours, and whether the team has clear agreements on when to be available. A yes/no question counts how many have been contacted in their free time with an answer expected – shown only as a count for the whole business. One of the suggestions is a team availability agreement.

items.looks: The laptop sits on the kitchen table, and “just one more thing” turns into an hour every evening. It is flexible – until it isn't.
items.fig: Among employees without management duties, 41% in professional occupations get work enquiries in their free time at least once a week, against 17% of operators and craft workers. Two in three managers with staff get such enquiries every week.
items.vl: in professional occupations without management duties get work enquiries in their free time at least once a week
items.law: Employees must have at least 11 consecutive hours off work in every 24 hours (WEA § 10-8, first paragraph). Working-time arrangements and the way work is organised must not expose employees to undue mental strain (§ 4-1, second paragraph).
items.solve: Work and private life asks whether the job leaves enough time for private life, and Recovery and switching off whether people manage to switch off in their free time. The suggestions include “Off means off” and a quarterly review of evening and weekend work together with the safety representative.

items.looks: Half the team is in on Tuesday, the rest on Thursday. The new hire hasn't met everyone yet, and sparring only happens when someone remembers to invite them.
items.fig: In Abelia's HR survey of technology and knowledge businesses, 40% of the businesses name weaker social cohesion from flexible and hybrid work as a major challenge. STAMI finds that working from home can give more control and flexibility, but is also linked to higher demands for availability, less support from colleagues and somewhat more role ambiguity and role conflict.
items.vl: of the businesses in Abelia’s HR survey see weaker social cohesion from hybrid work as a major challenge
items.ref: WEA § 4-3 fourth paragraph · home office regulation § 3
items.law: Work must as far as possible be designed to allow contact and communication with other employees (WEA § 4-3, fourth paragraph). For regular work from home, the employer must as far as practically possible make sure the working conditions are fully satisfactory, the psychosocial work environment included (home office regulation § 3).
items.solve: Hybrid collaboration asks whether collaboration works wherever people work, and Belonging and professional network whether people get informal contact and professional sparring. Role clarity and Support from colleagues in the main survey show the rest. The suggestions include a hybrid team agreement and a weekly one-to-one.

items.t: The client is always in a hurry
items.looks: The deadline was set in the sales meeting, the order changed along the way, and the hours still have to be logged as billable.
items.fig: About 1 in 10 employees regularly get work enquiries in their free time and are expected to answer. Most are managers or in particularly independent positions, spend at least 2 hours a week on it, and many report stress and working while ill.
items.vl: regularly get work enquiries in their free time and are expected to answer
items.ref: WEA § 4-3 second paragraph a and c
items.law: Unclear or conflicting demands and expectations, and workload and time pressure, are among the psychosocial factors the Act names (WEA § 4-3, second paragraph, letters a and c).
items.solve: In the extended set you can choose Client and delivery pressure: whether deadlines are realistic, whether people get support from their manager when a client makes unreasonable demands, and whether billable-hour targets are reasonable. Workload and time pressure and Conflicting demands in the main survey are included for everyone.

items.t: New systems, new structure, new AI
items.looks: A new system in spring, a reorganisation in autumn – and now everyone is to use AI, but nobody has said how.
items.fig: 55% of people in office workplaces have been through a reorganisation, against 48% of all employed. In banking, finance and insurance it is 65%. 9 in 10 businesses in information and communication use AI in 2026.
items.vl: have been through a reorganisation, against 48 % of all employed
items.law: Employees must be kept informed of the systems used in their work, get the training they need in them and take part in designing them (WEA § 4-2, first paragraph). During change, the employer must provide the information, participation and skills development needed for a fully satisfactory work environment (third paragraph).
items.solve: AI and changes in work tasks asks whether people know how to use AI safely, and whether they are involved when new technology changes their work. Job security and restructuring asks whether people feel their skills will be in demand, and in the extended set whether changes are explained. Participation and control in the main survey shows whether employees are heard.

items.looks: Eight hours at the screen, half the week at a kitchen table and a channel for every project. Nobody has asked how your neck is doing.
items.fig: 42% of people in office workplaces do repetitive arm and hand movements, PC work among them, against 25% of all employed. If someone works from home one day every week as a fixed arrangement, the home office regulation applies, the Labour Inspection Authority writes.
items.vl: do repetitive arm and hand movements, PC work among them, against 25 % of all employed
items.ref: WEA § 4-4 second paragraph · home office regulation § 3
items.law: The workplace must be designed so that employees avoid undue physical strain, with necessary aids and room for variety (WEA § 4-4, second paragraph). For regular work from home, the employer must as far as practically possible make sure the workplace, equipment and indoor environment cause no undue physical strain (home office regulation § 3).
items.solve: Physical workplace and equipment asks whether the office gives peace, and whether people have equipment that is good for the body – at home too. A yes/no question counts how many work from home regularly without a written agreement. Digital tools asks whether the tools make the job easier, and whether the volume of messages is manageable.

items.looks: In the video meeting, everyone says it's going fine. The one who is struggling says so at lunch – if she is in the office that day.
items.fig: Among managers whose staff can work from home, 47% find it demanding to manage employees who work from home, and 45% think it affects the work environment negatively.
items.vl: of managers whose staff can work from home find it demanding to manage them
items.law: Support and help at work is one of the psychosocial factors the Act names (WEA § 4-3, second paragraph, letter d). Employees have the right to report censurable conditions in the business (§ 2 A-1).
items.solve: Freedom to speak up and Support from manager in the main survey show whether people dare to speak up and whether the manager is there for them. Answers are anonymous and shown per team with enough answers – also for those the manager rarely sees. In the comment field they can write what they don't say out loud, and you can reply anonymously.

steps.title: From organisation number to report in four steps

items.d: Enter your organisation number and we fetch the name, address and industry from the Brønnøysund Register Centre. If the industry code belongs to knowledge and office work – IT, finance, consultancy or real estate, for example – Orgpuls suggests the office module.

items.t: Choose a variant and add your employees
items.d: Choose simplified or extended under Question set. Make one group per team or department, and send the invitation by e-mail or text message.
Each factor gets a score from 0 to 100 in green, yellow or red – for the whole business and for each team with enough answers.
Pick from the suggestions, give the measure an owner and a deadline, and let the pulse measure whether it worked. The report updates itself.

trust.title: Anonymous – even in a small team
trust.lead: No single answer can be traced back to a person. It is built into the way answers are stored, not just promised in a privacy policy.

items.d: No group is shown until at least 5 have answered. Small teams can lower the threshold to 3, never lower. The fewer the answers, the easier it is to recognise who said what.

A team with too few answers is not shown as a group of its own, but its answers count in the figures for the whole business. If a group could be worked out from the total and the other groups, one more group is held back.
The questions about contact in free time and a written home office agreement are shown only as counts for the whole business – never per team.

items.t: A department manager sees their team
items.d: A department manager sees only their own group. The safety representative sees the same figures as management.

faq.title: What leaders of knowledge businesses ask

items.q: Simplified or extended – which should we choose?
items.a: Simplified is 8 factors and 24 statements and takes about 3 minutes more. Extended has 15 factors and up to 62 statements and takes about 7 minutes. We recommend simplified for regular surveys and extended every other year, in depth. The 24 core statements are in both, so you can compare results over time.

items.q: Can we choose only the factors that fit us?
items.a: In extended, yes: you tick at least 8 of the 15 factors. The core statements are always included, and Fairness and career stays off until you turn it on. In simplified everyone gets the same eight factors. Single statements cannot be removed, but anyone who cannot answer a statement chooses “Not relevant to me”.

items.q: How long does it take for employees?
items.a: The main survey takes about 4 minutes. The office module adds about 3 minutes in simplified, with 24 statements and 2 short yes/no questions, and about 7 minutes in extended, with up to 62 statements and 4 yes/no questions.

items.q: What does it cost?
items.a: Small costs NOK 265 a month for up to 25 employees, and Usual NOK 565 for 26–100 employees. The office module is included in both. Prices exclude VAT, with no lock-in, and the first 15 days are free.

items.q: Does the manager see who was contacted in their free time?
items.a: No. The question is shown only as a count for the whole business, never per team. By default no group is shown until at least 5 have answered, and the threshold can never be set below 3.

items.q: We work from home a lot. Does the module fit?
items.a: Yes. The statements about collaboration, sparring, availability and equipment apply wherever people work. Anyone who doesn't use the office can answer “Not relevant to me” to the statement about their workplace there, and that answer does not count in the index. A yes/no question shows how many work from home regularly without a written agreement.

items.q: Can they answer in English?
items.a: Yes. The questionnaire is available in Norwegian, English, Polish and Lithuanian. A language is offered when every question in the survey has an approved translation. Ukrainian, Swedish and Danish are not ready yet.

items.q: Are the questions validated?
items.a: The office module's factors build on validated scales and research, but the wording is our own. The module is marked provisional until it has been tested in a pilot, and its risk levels are shown as provisional until then.

items.q: Will this hold if the Labour Inspection Authority comes?
items.a: Orgpuls covers the survey and risk assessment of the psychosocial work environment. The report brings together survey, risk assessment, measures and follow-up with dates. Home office agreements, routines and training live elsewhere, and the Authority expects the survey to draw on several sources – a questionnaire is one of them.

hero.k: Health and care · care, home care and clinics
hero.h1: The work environment in health and care: risks, figures and the law
hero.lead: Violence and threats, feelings you take home, too few on shift and heavy lifting shape the working day for many in health and care. This is what STAMI, Statistics Norway, Fafo and the Labour Inspection Authority have found about the work environment in the industry, and what the Working Environment Act requires of the employer.

figure.title: How your staff answer
figure.caption: The questionnaire on a phone, one theme per page.

tiles.d: The health and care module comes on top of the main survey and takes about {minutes} minutes more.
A link by text message or e-mail, or a QR poster in the staff room. No app, and nobody needs a work e-mail address.

tiles.t: Report for the Labour Inspection Authority
tiles.d: Survey, risk assessment and measures in one place, with the legal basis for each factor.

stats.title: The work environment in health and care: what the figures show
stats.lead: Around 588,000 people work in health and social services – about one in five of everyone employed in Norway. The figures come from Norwegian research and official statistics.

items.l: sickness absence in health and social services in the second quarter of 2026 – the highest of all industries, against an average of 6.6 %
of employees in nursing homes have been exposed to violence, against 5 % of everyone employed
in home care face high emotional demands, against 20 % of everyone employed
in health and social services work part-time, against 24 % in all industries

stats.note: Labour Inspection Authority inspectors describe relatively few incidents being reported in the work environment area in health and social services, even though many should have been. So the real state of the work environment does not become visible either.
stats.text: An anonymous questionnaire gives employees a way to say it without stepping forward. The health and care module asks about violence and threats that were not reported, and about shifts where the staffing was not responsible. The answers are shown only as a count for the whole business.

compare.title: Health and care against all employed

why.title: What the law requires of employers in health and care
why.lead: The Working Environment Act applies to every employer with employees, including the GP surgery with five staff and the personal assistance company with assistants in each user’s home. In work with people, the law points in particular to emotional demands, violence and threats, and working alone.

law.title: What the law requires in work with people

rows.t: Identify hazards and problems, assess the risk, make plans and put measures in place.
The psychosocial factors must be fully satisfactory – including unclear or conflicting demands, emotional demands and strain in work with people, and workload and time pressure.
Employees shall, as far as possible, be protected against violence, threats and adverse strain resulting from contact with others.
Assess whether working alone carries a particular risk, and put the necessary measures in place.
Identify and assess the risk of violence and threats – including working alone, working hours and staffing – and provide measures, training and follow-up.
The survey must be done together with the employees, repeated regularly and documented.

tilsyn.t: The Labour Inspection Authority prioritises nursing homes and home care
tilsyn.p: In 2025 nursing homes and home care were among the industries the Labour Inspection Authority prioritised in inspections of mental and musculoskeletal strain. In inspections of nursing homes and home care, violence and threats are often raised as a challenge, and in 2025 more than seven in ten businesses lacked an adequate survey, risk assessment, plan and measures against violence and threats.
tilsyn.d: In Orgpuls every measure gets an owner and a deadline, and the safety representative sees the same figures as management.

gap.t: Many small businesses have not done it
gap.p: About half of those working in health clinics – among them doctors’ and dentists’ practices and physiotherapy clinics – are in businesses with fewer than 10 employees. Among private businesses with fewer than 20 employees, 28 % run an employee survey, and 23 % carry out none of the surveys Fafo asked about.

items: 1 in 3 in nursing homes and 2 in 5 in home care who are on sick leave say the absence is related to their job. Absence like that can often be prevented at the workplace.
29 % of employees in home care services were no longer at the same workplace a year later, against 24 % in working life as a whole (2023). Among those under 30 it was 45 %.
Employees in large positions have the lowest drop-out, and workplaces with many full-time staff find it easier to build «the good shift», which both attracts and keeps people, Fafo writes.

challenges.title: Eight known risks in health and care – and what the rules say
challenges.lead: The challenges come from STAMI, Statistics Norway, Fafo and the Labour Inspection Authority. Under each one is what the Act and the regulation require of the employer.

items.t: Violence and threats – often alone with the service user
items.looks: A service user who becomes agitated during personal care, a night shift alone on the ward, a home visit where the door closes behind you. Often you are the only one there.
items.fig: 34 % in nursing homes have been exposed to violence, and 27 % to harassment or threats. In home care the figures are 12 and 18 %. The Labour Inspection Authority uses home care staff as an example of working alone.
items.vl: in nursing homes have been exposed to violence, against 5 % of all employed
items.ref: WEA § 4-3 sixth paragraph · § 4-1 third paragraph · regulation ch. 3A
items.law: Employees must as far as possible be protected from violence and threats (WEA § 4-3, sixth paragraph), and the employer must assess whether lone work carries a particular risk (§ 4-1, third paragraph). Chapter 3A of the regulation requires the risk to be surveyed and assessed, measures to be put in place, employees to be trained, and anyone affected to be followed up.
items.solve: The factor Violence and threats asks whether you have gone through the situations that can lead to violence, whether small incidents are reported too, and whether the person involved is followed up. A yes/no question counts incidents that were not reported. Contact and communication in the main survey asks whether you can call for help quickly when you are alone.

items.looks: A resident who dies, relatives in despair, a service user angry at everything. You have to stay professional the whole shift – and then drive home.
items.fig: 38 % in home care and 35 % in nursing homes face high emotional demands, against 20 % of everyone employed. In home care, 34 % are often mentally exhausted after work.
items.vl: in home care face high emotional demands, against 20 % of all employed
items.ref: WEA § 4-3 second paragraph b and d
items.law: The Act names emotional demands and strain in work with people, and support and help at work, as psychosocial factors (WEA § 4-3, second paragraph, letters b and d).
items.solve: The main survey measures Emotional demands: whether you are rarely left alone in emotionally demanding situations, whether you talk about difficult incidents afterwards, and whether you are allowed to react as a human being at work. The health and care module does not repeat these. Support from manager shows whether the manager is there when the job gets demanding.

items.looks: Two are off sick, the temp does not know the service users, and the list is just as long. Something has to wait – and you are the one who has to choose what.
items.fig: Labour Inspection Authority inspectors describe an industry with a high workload and time pressure, and an imbalance between tasks and resources.
items.vl: Labour Inspection Authority inspectors describe a high workload and time pressure, and an imbalance between tasks and resources.
items.law: Workload and time pressure is one of the factors the Act names (WEA § 4-3, second paragraph, letter c). Staffing is among what the risk assessment of violence and threats must look at (regulation § 3A-2).
items.solve: The factor Staffing and responsible care asks whether staffing makes it possible to give responsible care, whether you avoid going home with a bad conscience, and whether it is clear what can wait. A yes/no question counts shifts where staffing was not responsible. Time for the core tasks shows whether documentation and systems take time away from service users.

items.t: Between service user, relatives and manager
items.looks: Relatives want more than the service can give, the service user wants something else, and the manager has decided a third thing. And the comments about your body are laughed off.
items.fig: In nursing homes, 22 % experience a high degree of role conflict, against 13 % of everyone employed – including conflicting expectations from residents, relatives, managers and colleagues. 18 % are exposed to unwanted sexual attention, against 5 %.
items.vl: in nursing homes experience a high degree of role conflict, against 13 % of all employed
items.ref: WEA § 4-3 second paragraph a and fifth paragraph
items.law: Unclear or conflicting demands and expectations at work is one of the psychosocial factors the Act names (WEA § 4-3, second paragraph, letter a). Nobody may be subjected to harassment, including sexual harassment (fifth paragraph).
items.solve: The factor Boundaries with service users and relatives asks whether you have agreed what to do when someone crosses the line, whether sexual comments are taken seriously, and whether you get support to say no to relatives. Conflicting demands in the main survey shows whether it is clear who decides when two things collide.

items.looks: An evening shift until half past ten and a day shift at seven. The call about an extra shift comes on your day off – again.
items.fig: About 9 in 10 in nursing homes work outside normal daytime hours, and 1 in 3 work nights. 24 % report sleep problems caused wholly or partly by their job.
items.vl: in nursing homes work nights
items.law: If employees work at different times of day, there must be a work schedule drawn up with the employee representatives (WEA § 10-3). As a rule, employees must have at least 11 consecutive hours off in every 24 hours (§ 10-8), and night work is allowed only when the nature of the work makes it necessary (§ 10-11).
items.solve: The factor Rotas and rest asks whether the rota gives enough rest between shifts, whether you can influence it, and whether extra shifts at short notice are the exception. The suggested measures are concrete, such as a rota workshop and a fixed order for extra shifts. If the night shift is a group of its own, it gets its own figures once enough have answered.

items.looks: Many small positions, many temps and a few who take all the extra shifts. Those who work little miss the messages.
items.fig: Among rota-based staff in municipal nursing and care, nearly 35 % work full-time. Fafo describes employees who work part-time because the shifts feel too exhausting – an adaptation to a work environment they did not decide.
items.vl: Nearly 35 % of rota-based staff in municipal nursing and care work full-time.
items.law: Part-time employees have a preferential right to an extended position before the employer hires someone new (WEA § 14-3). A part-time employee who has regularly worked more than agreed over the last 12 months is, as a rule, entitled to a position matching the hours actually worked (§ 14-4 a).
items.solve: The factor Position and belonging asks whether you have the position size you want, whether important information reaches those who work little too, and whether you feel part of the professional community. One of the suggestions is to offer vacant position fractions to part-time employees first, as the preferential right requires.

items.t: New staff, temps and many languages
items.looks: The agency temp is here for the first time, and the new starter has done two shadow shifts. The handover is quick, and not everyone understands everything.
items.fig: Fafo describes how unskilled temps are often called in and have to take responsibility for tasks they lack formal competence for, and how colleagues then have to spend more time guiding them. 1 in 5 working in nursing homes are immigrants.
items.vl: working in nursing homes are immigrants
items.ref: WEA § 3-2 first paragraph a · § 4-2 second paragraph b
items.law: The employer must make sure employees get the training, practice and instruction they need (WEA § 3-2, first paragraph, letter a). Work must be organised with regard to each person’s working capacity, skills, age and other circumstances (§ 4-2, second paragraph, letter b).
items.solve: The factor Professional confidence asks whether new staff and temps get enough training before they are alone on shift, whether you have someone to consult, and whether you understand each other well enough for handovers and messages to be right. The questionnaire is available in Norwegian, English, Polish and Lithuanian.

items.t: Heavy lifting when it is busy
items.looks: The patient hoist is at the other end of the corridor, and it is busy. It is quicker to do it yourself.
items.fig: 30 % in nursing homes and 34 % in home care lift in awkward positions, against 14 % of everyone employed. 35 % in nursing homes report back pain caused wholly or partly by their job.
items.vl: in nursing homes lift in awkward positions, against 14 % of all employed
items.law: The workplace must be designed so that employees avoid undue physical strain. Necessary aids must be provided, and work must be arranged for variety and to avoid heavy lifting (WEA § 4-4, second paragraph).
items.solve: The factor Patient handling and heavy lifting asks whether you have the equipment you need, whether there is time to use it also when it is busy, and whether there are enough of you for heavy transfers. One of the suggestions is a handling plan per service user.
