steps.title: From organisation number to report in four steps

items.d: Enter your organisation number, and we fetch name, address and industry from the Brønnøysund Register Centre. If your industry code is in health and care, Orgpuls suggests the health and care module.
Make one group per department, ward or area. Send the link by text message or e-mail, or put up the QR poster in the staff room.
Each factor gets a score from 0 to 100 in green, yellow or red – for the whole business and for each department with enough answers.
Pick from the suggestions, give each measure an owner and a deadline, and let the pulse measure whether it worked. The report updates itself.

trust.title: Anonymous – even in a small department
trust.lead: No single answer can be traced back to a person. That is built into how answers are stored, not just promised in a privacy notice.

items.d: No group is shown until at least 5 have answered. Small teams can lower the limit to 3, never below. The fewer the answers, the easier it is to recognise who said what.

A department with too few answers is not shown as a group of its own, but its answers count in the figures for the whole business. If a group could be worked out from the total and the other groups, one more group is held back.
The questions about violence and threats that were not reported, and about shifts where staffing was not responsible, are shown only as a count for the whole business – never per department or shift.

items.t: The department manager sees their department
items.d: A department manager sees only their own group. The safety representative sees the same figures as management.

faq.title: What managers in health and care ask

items.q: How long does it take your staff?
items.a: The main survey takes about 4 minutes, and the health and care module about 3 minutes more: 24 statements and 2 short yes/no questions. The survey stays open for 14 days, so those on days, evenings, nights and weekends have time to answer.

items.q: What does it cost?
items.a: Small costs NOK 265 a month for up to 25 employees, and Usual NOK 565 for 26–100 employees. The health and care module is included in both. Prices exclude VAT, there is no lock-in, and the first 15 days are free.

items.q: Does the manager see who answered that staffing was not responsible?
items.a: No. The question is shown only as a count for the whole business, never per department or shift. By default no group is shown until at least 5 have answered, and the limit can never be set below 3.

items.q: Many have no work e-mail, and some work only a few shifts a month. Can we reach them?
items.a: Yes. Send the link by text message, or put up the QR poster in the staff room. The employee scans the code, enters a mobile number or e-mail address and gets their own link. Everything works on a phone, and the survey stays open long enough for every shift to answer.

items.q: Can they answer in Polish or Lithuanian?
items.a: Yes. The questionnaire is available in Norwegian, English, Polish and Lithuanian. A language is offered when every question in the survey has an approved translation. Ukrainian, Swedish and Danish are not ready yet.

items.q: We are a GP surgery or a dental clinic. Does the health and care module suit us?
items.a: The health and care module is made for care work with shifts, and today everyone gets the same eight factors – including patient handling, which matters little in a GP surgery. The main survey covers what applies to everyone, such as emotional demands, workload and support from your manager. You can also choose to survey without an industry module.

items.q: We are a healthcare staffing agency. Can we use the health and care module?
items.a: Yes. Orgpuls suggests the health and care module when your industry code is health and social services. If you have a different industry code, you can choose the health and care module yourselves under Setup. The survey goes to the people you add to your employee list, including those working at your clients.

items.q: Will this hold up if the Labour Inspection Authority visits?
items.a: Orgpuls covers the survey and risk assessment of the psychosocial work environment. The report brings together survey, risk assessment, measures and follow-up, with dates. Your deviation system, procedures for violence and threats and training live elsewhere, and the Labour Inspection Authority expects the survey to draw on several sources – a questionnaire is one of them.

seo.title: The work environment in kindergartens and schools: risks, figures and the law | Orgpuls
seo.description: Violence from children and pupils, staffing, documentation and difficult cases in kindergartens and schools: figures from STAMI, SSB, NIFU and Udir.

hero.h1: The work environment in kindergartens and schools: risks, figures and the law
hero.lead: Violence and threats, too few adults, documentation requirements and parents who get in touch after working hours shape the working day for many in kindergartens and schools. This is what STAMI, Statistics Norway, NIFU, the Directorate for Education and the Labour Inspection Authority have found about the work environment, and what the Working Environment Act requires of the employer.

figure.title: How your staff answer
figure.caption: The questionnaire on a phone, one theme per page.

tiles.d: The module comes on top of the main survey and takes about {minutes} minutes more. The statements say «the children» or «the pupils».
A link by text message or e-mail, or a QR poster in the staff room. No app, and nobody needs a work e-mail address.

tiles.t: Report for the Labour Inspection Authority
tiles.d: Survey, risk assessment and measures in one place, with the legal basis for each factor.

hero.jump: What Orgpuls does for kindergartens and schools

stats.title: The work environment in kindergartens and schools: what the figures show
stats.lead: Around 104,000 people work in kindergartens and after-school care, and around 232,000 in education. Just over half of all kindergartens are private. The figures come from Norwegian research, inspections and official statistics.

items.l: doctor-certified sickness absence in kindergartens in the first quarter of 2025, against 6.1 % in all industries
of primary and lower secondary teachers were exposed to violence at work in the past year – the highest of all occupations, against 5.7 % of everyone employed
in kindergartens and after-school care work squatting or kneeling, against 17 % of everyone employed
of primary and lower secondary teachers face high emotional demands, against 20 % in working life as a whole

stats.note: Nearly 9 in 10 upper secondary teachers say their school has a system for reporting violence and threats. Even so, it is little used, Fafo finds. Those who say it does not work point to too few using it, too few knowing it, and reported incidents not being followed up.
stats.text: An anonymous questionnaire gives employees a way to say it without stepping forward. The module asks about violence or threats from children or pupils that were not reported, and about days when absence was not covered by a substitute. The answers are shown only as a count for the whole organisation.

compare.title: Kindergartens and schools against all employed
compare.lead: The share in kindergartens and schools and among all employed. Under each row is the part of the sector the figure is for.
items: Exposed to violence at work in the past year
Work squatting or kneeling
Lift in awkward positions
Experience high noise levels
Face high emotional demands
Feel the job interferes with their private life

why.title: What the law requires of employers in kindergartens and schools
why.lead: The Working Environment Act applies to every employer with employees – including the small private kindergarten, the independent school and the after-school club. The children’s and pupils’ rights under the Kindergarten Act and the Education Act apply alongside the employees’ rights under the Working Environment Act, and in work with people the law points in particular to emotional demands and to violence and threats.

law.title: What the law requires – also in work with children

rows.t: Identify hazards and problems, assess the risk, make plans and put measures in place.
The psychosocial factors must be fully satisfactory – including unclear or conflicting demands, emotional demands and strain in work with people, and workload and time pressure.
Employees shall, as far as possible, be protected against violence, threats and adverse strain resulting from contact with others.
Identify and assess the risk of violence and threats – including working alone, working hours and staffing – and provide measures, training and follow-up.
The survey must be done together with the employees, repeated regularly and documented.

tilsyn.t: The Labour Inspection Authority found shortcomings at nearly 9 in 10 schools
tilsyn.p: In 2023–2025 the Labour Inspection Authority carried out more than 1,000 inspections of primary and lower secondary schools, after-school clubs and upper secondary schools. Nearly 9 in 10 had shortcomings in surveying, risk assessment and measures against violence and threats, and 8 in 10 had not made sure of the necessary training and practice. «Many jump straight from survey to measures», says an adviser at the Authority – and then the measures are too general or have nobody responsible.
tilsyn.d: In Orgpuls every measure gets an owner and a deadline, and the safety representative sees the same figures as management.

gap.t: Many small organisations have not done it
gap.p: Nearly 1 in 5 kindergartens have fewer than 26 children, and private primary and lower secondary schools are about 10 % of schools but have only 5 % of the pupils. Among private businesses with fewer than 20 employees, 28 % run an employee survey, and 23 % do none of the surveys Fafo asked about.

items: 1 in 2 in kindergartens and after-school care and 1 in 3 in education who are on sick leave say the absence is related to their job. Such absence can often be prevented at the workplace.

38 % of lower secondary teachers feel a lot of stress from extra work when colleagues are away, up from 26 % in 2018. The TALIS researchers see a risk of a vicious circle in which absence causes stress, which can cause more absence.

Substitutes cost more than wages. When kindergartens got permanent extra staff instead, they became less vulnerable to unexpected absence, and staff and managers saved time and energy on following up and guiding substitutes, Fafo finds.

challenges.title: Eight known risks in kindergartens and schools – and what the rules say
challenges.lead: The challenges come from STAMI, Statistics Norway, NIFU, the Directorate for Education and the Labour Inspection Authority. Under each one is what the Act and the regulation require of the employer.

items.t: Violence and threats from children and pupils
items.looks: A child who bites and kicks in the cloakroom, a pupil who throws a chair when a transition comes too fast. Often it is the same situations that come back.
items.fig: 28 % of primary and lower secondary teachers and nearly 1 in 5 kindergarten teachers and kindergarten and school assistants were exposed to violence at work in the past year, against 5.7 % of everyone employed. 8 in 10 primary and lower secondary school leaders report violent incidents in the past year.
items.vl: of primary and lower secondary teachers were exposed to violence at work in the past year, against 5.7 % of all employed
items.law: Employees must as far as possible be protected from violence and threats (WEA § 4-3, sixth paragraph). Chapter 3A of the regulation requires the risk to be surveyed and assessed, measures to be put in place, employees to be trained, and anyone affected to be followed up.
items.solve: The factor Violence and threats asks whether the routines are known, whether people know what room they have to step in when a situation becomes dangerous, and whether the person involved is followed up. A yes/no question counts incidents that were not reported. The statement says «a child» in a kindergarten and «a pupil» in a school.

items.t: Too few adults at the edges of the day
items.looks: The norm holds on paper. But at opening time, during breaks and when the last children are collected, one adult is alone with more children than anyone can keep track of.
items.fig: 99 % of kindergartens meet the staffing norm. But in a 2019 survey, 86 % of heads said they are fully staffed for less than 6 hours of the day, and the Directorate for Education writes that staffing on paper can be something other than staffing in reality.
items.vl: of kindergartens were fully staffed for less than 6 hours of the day in 2019
items.law: Workload and time pressure is one of the factors the Act names (WEA § 4-3, second paragraph, letter c). Staffing is among what the risk assessment of violence and threats must look at (regulation § 3A-2).
items.solve: The factor Staffing and substitutes asks whether staffing makes it possible to give the children what they need, whether a substitute is brought in when someone is away, and whether people are seldom alone with more children than they can keep track of. A yes/no question counts days when absence was not covered by a substitute. Workload and time pressure in the main survey shows whether the pace is too high.

items.t: Documentation and assessment take the time
items.looks: Plans, assessments, minutes and messages. The time for following up the pupil who needs it is what is left over.
items.fig: More than half of lower secondary teachers feel a lot of stress from the amount of administrative work and from assessment and grading. «Teachers have many roles and documentation requirements, they work a lot and have little time for breaks in their day», says an inspector at the Labour Inspection Authority.
items.vl: More than half of lower secondary teachers feel a lot of stress from the amount of administrative work.
items.ref: WEA § 4-3 second paragraph c · § 4-2 second paragraph c
items.law: Workload and time pressure is one of the psychosocial factors the Act names (WEA § 4-3, second paragraph, letter c). Weight must be given to each person’s opportunity for self-determination, influence and professional responsibility (§ 4-2, second paragraph, letter c).
items.solve: The factor Time for the core tasks asks whether people have time to plan and prepare the work with the pupils, whether documentation and reporting are worth the effort, and whether meeting time is used for what matters most. One of the suggestions is protected planning time. Workload and time pressure in the main survey shows the overall pressure.

items.looks: A message late in the evening, a worried parent at the gate, a conversation that gets stuck. The cooperation matters – and is sometimes the heaviest part of the week.
items.fig: About half of lower secondary teachers feel a lot of stress from handling parents’ concerns, and this has grown since 2018. At the same time, 76 % feel valued by parents. 41 % in education feel that the job interferes with their private life, partly because pupils and parents get in touch after working hours.
items.vl: in education feel the job interferes with their private life, against 31 % of all employed
items.law: Employees must as far as possible be protected from undue strain from contact with others (WEA § 4-3, sixth paragraph). They must have at least 11 consecutive hours off work in every 24 hours (§ 10-8, first paragraph).
items.solve: The factor Cooperation with parents asks whether it is clear what parents can expect, whether people get support from management when the cooperation becomes demanding, and whether they are spared answering parents outside working hours. The suggestions include reply times within working hours and the manager joining the demanding meetings.

items.t: Children and pupils who need more than you can give
items.looks: A child who needs an adult all day, a pupil waiting for an assessment. The adaptation happens in an ordinary group, with the adults who are there.
items.fig: More lower secondary teachers than in 2018 report a more varied pupil group and a need for more competence in adapting teaching. NIFU finds that pupils who need individually adapted education are often involved in violent incidents, and that special needs teachers and assistants who work closely with them are the most exposed.
items.vl: Pupils who need individually adapted education are often involved in violent incidents, and those who work closest to them are the most exposed, NIFU finds.
items.ref: WEA § 4-3 second paragraph b and d · § 3-2 first paragraph a
items.law: Emotional demands and strain in work with people, and support and help at work, are among the psychosocial factors the Act names (WEA § 4-3, second paragraph, letters b and d). The employer must provide the training, practice and instruction needed (§ 3-2, first paragraph, letter a).
items.solve: The factor Adaptation and inclusion asks whether people get enough support to meet children or pupils with special needs, whether you have access to special needs expertise, and whether people know whom to contact when a child needs more help than you can give. One of the suggestions is regular meetings with the support services.

items.t: Many without teaching qualifications – and new people all the time
items.looks: The permanent assistant knows the children best, the substitute is here for the first time, and it is unclear who is responsible for what.
items.fig: In kindergartens, 42.2 % of the core staff are kindergarten teachers and 22.8 % are child and youth workers – 35 % are neither. In primary and lower secondary school the law sets no education requirement for assistants, and assistants and others account for nearly a third of the annual hours of pupil-related work.
items.vl: of the core staff in kindergartens are neither kindergarten teachers nor child and youth workers
items.ref: WEA § 3-2 first paragraph a · § 4-2 second paragraph b
items.law: The employer must make sure employees get the training, practice and instruction they need (WEA § 3-2, first paragraph, letter a). Work must be organised with regard to each person’s working capacity, skills, age and other circumstances (§ 4-2, second paragraph, letter b).
items.solve: The factor Skills and community among staff asks whether new staff and substitutes are trained before they are responsible for children alone, whether you have time for professional conversations, and whether it is clear how tasks are divided between teachers and other staff. One of the suggestions is a substitute folder and a fixed walk-through on the first day. Support from colleagues in the main survey shows how the team works.

items.looks: Dressing children while squatting, a two-year-old on the hip and an adult on a child’s chair at lunch. And the sound of a full unit in one room.
items.fig: In kindergartens and after-school care, 60 % work squatting or kneeling and 38 % lift in awkward positions, against 17 and 14 % of everyone employed. 35 % report back pain caused wholly or partly by the job. 24 % experience high noise levels, against 8.6 % – measurements show a low risk of hearing damage, but the noise can be mentally draining.
items.vl: in kindergartens and after-school care work squatting or kneeling, against 17 % of all employed
items.law: Noise and other physical conditions must be fully satisfactory (WEA § 4-4, first paragraph). The workplace must be designed so that employees avoid undue physical strain, with necessary aids and arrangements to avoid heavy lifting (second paragraph).
items.solve: The factor Noise, physical strain and breaks asks whether the noise level is bearable, whether you have furniture and equipment that let people work in a way that is good for the body, and whether people get their breaks. The suggestions are concrete: a noise map, breaks where someone takes over, and adult chairs and height-adjustable changing tables.

items.t: Difficult cases and the feelings you take home
items.looks: A worry about how a child is doing at home, a bullying case that does not let go. You are meant to stay calm and professional – and then go home.
items.fig: 31 % in kindergartens and after-school care and 32 % in education face high emotional demands, against 20 % of everyone employed. In kindergartens and after-school care, 41 % are often mentally exhausted after work.
items.vl: in kindergartens and after-school care are often mentally exhausted after work
items.ref: WEA § 4-3 second paragraph b and d
items.law: The Act names emotional demands and strain in work with people, and support and help at work, as psychosocial factors (WEA § 4-3, second paragraph, letters b and d).
items.solve: The factor Difficult cases asks whether people know how you proceed when you are worried about how a child is doing at home, whether people are left alone with cases of bullying and harassment, and whether you have time to follow them up. One of the suggestions is two people responsible for every case, never one. The main survey measures Emotional demands, so the module does not repeat them.

orgpuls.title: How Orgpuls measures this in kindergartens and schools
orgpuls.lead: Orgpuls is a work environment survey built on QPS Nordic, with its own module for kindergartens and schools on top of the main survey. This is what it asks about, and how the answers become measures.

steps.title: From organisation number to report in four steps

items.d: Enter your organisation number, and we fetch name, address and industry from the Brønnøysund Register Centre. If your industry code is a kindergarten, school or after-school club, Orgpuls suggests the module and the wording.
Make one group per unit, year group or after-school club. Send the link by text message or e-mail, or put up the QR poster in the staff room.
Each factor gets a score from 0 to 100 in green, yellow or red – for the whole organisation and for each group with enough answers.
Pick from the suggestions, give each measure an owner and a deadline, and let the pulse measure whether it worked. The report updates itself.

trust.title: Anonymous – even in a small kindergarten
trust.lead: No single answer can be traced back to a person. That is built into how answers are stored, not just promised in a privacy notice.

items.d: No group is shown until at least 5 have answered. Small teams can lower the limit to 3, never below. The fewer the answers, the easier it is to recognise who said what.

items.t: Units and year groups with few answers
items.d: A unit or year group with too few answers is not shown as a group of its own, but its answers count in the figures for the whole organisation. If a group could be worked out from the total and the other groups, one more group is held back.

The questions about violence and threats that were not reported, and about days when absence was not covered by a substitute, are shown only as a count for the whole organisation – never per unit or year group.

items.t: The unit manager sees their unit
items.d: A unit manager sees only their own group. The safety representative sees the same figures as management.

faq.title: What heads of kindergartens and schools ask

items.q: Does it suit both kindergartens and schools?
items.a: Yes. The statements are the same, but the wording follows the organisation: «the children» in a kindergarten, «the pupils» in a school and after-school club, and «the children or the pupils» where you have both. Orgpuls suggests the wording from your industry code, and you can change it under Measurements. A survey that has opened keeps its wording. The module is provisional: the pilot tests that the three versions work alike.

items.q: How long does it take for staff?
items.a: The main survey takes around 4 minutes, and the kindergarten and school module around 3 more: 24 statements and 2 short yes/no questions. The survey stays open for 14 days, so people who work part-time or only in the after-school club have time to answer.

items.q: What does it cost?
items.a: Small costs NOK 265 a month for up to 25 employees, and Usual NOK 565 for 26–100 employees. The kindergarten and school module is included in both. Prices exclude VAT, with no lock-in, and the first 15 days are free.

items.q: We are a small kindergarten. Can the head see who answered?
items.a: No. By default no group is shown until at least 5 have answered, and a unit with fewer answers counts only in the figures for the whole kindergarten. Small teams can lower the limit to 3, never below – but the fewer the answers, the easier it is to recognise who said what.

items.q: Assistants and substitutes have no work e-mail. Can we reach them?
items.a: Yes. Send the link by text message, or put up the QR poster in the staff room. The employee scans the code, enters a mobile number or e-mail address and gets their own link. The survey goes to the people you add to the staff list, and everything works on a phone.

items.q: Can they answer in Polish or Lithuanian?
items.a: Yes. The questionnaire is available in Norwegian, English, Polish and Lithuanian. A language is offered when every question in the survey has an approved translation. Ukrainian, Swedish and Danish are not ready yet.

items.q: We already have routines for violence and threats. Do we need this as well?
items.a: The routines are part of what the regulation requires. Orgpuls surveys the psychosocial work environment together with the employees, as the law requires in § 4-3 and chapter 1A of the regulation – violence and threats, staffing, cooperation with parents, time and support. The answers show whether the routines are known and whether the person involved is followed up.

items.q: Will this hold if the Labour Inspection Authority comes?
items.a: Orgpuls covers the survey and risk assessment of the psychosocial work environment. The report brings together survey, risk assessment, measures and follow-up with dates. Routines for violence and threats, incident reporting and training and practice live elsewhere, and the Labour Inspection Authority expects the survey to draw on several sources – a questionnaire is one of them.

bransjer.h1: A work environment survey that knows your industry
bransjer.lead: The main survey covers what applies to every workplace. An industry module also asks about what is most risky where you work – lone shifts in shops, violence in care, time pressure on building sites – and suggests measures that fit your everyday work.

pastander.d: Added to the main survey, about 3 minutes extra.

tiltak.d: Suggestions written for everyday work in your industry.

hjemmel.d: The report shows which legal rule each factor rests on.

cards.k: Health, care and work with people

other.title: One tool, different working days
other.p: The questions are the same everywhere, so you can compare the figures over time. What sets industries apart is which factors are often worth watching, and how you reach people.
other.d: The survey requirements are the same for everyone, and the main survey covers them. See the <link>use cases</link> for pages by need, role and size.

bygg.d: Teams with different days – workshop, projects and operations. The heat map shows where the differences are, without pointing at people.

helse.d: Shifts, and many without a screen at work. Sent by SMS, and the pulse follows up measures on emotional demands through the year.

kommune.d: Clear requirements for participation and documentation. Consultation and notice to the safety representative are logged in the report.

teknologi.d: Fast growth and frequent change. Extra pulses after a reorganisation show whether the new structure has settled.

industri.d: Shifts and physical work. A short survey on the phone, and steady follow-up of freedom to speak up.

why.title: What a general survey does not ask
why.lead: The law requires you to survey the risk where it is. An industry module does that without you writing your own questions.

cards.t: Risk differs from industry to industry
cards.p: In shops many stand alone at the till, in care staff meet violence from service users, and on building sites time pressure is a safety issue.
cards.s: Each module adds 8 factors or more for the industry's own risks, on top of the main survey's 11.

cards.t: The law points to the industry's risks
cards.p: The regulation requires a separate risk assessment of violence and threats, and the Working Environment Act § 4-1 one of lone work. Both have to show up in the survey.
cards.s: The report shows the legal basis for each factor, and the module gets its own part of the report.

cards.t: Measures have to fit everyday work
cards.p: «Better communication» does little for the person closing the shop alone at nine in the evening.
cards.s: Each factor has 3 suggested measures written for the industry, and the pulse measures whether a measure worked.

items.d: 33 statements on 11 factors, the same for everyone, so you can compare figures over time. About 4 minutes.
The industry's statements come in the same questionnaire, on the same scale. About 3–7 minutes more.
The module's factors get the same 0–100 index, suggested measures of their own and their own part of the report.

items.q: Does an industry module cost extra?
items.a: No. The industry modules are included in Small and Usual, from NOK 265 a month excluding VAT. The free plan has the standard main survey without modules.

items.q: How do we get the right module?
items.a: Orgpuls suggests the module from your industry code in the Brønnøysund Register Centre. You can choose another module, or none, under Setup.

items.q: Do we have to use an industry module?
items.a: No. The main survey covers WEA § 4-3 on its own. The module goes deeper where your industry has risks of its own.

items.q: Does the survey get much longer?
items.a: About 3 to 7 minutes more, depending on the module. The main survey takes about 4 minutes.

items.q: Is it anonymous in small teams?
items.a: Yes. By default no group is shown until at least 5 have answered. Small teams can lower the limit to 3, but the fewer the answers, the easier it is to recognise who said what.
